figures.card: **Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī** (1369–1432), Chief Judge of Isfahan and Yazd. The foremost occult philosopher of Timurid Iran and the first to systematize Islamic lettrism (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*) into a coherent, Pythagorean-modeled philosophical cosmology. Leader of the Isfahan Circle and spiritual heir to Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī, Ibn Turka authored over 45 works across philosophy, mysticism, grammar, rhetoric, and occult science. His synthesis of lettrism and Neoplatonic philosophy became canonical; virtually every Islamic thinker engaging with lettrism after 1450 worked through his categories.
figures.body:
## Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432)

### Opening

Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī (also known as Khwāja Turka, born 770/1369, died 835/1432) was a Persian scholar, mystic, and occult philosopher who stands at the intersection of Islamic philosophy, Sufism, and lettrist theurgy. Born in Isfahan during the reign of the Timurid dynasty, Ibn Turka emerged as the intellectual leader of a network of scholars—the Isfahan Circle—based in Isfahan and Yazd. He served as Chief Judge (*qāḍī*) of both Isfahan and Yazd, positions that allowed him to accumulate extraordinary political and intellectual influence. Over four decades of scholarly work, Ibn Turka authored approximately 45 works in Persian and Arabic spanning philosophy, mystical theology, occult science, rhetoric, and grammar—a polymath output unmatched by his contemporaries.

Ibn Turka's significance lies not in abstract innovation but in synthesis and systematization. Drawing directly from his teacher Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (d. 1397), Ibn Turka transformed oral teachings into a written, rigorous philosophical system. His central project was demonstrating that Islamic lettrism (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*)—the science investigating divine and cosmological meanings encoded in the Arabic alphabet—was not mystical esotericism but a universal science as valid as mathematics or logic for understanding reality itself. By modeling this system explicitly on Pythagorean principles, Ibn Turka created the only fully coherent Pythagorean cosmology between Porphyry (3rd century) and Giordano Bruno (16th century), and the only one operating at imperial scale.

Modern scholarship, particularly Matthew Melvin-Koushki's revisionist work, has elevated Ibn Turka from a minor figure in Islamic philosophy to a central thinker in global intellectual history. He stands alongside Pico della Mirandola, John Dee, and Bruno as a theorist of magical-mathematical empire and a figure exemplifying the "will to synthesis" that characterized Renaissance and early modern universalist thought.

### Formation and Education (1369–1387)

The Turka family had been noted for producing scholars since Ilkhanid times. Ṣāʾin al-Dīn was born in Isfahan in 770/1369, when the city was still recovering from Mongol devastation. His elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn, who would later become a *qāḍī* at Samarkand in Temur's court, was an early intellectual influence. The family's fortunes changed catastrophically in 789/1387 when Temur took Isfahan and massacred most of its inhabitants. Yet the Turka family was spared and brought to Temur's court at Samarkand—an intervention that points to existing ties with power and suggests Ṣāʾin al-Dīn's family was already distinguished.

The key turning point came when Ibn Turka encountered Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī in Cairo. While the exact date of Ibn Turka's arrival in Cairo is uncertain, he spent formative years there absorbing Akhlāṭī's teachings on lettrism, alchemy, and talismanic magic. Akhlāṭī, a Kurdish occultist-physician who served the Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 1382–1399), was the intellectual pivot of a vast network of scholars calling themselves cryptically the "New Brethren of Purity" (*Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ al-jadīd*). This network stretched from Cairo through Anatolia and westward to Iran, Central Asia, and India. Akhlāṭī proclaimed a new era of human development through retrieval and open promulgation of the occult sciences—a mission Ibn Turka would spend his life fulfilling.

### The Isfahan Circle and Intellectual Leadership (1400–1432)

By 1400, Ibn Turka had returned to Isfahan, where he established himself as the intellectual leader of a circle of heavyweight thinkers. This "Isfahan Circle" included [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]] (d. 1454), author of the *Ẓafarnāma* (a universal history from an astrological-lettrist perspective), and [[qazizada-rumi]] (d. 1432), the celebrated mathematician and astronomer. Unlike earlier lettrist movements rooted in popular mysticism or messianic claims, Ibn Turka's Isfahan Circle practiced an explicitly intellectual, mathematicized lettrism grounded in rigorous philosophical training.

Ibn Turka's tenure as Chief Judge gave him unprecedented opportunity to institutionalize his teachings. He could appoint scholars, establish study circles (*majālis*), and protect heterodox intellectual work from both religious orthodoxy and political instability. His court became a center for Pythagorean occultism and philosophical innovation. Contemporary accounts describe him holding regular scholarly gatherings where the latest works in logic, metaphysics, and lettrism were debated.

### The Lettrist Project: Systematizing the Occult

Ibn Turka's life work was transforming lettrism from an esoteric, orally-transmitted teaching (as it existed in Akhlāṭī's circle) into a transparent, scientifically rigorous philosophy. He argued that lettrism—understood as the systematic investigation of how the letters of the Arabic alphabet encode divine names, cosmological principles, and operative powers—was superior to both philosophical speculation and mystical intuition alone. As Melvin-Koushki notes, Ibn Turka saw an "invidious comparison" between lettrism and philosophy: while philosophy aspired to universality but failed, only lettrism actually encompassed all that is and is not, all that can and cannot be. The letter alone is the *coincidentia oppositorum* (the coincidence of opposites), the only truly universal science.

Ibn Turka accomplished this through an explicitly **Pythagorean model**. Drawing on late-antique Neoplatonic lettrism (transmitted through Hellenistic Greek texts, Islamic reception, and Ibn ʿArabī's intuitive lettrist insights), he argued that reality is fundamentally **mathematical-linguistic**. Numbers, letters, divine names, and cosmic principles form a unified system where:

1. The 28 Arabic letters correspond to 28 divine names, celestial bodies, elements, minerals, plants, animals, and human attributes.
2. Each letter has a numerical value (*abjad* system) that connects it to cosmological scales and operative powers.
3. The cosmos itself is an endless text (*kitāb*) written in letters; mastery of letters grants mastery over the unfolding of creation.
4. Operations that recombine letters—anagrams, numerical rearrangements, geometric configurations—are not magical superstitions but interventions in the fundamental structure of reality.

His magisterial treatise *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) stands as the summa of this system—a comprehensive, technically precise, philosophically cutting-edge treatment of lettrism that remained the canonical reference for centuries.

### Writings and Influence

Ibn Turka authored approximately 45 works, though only about half survive in manuscript. His major lettrist treatises include:

- *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) — the magisterial summa of intellectual lettrism
- *Risālat al-Barzakh* (Treatise on the Isthmus) — philosophical treatment of the intermediate realm between matter and spirit
- *Kitāb al-Nūr* (Book of Light) — cosmological and metaphysical doctrines
- Multiple treatises on the properties of divine names and the occult sciences

Beyond his lettrist works, Ibn Turka wrote extensively on:
- Peripatetic-Illuminationist philosophy (synthesizing Ibn ʿArabī and Suhrawardī)
- Sufi mystical theology
- Rhetoric and literary theory (*ʿilm al-bayān*)
- Grammar and semantics (*ʿilm al-ṣarf wa-l-naḥw*)

His prose style was famous in the Islamic world—Melvin-Koushki describes it as "stylistically gorgeous, philosophically cutting-edge, and wonderfully accessible in a way no previous treatments had been." This combination—technical rigor married to elegant prose—allowed him to appeal to both scholars and educated courtiers, democratizing what had been esoteric knowledge.

Ibn Turka's influence proved enormous. Within a century, his framework became canonical in Islamic lettrism. Every major lettrist after 1500—whether in Safavid Iran, Ottoman Anatolia, or Mughal India—engaged with his categories, debated his arguments, and built on his synthesis. He shaped not only occult philosophy but Islamic literary theory, rhetoric, and mysticism.

### Historiographical Significance

Traditional Islamic historiography, focused on theology and jurisprudence, largely sidelined Ibn Turka as a curiosity. European orientalism dismissed Islamic occultism as superstition, further marginalizing him. The turning point came with Matthew Melvin-Koushki's scholarly work, especially his Yale dissertation *The Quest for a Universal Science* (2012), which demonstrated that:

1. Ibn Turka was not an exception but the systematizer of a vast network of occultists operating at the highest levels of power across the Islamic world.
2. His lettrist philosophy was not mystical superstition but a rigorous intellectual system with its own internal logic and demonstrable consequences.
3. His project of magical-mathematical empire paralleled and arguably exceeded the ambitions of contemporary European figures (Pico, Dee, Bruno).
4. Understanding Ibn Turka is essential for understanding post-Mongol intellectual history, the emergence of occult philosophy as a legitimate science, and the global early modern period.

Recent scholarship (Melvin-Koushki, 2023–2025) has repositioned Ibn Turka as a central figure in a "Persianate Neopythagorean Renaissance"—a transregional intellectual movement dedicated to reviving Pythagorean-Neoplatonic philosophy as a tool for understanding and transforming the world.

### Sources and Death

Ibn Turka lived through the dynastic instability of the late Timurid period. After Timur's death (1405), his empire fragmented. The last years of Ibn Turka's life were marked by political decline and personal exile. He died in 835/1432, in poverty and political limbo, five years after losing his third state inquisition—persecuted for teaching occult philosophy to the elite. Yet his writings survived, and within a generation, his fame had only grown.

According to Melvin-Koushki's dating, Ibn Turka wrote *Nafsat al-Masṭūr* (Breath of the Hidden) around 829/1426, at age 59, providing his own reflection on his life and work. In this late treatise, he reasserted the superiority of lettrism over philosophy and mysticism alone, confident that his synthesis would outlive the political powers that opposed him.

## The household

Ibn Turka states that he had **ten children, three sons and seven daughters**. Two sons are known by name. For **Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad** he wrote his manual of logic, the *Kitāb al-Manāhij*, during the winter at Natanz in the exile years. **Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb Allāh** appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise of his own, the *Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ* — the science continued inside the family for at least one further generation, though nothing else is known of him (*The Quest*, 41).

His office is worth stating exactly: **Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and Yazd**. Everything in the [[kitab-al-mafahis|summa]] was written around a working senior magistracy in two cities.

## The thesis of the science, in his own terms

Everything Ibn Turka argues rests on one claim about letters, and it is worth stating in
the sharpest form the dissertation gives it. Against philosophy — and the comparison is
explicitly invidious — **the faux-universal concepts of philosophical speculation
notwithstanding, only the letter encompasses all that is and is not, all that can and
cannot be; it alone is the *coincidentia oppositorum*; hence lettrism is the only truly
universal science** (*The Quest*, iii).

Three things are packed into that sentence and each is doing work.

**First, the comparison is with philosophy, not with magic.** Ibn Turka is not defending a
practice against the charge of superstition; he is claiming a crown that peripatetic
philosophy had assumed was its own. Philosophy's concepts *aspire* to universality and fail,
because a concept ranges only over what is and what can be. The letter ranges further,
covering also what is not and what cannot be.

**Second, the *coincidentia oppositorum*.** The letter is the point at which opposites
coincide — being and non-being, possibility and impossibility — and a science of the letter
is therefore a science of the whole. Melvin-Koushki's choice of the Latin phrase is
deliberate and comparative: it is Nicholas of Cusa's term, and the essay
[[ilm-al-huruf|on the Pythagorean revival]] sets Isfahan 1420 against Cusa 1440 without
ever asserting contact between them.

**Third, the word "only".** This is a maximal claim. It is why the project could not settle
for being tolerated, and why the tribunals were, in a sense, correctly aimed. A man
claiming that his discipline supersedes philosophy has said something about the order of
the sciences that other people hold offices within.

## Three lettrisms, and which one is his

The single most important distinction in reading Ibn Turka is that **lettrism in this
period is not one thing**, and he belongs to a strand that is routinely confused with the
other two.

Melvin-Koushki argues that Ibn Turka's unprecedented lionization of lettrism vis-à-vis
philosophy represents **a specifically *intellectual* form of the science, distinct from
its originary gnostic-messianic and Sufi strains** (*The Quest*, iii). The three run
alongside each other:

- **Gnostic-messianic lettrism** — the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfiyya]] of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī:
  letters as the announcement of a new dispensation.
- **Sufi lettrism** — letters within a devotional and contemplative discipline, the strand
  running from Ibn ʿArabī through the orders.
- **Intellectual lettrism** — Ibn Turka's: letters as the object of a rigorous,
  mathematically grounded universal science.

He then makes a point about the historiography that matters for anyone reading this portal.
**It is typically — and erroneously — assumed that the Ḥurūfī movement defines later
Islamicate lettrism.** It does not. It is an example of *popular* gnostic-messianic-Sufi
lettrism, and what its vigour actually demonstrates is the religio-cultural valency of
lettrism in Iran **at all levels** of society (*The Quest*, iii). The Ḥurūfīs are evidence
of how widely the material circulated, not of what it fundamentally was.

This is the distinction his prosecutors collapsed, and the one his own defence depended on
holding open.

## The two Books

Melvin-Koushki places Ibn Turka's significance in late medieval intellectual history in a
frame that is deliberately global. His importance centres on his status as **one of a
panoply of late medieval and early modern thinkers to understand reality in textual terms,
driven by the prospect of decoding and recoding the twin Books, the Qur'an and the cosmos**
(*The Quest*, iii).

Two moves are worth separating there. *Decoding* is hermeneutic: creation and scripture are
both texts, and both can be read. *Recoding* is operative: a reader who understands the
notation can write in it. The second is what makes this an occult science rather than an
exegetical one, and it is the whole distance between reading the world and
[[talismanic-science|acting on it]].

The frame also explains why the comparison with Renaissance Europe recurs throughout
Melvin-Koushki's work without ever becoming a claim of influence. Cusa, Pico, Bruno and Dee
were doing something structurally similar with a different scripture and a different
alphabet. The parallel is real; the contact is not asserted.

## What the lettrists thought they were doing

Against the picture of fringe cranks, the dissertation is emphatic: **far from being fringe
thinkers, Muslim lettrists of Ibn Turka's stripe saw themselves as both advancing human
knowledge of the cosmos and demonstrating the miraculous inimitability of the Qur'an
(*iʿjāz*) as the clearest transcript of divine Speech in history** (*The Quest*, iii).

The second half of that is easy to miss and is load-bearing. *Iʿjāz* — the doctrine that
the Qur'an's perfection is itself the proof of its divine origin — is a mainstream, indeed
conservative, theological commitment. Ibn Turka's science is offered as its
**demonstration**: if the letters of scripture are the constitutive principles of creation,
then the Qur'an's inimitability is not a literary judgement but a cosmological fact. This is
why the project reads as pious from the inside and as dangerous from the outside. He is not
smuggling foreign material into Islam; he is claiming to prove Islam's central textual
doctrine by mathematical means.

It also explains the dependence, noted in the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]], on the
doctrine of the **uncreatedness of the Qur'an**. Created letters could not carry this
weight.

## The prose

One further consequence, and it is not decorative. Melvin-Koushki argues that **lettrist
theory informs the ornate literary practice of the period**, and points to Ibn Turka's own
standing as a **vaunted stylist of Persian prose** (*The Quest*, iii).

If letters are ontological entities, then the arrangement of letters on a page is not
presentation but participation. The elaborate prosimetric style of his work — verse set
into prose, the sound and shape of the words carrying argumentative weight — is a
consequence of the doctrine rather than an ornament laid over it. The
[[sharh-nazm-al-durr|*Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr*]], which brings each line of Ibn al-Fāriḍ's
poem into conjunction with several further lines of Persian and Arabic verse, is the
method in its literary form.

## What we do not know

- **Over half the oeuvre is unedited.** Some twenty-three or twenty-four of his roughly
  forty-five works remain in manuscript, and the lettrist works are disproportionately
  among them — on the assumption, which this portal exists to contest, that they are the
  marginal part.
- **The conjunction is uncertain.** Melvin-Koushki says plainly that he is not entirely
  sure which conjunction Ibn Turka has in mind for the portent of 767/1365.
- **The second and third tribunals are undated.** The chronology fixes the first, around
  825/1422; the sequence and years of the later two are not established in the sources in
  hand.
- **Composition versus transcription.** For much of the oeuvre the colophons of
  MS Majlis 10196 cannot distinguish when a work was written from when it was copied.
- **Eight of ten children are unnamed**, and nothing further is known of Najīb al-Dīn
  Ḥabīb Allāh beyond the one lettrist treatise attributed to him.
- **Whether he ever met [[bistami|Bisṭāmī]]** during their overlapping Cairo years is
  unclear, and so is whether he ever met Ibn Khaldūn, who lived in the city throughout.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran.* PhD Dissertation, Yale University, 2012.

Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context.* In *Islamicate Occult Sciences in Theory and Practice*, edited by Saif, Leoni, Melvin-Koushki, and Yahya, pp. 127–199. Berlin: De Gruyter, 2017.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism, Definitively Synthesizes, Fully Works Out, and Productively Extends the Lettrist Implications.* Forthcoming.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology: Lettrism, Alchemy, and the Secrets of the Letters in Medieval Islam.* Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.

figures.name: Akhlati
figures.card: **Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī** (d. 1397), Kurdish occultist, alchemist, and lettrist mystic. The pivot of the "New Brethren of Purity" network stretching from Cairo through Anatolia to Iran, Central Asia, and India. Served as physician and confidant at the court of Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 1382–1399). Akhlāṭī's oral teachings on lettrism, alchemy, and talismanic magic shaped Ibn Turka, who became his principal systematizer and heir. Though Akhlāṭī left few written works, his influence on Islamic occultism proved foundational and lasting.
figures.body:
## Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (d. 1397)

### The Pivot of the Network

Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī (also known as the Tabrizi, a reference to his Kurdish origins in Tabriz/Ahlat region) died in Cairo in 799/1397, at an unknown age. Yet despite the paucity of biographical detail—his birth date is unknown, few of his writings survive—Akhlāṭī stands as the intellectual and spiritual center of what Melvin-Koushki calls the "New Brethren of Purity," a transregional network of occultists operating at the highest levels of power across the late medieval Islamic world.

The network stretched from Cairo (where Akhlāṭī held court) northward to Ottoman Anatolia and eastward through western Iran, Central Asia, and eventually India. Its members called themselves cryptically the *Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ* (Brethren of Purity)—deliberately invoking the medieval encyclopedists of the 10th century—and shared a common project: the retrieval, systematization, and open promulgation of the occult sciences (*ʿulūm al-gharība*) as a tool for human evolution and imperial power.

### Life and Position

Akhlāṭī's prominence in Mamluk Cairo is documented in contemporary sources and visual art. A manuscript of the *Majālis al-ʿUshshāq* (Assemblies of Lovers) from Shiraz (BL Or. 11837 f. 117, ca. 1560) depicts an illumination showing Akhlāṭī receiving gifts from the Mamluk sultan Barqūq (r. 784–801/1382–1399). Two figures who may represent Ibn Turka and [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]] look on as their master is honored by the sultan—a visual record of Akhlāṭī's extraordinary status as both scholar and court confidant.

Akhlāṭī served as physician to Barqūq and held intellectual authority on matters of alchemy, medicine, geomancy, and lettrism. The sources consistently describe him as a *muʿajjiz* (miracle-worker), indicating that his reputation extended beyond scholarly circles into the world of practical theurgy and wonder-working. He was, in short, a public intellectual at the apex of political power, able to advocate openly for the occult sciences in an environment where such advocacy could be dangerous.

### Teachings and Method

Akhlāṭī's primary influence came through oral teaching rather than written treatises. He conducted regular scholarly gatherings (*majālis*) where he taught lettrism, alchemical theory, and talismanic operation. Unlike the gnostic-messianic lettrist movement of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 1394), which emphasized popular mysticism and ecstatic experience, Akhlāṭī's teaching was philosophical and technical. He integrated lettrist theory with Neoplatonic metaphysics, Islamic peripatetic philosophy, and practical alchemy—demonstrating that letters, divine names, and numerical values form a coherent system for understanding and manipulating reality.

Ibn Turka, who absorbed these teachings directly in Cairo before Akhlāṭī's death in 1397, repeatedly credits Akhlāṭī in his own writings. In the introduction to his magisterial *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries), Ibn Turka names Akhlāṭī as one of his three primary sources (alongside Ibn ʿArabī and Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya). Yet while Ibn Turka consistently emphasizes that he is merely "the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's teachings," the reality is more subtle: Akhlāṭī provided the intellectual raw material and the occultist worldview, but Ibn Turka transformed oral teachings into a written, rigorous, Pythagorean-modeled philosophical system. Akhlāṭī pioneered; Ibn Turka systematized.

### Influence and Legacy

Akhlāṭī's death in 1397 marked a turning point. With him gone, the New Brethren network began to decentralize. Yet his influence spread outward rather than contracting. Ibn Turka carried his teachings to Isfahan and Yazd, establishing them at the highest levels of Timurid power. Other disciples—[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi]], [[qazizada-rumi]], and unnamed others—propagated his methods across the Islamic world. By the 15th and 16th centuries, Akhlāṭī's fame had grown even as his original writings disappeared. Every Islamic occultist engaging with lettrism at scholarly levels was working within a framework Akhlāṭī had established.

Modern historiography, influenced by orientalist dismissal of "Islamic superstition," long sidelined Akhlāṭī as a marginal figure. Melvin-Koushki's work has demonstrated that Akhlāṭī was in fact a central intellectual figure—not in the narrow sense of academic philosophy, but in the broader sense of late medieval intellectual history. He was doing what Renaissance mages in Europe would later do: attempting to create a universal science integrating reason, mysticism, natural magic, and mathematics into a coherent system for understanding and transforming the world.

### Sources

Akhlāṭī is mentioned frequently in Ibn Turka's surviving works and in the writings of other members of the Isfahan Circle. Some short treatises attributed to him survive in manuscript, particularly on the properties of letters and divine names. The most sustained modern treatment remains Melvin-Koushki's dissertation and subsequent articles, which have excavated Akhlāṭī from near-total obscurity and positioned him as the intellectual hub of a vast occultist network.

## The office that put him at the centre

The single fact that organises Akhlāṭī's career is institutional rather than doctrinal: he
was **summoned to Cairo to serve as personal physician to Sultan Barqūq** (r. 784–801/
1382–1399), and Melvin-Koushki calls him more precisely Barqūq's **personal
physician-alchemist** (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70; *Powers of One*, 6).

A court physician has something no other kind of scholar has: unsupervised, repeated,
private access to the ruler's body. That access is the mechanism behind everything else.
Under his influence **Barqūq seems to have developed a keen interest in the occult
sciences**, and the evidence Melvin-Koushki adduces is exactly the evidence a historian
would want — not testimony about the sultan's opinions but **his personal library and his
choice of courtiers**, among whom was Ibn Turka himself.

From this Melvin-Koushki puts a question and answers it: **was Barqūq the first Mamluk
sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and so an inspiration for Timurid rivals?
Likely so.** If that is right, Akhlāṭī did not merely teach a generation of occultists; he
converted a throne, and the model of the occult court that the Timurids would develop has a
Cairene prototype.

## Heir of two traditions at once

Melvin-Koushki's characterisation is compact and worth spelling out: Akhlāṭī is the
**conscious heir of both al-Būnī and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]]**, and master to the most
important occult philosophers of the following generation (*Powers of One*, 6).

Those are two different inheritances and they do not obviously combine.

- **From al-Būnī** comes operative talismanic lettrism: the *Shams al-Maʿārif* tradition,
  magic squares, divine names deployed for effect, a practical literature of procedures.
- **From Ibn ʿArabī** comes a metaphysics: the [[divine-names|divine names]] as the
  structure through which being manifests, the [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]], a
  contemplative rather than operative orientation.

Holding both **consciously** is the achievement. The manual and the metaphysics are joined
in one teacher before Ibn Turka receives them, which is why his own synthesis can take the
combination for granted and spend its effort on the [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematics]]
instead.

## The pivot of a network

The dissertation describes Akhlāṭī as **the pivot** of the network that would call itself,
cryptically, the [[new-brethren-purity|Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ]] — a network stretching from
Anatolia through Cairo to Iran and India. He **proclaimed a new era of human development
through the retrieval and open promulgation of the occult sciences** (*The Quest*, 2).

Two heirs matter most, and their divergence is the network's central comparative fact. Ibn
Turka is the eastern arm; **[[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]]** is the Ottoman one. They
were **both the intellectual heirs of Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī**, and it is unclear whether
they met during their respective long residences in Mamluk Cairo (*The Quest*, 2). The same
teaching went west and east; Melvin-Koushki judges the western outcome **more successful**.

## How Ibn Turka positioned himself in relation to him

Not as an innovator. **Ibn Turka presents himself as simply the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's
teachings, and was received as such in the later lettrist tradition** (*The Quest*, 2).

This self-presentation should be read with care in both directions. It is partly genuine
intellectual debt and partly the ordinary prudence of a man in a dangerous field, for whom
a chain of transmission is a defence. But it also understates what he did: Akhlāṭī does not
appear to have grounded lettrism in Pythagorean mathematics or argued it into the
[[occult-science-universal|mathematical sciences]]. The systematiser's modesty conceals a
reclassification.

## What we do not know

- **Almost nothing of Akhlāṭī's own writing** is discussed in the sources in hand; he is
  known chiefly through his students and his position.
- **Whether Bisṭāmī and Ibn Turka met** under him is unresolved.
- The claim that **Barqūq aspired to occult-philosopher-kingship** is offered as "likely",
  not as established.
- His death in **799/1397** in Cairo is firm; his birth and origins are not treated in these
  sources.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran.* PhD Dissertation, Yale University, 2012. [See especially Chapter 1 on Akhlāṭī and the Cairo Circle.]
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'The New Brethren of Purity: Intellectual Lettrist Networks in the Fifteenth-Century Islamic World.' *Journal of the American Oriental Society* 139, no. 3 (2019): 541–572.

figures.name: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi
figures.card: **Sharaf al-Dīn ʿAlī Yazdī** (c. 1370s–1454), scholar, historian, and occult philosopher. One of the two most prominent intellectuals of Shahrukhid Iran (identified with Ibn Turka by Dawlatshah Samarqandi). Member of the Isfahan Circle; author of the *Ẓafarnāma* (universal history from an astrological-lettrist perspective). Integrated [[ilm-al-huruf]] with historical and political analysis. Represents the application of lettrist philosophy to the writing of history and the interpretation of empire.
figures.body:
**Sharaf al-Dīn ʿAlī Yazdī** (c. 1370s–1454) was among the most accomplished intellectuals of 15th-century Iran. Born in Yazd, he emerged as one of the two leading figures of his age, identified by the historian Dawlatshah Samarqandi (d. 1494–1507) as equal in prominence to [[ibn-turka]] himself. Unlike Ibn Turka, who was primarily a philosopher and occultist, Sharaf al-Dīn applied lettrist and astrological principles to the practice of history-writing and political analysis. His magnum opus, the *Ẓafarnāma* (Book of Victories), is a universal history organized according to astrological and lettrist principles—demonstrating that history itself unfolds according to cosmic cycles encoded in letters and divine names. This work became canonical in the Timurid and Safavid periods. Sharaf al-Dīn's synthesis of lettrism, astrology, and historiography shows how Ibn Turka's philosophical framework could be applied practically to statecraft and the interpretation of events.

**Correction on the relationship.** An earlier version of this entry described Yazdī as Ibn Turka's peer. The dissertation is more specific: he is *his disciple and closest associate*. The *Munshaʾāt-i Yazdī* preserves eight items relating to Ibn Turka or his immediate family, showing Yazdī's attendance at his teacher's *majālis*, his accompanying Ibn Turka on journeys to Herat, and his concern for Ibn Turka's children (*makhdūm-zādagān*) after their father's death (*The Quest*, 135–36). The bond is pedagogical and personal, not collegial — which is what makes Yazdī the one figure positioned to carry the system forward.

## The relationship, documented from his side

The evidence for the closeness is unusual in shape: it survives chiefly in **Yazdī's**
archive rather than Ibn Turka's. Only one letter to Yazdī appears in the
[[munshaat-i-turka|*Munshaʾāt-i Ṣāʾin-i Turka*]], from the first stage of Ibn Turka's career
in Fars; Melvin-Koushki suggests the rest were simply too informal to be thought worth
preserving.

The ***Munshaʾāt-i Yazdī***, by contrast, contains **eight items** relating to Ibn Turka or
his immediate family, and they sketch the relationship far more adequately: Yazdī's
**attendance at his teacher's *majālis***, his **accompanying Ibn Turka on journeys to
Herat**, and his **concern for Ibn Turka's children (*makhdūm-zādagān*) after their father's
death** (*The Quest*, 135–36).

That last item is the one that settles the character of the bond. Looking after a dead
colleague's children is not a professional courtesy.

## From the beginning of the journey

The association predates the Timurid courts entirely. The chronology places it at the start:
around **795/1393 Ibn Turka leaves Samarkand for Mecca and Cairo, and Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī
accompanies him**. Yazdī spent at least part of the period 795–810/1393–1408 in Cairo with
him (*Powers of One*, 37).

So the fifteen years of formation under [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] were shared. Yazdī
is not a disciple acquired at the height of Ibn Turka's career; he is the man who was there
for the whole of it.

## The Cairo overlap with Ibn Khaldūn

One tantalising possibility follows. **Ibn Khaldūn lived in Cairo from 785/1383 until his
death in 808/1406**, overlapping Yazdī's residence there, and Melvin-Koushki notes that
**the two historians possibly met** (*Powers of One*, 37).

The interest is obvious: Ibn Khaldūn is the most formidable critic of the occult sciences in
the tradition, and Yazdī would go on to write in defence of divination against exactly that
critique. Whether the defence was written by a man who had argued with him in person is
unknown and would change how one reads it.

## What we do not know

- **Whether he and Ibn Khaldūn actually met** — "possibly" is as far as the evidence goes.
- **The bulk of the correspondence between him and Ibn Turka** is lost.
- **How far he shared the lettrist doctrine** as opposed to applying its methods to history
  is not resolved in the sources in hand.


## The historian, and the argument he is used to make

Yazdī is described as **dynastic historian to the Timurids and committed occultist**
(*In Defense of Geomancy*, 349) — and the two halves of that description are not in tension
for him, which is the point.

His best-known work is the ***Ẓafarnāma***, an **ornate, long-admired and much-imitated
account of Tīmūr's career**. Less widely known: it is **one of five separate chronicles he
began** (ibid., n.3). The output is that of a professional historian, not an occultist with
a sideline.

## Against Ibn Khaldūn — but not in the expected direction

Melvin-Koushki stages Yazdī against **Ibn Khaldūn** (d. 808/1406), and the confrontation
inverts both reputations.

Ibn Khaldūn's supposed skepticism about the occult sciences is **much admired, held up as a
shining, solitary example of rationality amidst rampant superstition**. What is less
acknowledged is that he **argues forcefully, and at length, for the incontrovertible reality
of magic and divination, with the selfsame sober objectivity**. He rejected astrology and
alchemy; he did not reject the occult as such.

And Yazdī, from the other side, produces **theories of historical evolution and human
potential not dissimilar to Ibn Khaldūn's more famous formulations** — yet **predicated
precisely on a thoroughgoingly occultist outlook**.

Two historians of one generation reaching comparable accounts of how societies develop from
opposite metaphysical premises. Both men's views on occultism **go to the heart of their
respective sociologies and political theologies, which accordingly converge and diverge in
instructive ways**.

This is what the portal's intersection essay on the defence of divination is about, and it
is a better story than rationalism versus credulity.

## The Cairo overlap again

Ibn Khaldūn lived in Cairo from 785/1383 until his death in 808/1406; Yazdī spent at least
part of 795–810/1393–1408 there with Ibn Turka, and Melvin-Koushki notes **the two
historians possibly met** (*Powers of One*, 37). If the *Ẓafarnāma*'s occultist philosophy of
history was written by a man who had argued with Ibn Khaldūn in person, it reads
differently.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi and the Occult Sciences in Timurid Iran.' Journal of the American Oriental Society.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 135–36.

figures.name: Qazizada Rumi
figures.card: **Qāżīzāda Rūmī** (c. 1380–1432), celebrated mathematician and astronomer. Member of the Isfahan Circle; friend and colleague to [[ibn-turka]]. Active in Samarkand at Timur's court and later in Isfahan and Yazd. Pioneer of mathematical methods in astronomy; integrated mathematical and occult approaches to celestial phenomena. Represents the mathematicization of Islamic astronomy during the early Timurid period.
figures.body:
**Qāḍīzāda Rūmī** (also known as Ṣāliḥ al-Dīn Mūsā Qāḍīzāda, c. 1380–1432) was one of the most accomplished mathematicians and astronomers of the Timurid age. Born in Anatolia, he rose to prominence at Timur's court in Samarkand and later became a close colleague of [[ibn-turka]] in Isfahan and Yazd. Qazizada was renowned for advancing mathematical methods in astronomy—bringing rigorous calculation to celestial observations. He shared with Ibn Turka a commitment to integrating rational mathematical analysis with occult philosophy. Where Ibn Turka pursued lettrism as the universal science, Qazizada pursued mathematics and astronomy as paths to understanding cosmic principles. The two represent complementary approaches within the Isfahan Circle: Ibn Turka's linguistic-lettrist method and Qazizada's mathematical-astronomical method, both grounded in the belief that creation is knowable through precise systematic inquiry into its underlying patterns.

**They were schoolfellows.** The dissertation records that Ibn Turka studied under his elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] for the first twenty-five years of his life **along with Qāḍīzāda Rūmī** (*The Quest*, ch. 1). The two were not colleagues who converged at a Timurid court but students taught side by side in the same Isfahani household for a quarter of a century — which makes the later division of labour between them, one taking the letters and one the stars, look less like coincidence and more like two answers to the same teaching.

**Two precisions.** He was the **second** director of Ulugh Beg's observatory at Samarkand, not its first. And he died in **835/1432 — the same year as Ibn Turka** (*The Quest*, 41 n.17, citing Ragep, 'Ḳāḍī-zāda Rūmī', EI2). Two men taught side by side for twenty-five years, who then divided the century's work between the stars and the letters, died in the same season.

## The schooling, and what it implies

The fact that reorganises this entry: Qāḍīzāda studied under
[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn Turka]] **alongside Ibn Turka**, for the first twenty-five
years of Ibn Turka's life (*The Quest*, 41 n.17, citing Eichner, 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka', EI3,
and Ragep, 'Ḳāḍī-zāda Rūmī', EI2).

They were not colleagues who converged at a Timurid court. They were taught in the same
household, by the same man, for a quarter of a century — an education that stopped
deliberately at the outward sciences because their teacher **deemed it too dangerous to delve
into esoteric matters in public**.

Both pupils then spent their careers on disciplines by which the hidden order of things might
be made **calculable**. One took the stars and the other the letters, and
[[observatory-founded|the observatory]] and [[mafahis-completed|the summa]] were begun in the
same year, 1420. Melvin-Koushki's thesis — that the mathematization of astronomy and the
mathematicalization of the occult sciences are one movement studied in atomistic isolation —
has, in these two men, a shared classroom underneath it.

## The office

He was the **second** director of [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg's]]
[[samarkand-observatory|observatory at Samarkand]] — a precision worth keeping, since he is
often described simply as its director. The observatory's staff over its short life included
Jamshīd al-Kāshī and ʿAlī Qushjī; Qāḍīzāda belongs to the first generation of that
institution rather than to its founding.

## The coincidence at the end

He died in **835/1432**, the same year as Ibn Turka. One in an observatory that would be
dismantled within two decades of his death, the other in an antechamber at Herat waiting on a
case review that never came.

## What we do not know

- **Whether they remained in contact** after the Isfahan schoolroom.
- **What he thought of lettrism.** The link between the two disciplines is argued at the level
  of intellectual context, not documented as an exchange of views between these two men.
- **His birth date** is not given in these sources.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. 'Qazizada Rumi and the Mathematical Sciences in Timurid Iran.'
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), ch. 1.

figures.name: Ibn Arabi
figures.name_full: Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿArabī
figures.card: **Muḥyī al-Dīn Ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240), Andalusian mystic and philosopher. Founder of the metaphysical school most influential on later Islamic occultism and mysticism. Author of the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations) and other foundational works. His doctrines of [[divine-names|divine names]], the imaginal realm, and the macrocosm-microcosm correspondence profoundly influenced [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka's]] theoretical framework. Via the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-[[jandi|Jandī]] transmission, Ibn Arabi's philosophy became the philosophical grounding for Ibn Turka's lettrist innovations.
figures.body:
## Ibn ʿArabī: The Shaykh al-Akbar and His Legacy

**Muḥyī al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240) was born in Murcia, Andalusia, during the waning years of Islamic rule in medieval Spain. He lived through an era of profound intellectual ferment—the collision of Islamic mysticism, philosophy, and theology in a period of cultural upheaval. By the end of his life, based in Damascus, Ibn Arabi had become the most influential mystical-philosophical voice in the Islamic world, with a legacy that would shape Islamic thought for centuries.

### The Metaphysical System

Ibn Arabi's magnum opus, the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations), presents a comprehensive metaphysical system grounded in several key doctrines:

1. **The Unity of Existence** (*Waḥdat al-Wujūd*): All being is fundamentally one; the apparent multiplicity of creation is manifestation of the single divine reality.

2. **The Divine Names** (*Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya*): God is known through 99 (or 28) divine names and attributes. Each name expresses a dimension of the divine. Creation itself unfolds through these names.

3. **The Perfect Human** (*Al-Insān al-Kāmil*): The human being is the microcosm that mirrors the macrocosm. In the perfected human, all divine names are manifest.

4. **The Imaginal Realm** (*Al-Khalīqa al-Mutawassita*): Between pure intellect and material sense exists an intermediate realm of subtle forms—the imaginal world where mystical visions and symbolic knowledge occur.

### Transmission Through Qūnavī and Jandī

Ibn Arabi's thought did not reach later occultists directly. Instead, it was systematized and reinterpreted by two crucial transmitters:

- **Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnavī** (d. 1274), Ibn Arabi's leading disciple, who codified and organized his teachings into a more scholastic philosophical framework.

- **ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th century), who further elaborated Qūnavī's synthesis, emphasizing the metaphysical correspondences and the operations of divine names.

This Qūnavī-Jandī school tradition became the conduit through which Ibn Arabi's metaphysics reached [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] and the later Islamic occult philosophers. When Ibn Turka integrated [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]] with Islamic mysticism, he was building on the Ibn Arabi–Qūnavī–Jandī foundation.

### Ibn Arabi and Ibn Turka: The Philosophical Genealogy

Matthew Melvin-Koushki's historical reconstruction clarifies Ibn Turka's relationship to Ibn Arabi. Scholars had long viewed Ibn Turka primarily as a Sufi-philosopher in the Ibn Arabi tradition—a continuator of mystical-scholastic synthesis. However, this framework obscured Ibn Turka's more radical project. Ibn Turka was not simply synthesizing Ibn Arabi with peripatetic philosophy; he was deploying Ibn Arabi's metaphysics (especially the doctrine of divine names) as the theoretical foundation for a new kind of operative science: [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist cosmology]].

The key insight: For Ibn Arabi, the divine names were primarily objects of mystical knowledge and contemplation. For Ibn Turka, they become operative principles encoded in the structure of letters and numbers. This is not a contradiction but a systematic application of Ibn Arabi's principles to the domain of practice and causation.

### Historical Significance

Ibn Arabi stands at the head of a tradition that includes mysticism, Sufism, Islamic philosophy, and occultism. He demonstrated that Islamic thought could achieve a synthesis of reason and intuition, philosophy and gnosis, theology and practice. His rehabilitation of the imaginal realm and his systematization of [[divine-names|divine attributes]] created the conceptual apparatus that later occultists like Ibn Turka would weaponize.

In the history of Islamic occult philosophy, Ibn Arabi is the foundational figure. Every subsequent occultist, from Safavid mystical philosophers to Ottoman talismanic practitioners, operated in the shadow of his legacy—and often in direct dialogue with his texts.

## What Ibn Turka took, and what he did not

The portal's [[hurufism|three-strand]] account of lettrism makes the debt precise. From the
Akbarian tradition Ibn Turka takes a **metaphysics of the [[divine-names|divine names]]** —
the doctrine that creation unfolds as the self-disclosure of divine attributes, and that the
[[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]] is where that disclosure takes form. Without this there is
nothing for letters to *be*.

What he does not take is the orientation. Ibn ʿArabī's names are objects of contemplation
approached through spiritual discipline; the knower is transformed by knowing. Ibn Turka's
are **operative principles** encoded in a notation, approached through calculation; the
knower acts. The intersection essay on the Akbarian inheritance calls this contemplation
converted to computation, and the phrase is exact.

This is why the entry insists on *two fathers*. Akbarian metaphysics alone does not produce
an operative science. It needs the second inheritance —
[[saad-al-din-hamuyya|Ḥamūya's]] lettrist application, and behind it the al-Būnī tradition
that [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] held together with Ibn ʿArabī in a single teaching.

## The school, not the man

A point about transmission that matters for reading this portal. Ibn Turka does not receive
Ibn ʿArabī raw. He receives the **Ibn ʿArabī school tradition as formulated by
[[qunavi|Qūnavī]] and [[jandi|Jandī]]** — this is the formula the dissertation uses of the
[[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]], which relies on precisely that lineage
(*The Quest*, 6).

The distinction is not pedantic. Ibn ʿArabī's own writing is vast, associative and
resistant to system; what reached fifteenth-century Iran was a scholasticised version,
organised into arguments that could be taught, defended and built on. Ibn Turka argues with
the school's Ibn ʿArabī.

## The reception problem this created

There is an irony the portal should name. Because Ibn Turka is demonstrably an Akbarian, and
because the *Tamhīd* — his most Akbarian book — became his most famous, he was filed as a
link in a chain: the synthesizer connecting Ibn ʿArabī to Mullā Ṣadrā. Melvin-Koushki's
verdict is that this acclaim is **what marginalised him**, obscuring the occultist tenor of
the larger project, abstracting it from its historical context and robbing it of its
animating virtue (*The Quest*, ii).

Being correctly identified as Ibn ʿArabī's heir is what stopped people looking at what he
did with the inheritance.

## What we do not know

- **Which of Ibn ʿArabī's works Ibn Turka read directly**, as against through Qūnavī and
  Jandī, is not established in these sources.
- **How Ibn ʿArabī's own attitude to operative practice** should be characterised is a large
  contested question this portal does not attempt to settle.
literature: Ibn Arabi. *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (The Meccan Illuminations). Damascus: al-Dar al-Qawwama, 2010.
Ibn Arabi. *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam* (The Bezels of Wisdom). Translated by Ralph Austin. Oxford: Muhammadi Trust, 1980.
Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 45–90.

figures.name: Qūnavī
figures.name_full: Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Qūnavī
figures.card: **Ṣadr al-Dīn al-Qūnavī** (1210–1274), leading disciple and systematizer of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics. Through his philosophical elaboration of Ibn Arabi's doctrines, Qūnavī created the scholastic framework that transmitted Ibn Arabi's thought to later Islamic philosophers and occultists. His work provided the philosophical grounding for [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka's]] integration of divine-names doctrine with lettrist and Pythagorean theory. A central figure in the Qūnavī-[[jandi|Jandī]] school tradition.
figures.body:
**Ṣadr al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq al-Qūnavī** (1210–1274) was the most important early systematizer of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysical doctrines. Born in Konya, Anatolia, Qūnavī became Ibn Arabi's foremost disciple and literary executor, tasked with organizing, elaborating, and defending his master's vision. Whereas Ibn Arabi's own writings are voluminous, imaginative, and often enigmatic, Qūnavī's works present Ibn Arabi's metaphysics in a rigorous, scholastic form, amenable to philosophical analysis and teaching. This systematization proved decisive: it was Qūnavī's articulation of Ibn Arabi's thought—not Ibn Arabi's own texts directly—that shaped the transmission of Ibn Arabi's legacy to later philosophers, Sufis, and occultists. Qūnavī's central contributions include: (1) the codification of the doctrine of the [[divine-names|divine names]] as the mechanism of creation; (2) the elaboration of the imaginal realm (*malakūt*) as the intermediate domain where mystical knowledge operates; (3) the establishment of the Perfect Human (*al-insān al-kāmil*) as the microcosm in which all divine attributes are manifest. Through the Qūnavī-[[jandi|Jandī]] school tradition, these doctrines reached Ottoman and Persian philosophers, providing the theoretical foundations that [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] would deploy in systematizing [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist occultism]] as the operative application of divine-names metaphysics.

## Why systematisation was the decisive act

The usual way of describing a disciple is that he preserved his master's teaching. Qūnavī
did something more consequential and more distorting: he **made it arguable**.

Ibn ʿArabī writes in a mode that is visionary, associative and enormous. It can be read,
quoted and meditated on; it cannot easily be *disputed*, because it does not present itself
as a sequence of claims with grounds. Qūnavī reorganised it into the form a scholastic
philosopher could use — definitions, distinctions, positions taken against named opponents.

The gain is transmissibility: after Qūnavī, Akbarian metaphysics can be taught in a madrasa
and defended in a disputation. The cost is that the version transmitted is Qūnavī's. When
[[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] argues with Ibn ʿArabī he is arguing with a text that has already
been through this process — the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]] relies specifically
on **the Ibn ʿArabī school tradition as formulated by Qūnavī and [[jandi|Jandī]]**
(*The Quest*, 6).

## What the school supplied to lettrism

Three things, each load-bearing for the later science:

1. **The [[divine-names|divine names]] as an ordered structure** rather than a devotional
   list — nameable, relatable, and therefore mappable onto something else.
2. **The [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]] given a defined ontological status**, which is
   what allows [[barzakh|the intermediate]] to be treated as a location where causation
   operates rather than a metaphor.
3. **A scholastic vocabulary** in which mystical claims could be stated as philosophical
   ones — the precondition for arguing that lettrism outranks philosophy on philosophy's own
   ground.

## What we do not know

- **Which specific works of Qūnavī** Ibn Turka used is not identified in these sources.
- **How far Qūnavī's version departs from Ibn ʿArabī's own** is a live scholarly question
  outside this portal's corpus.
- The relationship between Qūnavī and **Jandī** — who elaborated whom, and in what order —
  is treated here only in outline.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.

figures.name: Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya
figures.name_full: Saʿd al-Dīn Muḥammad b. al-Muʾayyad Ḥamūya
figures.card: **Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya** (d. 649/1252), Kubrawi shaykh and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī's]] Iranian contemporary — and, with Ibn ʿArabī, **Ibn Turka's favourite lettrist source**. Melvin-Koushki calls him Ibn Turka's **only other identified source**, with an oeuvre **even more centrally lettrist, and even more slippery**, than Ibn ʿArabī's. He once criticised Ibn ʿArabī by letter for being **too rigid in his lettrism**.
figures.body:
## The second father

The portal's intersection essay on the Akbarian inheritance is subtitled *two fathers for one science*, and this is the other one. Melvin-Koushki is precise about his standing: besides [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]], **Ḥamūya is Ibn Turka's only other identified source**, a Kubrawi shaykh and Ibn ʿArabī's Iranian contemporary **whose oeuvre is even more centrally lettrist, and even more slippery** (*Being with a Capital B*, 10). Elsewhere the two together are named **Ibn Turka's favourite lettrist source**
(*Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 6).

That pairing is the point. Akbarian metaphysics alone does not produce an operative science of letters; it produces a metaphysics of [[divine-names|names]]. Ḥamūya supplies the half where letters are already the centre of the enterprise rather than a consequence of it.

## Too rigid in his lettrism

The detail that makes him vivid: Ḥamūya **went so far as to personally criticize Ibn ʿArabī in a letter as being too rigid in his lettrism** (*Being with a Capital B*, 10 and n.6).

Read that from Ibn Turka's position. The two authorities behind his science were not in agreement, and their disagreement was about **method in the very discipline he was systematising** — one of them thinking the other insufficiently free with it. An heir who inherits a quarrel has to adjudicate it, and the fourfold analysis of the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] can be read as an adjudication: a scheme rigorous enough to satisfy the systematiser and capacious enough to hold what the free player was doing.

## Jazz philosophers, and a philosopher of jazz

Melvin-Koushki's formulation for the relationship is deliberately unexpected and worth quoting: what the critique makes clear is that **both Ibn ʿArabī and Ḥamūya can be usefully read as jazz philosophers — and Ibn Turka, their systematizing and Pythagoreanizing lettrist heir, as a philosopher of jazz** (*Being with a Capital B*, 10).

The distinction is exact and it is the best short account of what Ibn Turka did. His predecessors *improvised* on the letters — Ḥamūya's stylings are described as **radically free-playing, Mind-manifesting**, riffing on the visual and the aural simultaneously. Ibn Turka did not improvise. He wrote the theory of the improvisation: what the changes are, why they work, and what makes a run of them right rather than merely striking. A philosopher *of* jazz is not a jazz musician, and the difference is the whole of his originality.

## Where he sits in the canon

A later lettrist genealogy preserved through Kāshifī's works lists the canonical authorities in order: [[al-ghazali|Abū Ḥāmid Ghazālī]] (d. 1111), Fakhr al-Dīn Rāzī (d. 1210), **Aḥmad al-Būnī** (d. between 1225 and 1233), **Ibn al-ʿArabī** (d. 1240), **Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya** (d. 1252), Ibn Tamīmī al-Yāfiʿī (d. 1367), **[[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Ḥusayn Akhlātī]]** (d. 1397), Abū Yaʿqūb al-Kūmī (fl. 1407), **Ibn Turka** (d. 1432), and Yaʿqūb Charkhī (*Qizilbash Magic*, 4).

Two things stand out. Ibn Turka appears in it as a canonical authority — the tradition itself placed him in the line, whatever modern reception did. And Ghazālī heads the list, which sits oddly against his place in the [[peripatetic-philosophy|anti-occultist coalition]]: later lettrists claimed him as a predecessor whether or not he would have accepted the role.

## The dissertation's treatment

Chapter 4 of *The Quest* gives him a section of his own, §4.1.2.3, between al-Būnī and letter magic (§4.1.2.1) and Ibn ʿArabī and letter theory (§4.1.2.2) on one side, and — unexpectedly — **§4.1.3, Ibn Sīnā's philosophical lettrism**, on the other. Even the arch-opponent turns out to have a lettrism worth a section.

## What we do not know

- **Which of his works Ibn Turka used**, and in what form.
- **What the letter criticising Ibn ʿArabī actually argued** beyond the charge of rigidity.
- **How much of the Kubrawi context** came with the doctrine; the order's own lettrist tradition is not detailed in the corpus in hand.
- His oeuvre is described as **slippery**, which is a warning about attribution as much as about style.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Being with a Capital B*, 10 and n.6.
Melvin-Koushki, *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 6.
Melvin-Koushki, *Qizilbash Magic*, 4.
Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), §4.1.2.3.

figures.name: Al-Ghazali
figures.name_full: Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-Ghazālī
figures.card: **Abū Ḥāmid al-Ghazālī** (1058–1111). Theologian-philosopher whose *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* reconciled Sufi mysticism with Islamic orthodoxy. For this portal his importance is **adversarial, not enabling**: Melvin-Koushki lists him among the anti-occultist polemicists — with Ibn Sīnā, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Khaldūn — whose four centuries of attack on the 'strange sciences' is precisely what Ibn Turka's mathematicalization of the occult sciences was built to answer.
figures.body:
**Abū Ḥāmid Muḥammad al-Ghazālī** (1058–1111), born in Tus, taught at the Niẓāmiyya of Baghdad before a spiritual crisis drove him from public life into mystical retreat. His *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* argued that reason has limits, that mystical knowledge (*dhawq*, 'tasting') is genuine knowledge, and that Islamic intellectual life requires both. It became one of the most widely copied books in Islamic history, and the reconciliation it effected between Sufism and orthodoxy shaped everything after it.

**Why he appears in a portal on Ibn Turka — and why not for the reason one expects.** It is tempting to cast Ghazālī as the figure who cleared space for later occultists by vindicating mystical knowledge. Melvin-Koushki's account does not support that reading. He places Ghazālī squarely in the **anti-occultist camp**, observing that hostility to the *ʿulūm al-gharība* is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā, theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn find common cause — a camp further boasting al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār (*Powers of One*, 1).

**The consequence.** Ghazālī belongs to the four centuries of polemic that Ibn Turka's generation had to answer, not to the resources it drew on. Vindicating mystical experience is not the same as vindicating an operative science of letters, and Ghazālī did the first while attacking the second. This is what makes the [[neoplatonism|move into the mathematical sciences]] necessary rather than merely elegant: the occultists needed ground that Ghazālī's own arguments could not reach. Reading him as an enabler obscures the very problem Ibn Turka set out to solve.

## Why the correction matters beyond this entry

An earlier version of this page had Ghazālī enabling later occultists by vindicating
mystical knowledge. That is a natural reading and it is wrong, and the reason it is wrong is
worth stating because the same mistake is easy to make elsewhere in this material.

**Vindicating mystical experience is not the same as vindicating an operative science.**
Ghazālī argued that *dhawq* — direct experiential knowledge — is genuine knowledge, and that
reason has limits. Both claims are useful to a later occultist, and Ibn Turka's tradition
does draw on the space they opened. But Ghazālī himself drew the opposite conclusion about
the occult sciences, and Melvin-Koushki places him in the **anti-occultist camp**: hostility
to the *ʿulūm al-gharība* is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā,
theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn
find common cause, joined by al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār
(*Powers of One*, 1).

## The size of the opposition

That list is the point of this entry. It is not a fringe of hostile jurists; it is the
mainstream of Islamic intellectual life across four centuries and every major discipline —
philosophy, theology, traditionism, historiography, and the two great schools of *kalām*.
Anti-occultism was the common ground on which figures who agreed about almost nothing else
could stand together.

Understanding that changes how Ibn Turka's project reads. He was not defending a
comfortable orthodoxy against cranks. He was attempting to move a body of disciplines out of a
category in which the entire prestige structure of his tradition had placed them — which is
why the answer had to be [[pythagorean-cosmology|jurisdictional]] rather than merely
argumentative. Persuading this coalition on its own terms was not available; reclassifying
the sciences into a field whose credentials it did not dispute was.

## What Ghazālī does supply

The *Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn* remains one of the most widely copied books in Islamic history, and
the settlement it effected between Sufism and orthodoxy is the intellectual weather every
later figure works in — including Ibn Turka, whose relations with [[sufism|organised Sufism]]
are conducted inside a framework Ghazālī largely built. The debt is real. It is simply not a
debt about the occult sciences.

## What we do not know

- **What Ghazālī says specifically about lettrism**, as against the occult sciences
  generally, is not detailed in the corpus in hand.
- **Whether Ibn Turka answers him by name** anywhere in the unedited works.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.

figures.name: Suhrawardi
figures.name_full: Shihab al-Din Yahya ibn Habash al-Suhrawardi
figures.card: **Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi** (1154–1191). Founder of Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) philosophy. Synthesized Neoplatonic emanationism with Islamic theology, emphasizing direct mystical intuition (*ishraq*; illumination) of divine light and angelic powers. Executed in Aleppo for his teachings. His system profoundly influenced later Islamic philosophers and occultists, including Ibn Turka, who adopted Illuminationist vocabulary and framework to ground lettrist doctrine.
figures.body:
**Shihab al-Din Yahya al-Suhrawardi** (1154–1191), known as Shaykh al-Ishraq (Master of Illumination), was born in Suhrawardi, Persian Azerbaijan. He became the founder of the Illuminationist (*Ishraqi*) school of Islamic philosophy—a synthesis of Neoplatonic emanationism, Islamic theology, and visionary mysticism. Suhrawardi's key innovation: reality unfolds through levels of light. The divine is pure light (*nur*); creation emanates downward through successively dimmer grades of illumination; each level manifests divine attributes. Crucially, knowledge of these levels is not rational inference but direct mystical intuition (*ishraq*—illumination, sudden gnosis). In Suhrawardi's system, the soul possesses the capacity for immediate perception of intelligible forms, celestial beings, and divine light. This is not imagination but genuine knowledge. Suhrawardi was executed in Aleppo in 1191, likely for heterodox teachings. Yet his influence proved immense: Illuminationism became the dominant philosophical framework for later Islamic thinkers. Ibn Arabi adopted Illuminationist language; Qunavi built on it; Safavid philosophers canonized it. For Ibn Turka, Suhrawardi's framework was essential: the doctrine that reality manifests through levels of light, that the soul can directly perceive intelligible realities, and that mystical intuition is genuine knowledge—all this authorized Ibn Turka's claim that letters are cosmic principles knowable through direct gnosis and operative through talismanic technique.

## What Illuminationism supplied

Two things Ibn Turka's project could not do without.

**First, the legitimation of non-discursive knowledge.** Suhrawardi's *ishrāq* is
illumination — knowledge that arrives by direct presence rather than by inference. Once
that is granted standing as knowledge rather than as private experience, the whole
[[walaya|category of sanctified knowing]] has a philosophical basis, and a science that
claims access unavailable to ordinary reasoning is not thereby disqualified.

**Second, a graded cosmos of light.** Reality as hierarchies of luminosity, each level
receiving from the one above, gives the framework in which
[[barzakh|an intermediate domain]] is a natural feature rather than an ad-hoc addition. The
*Kitāb al-Nūr* takes up this vocabulary directly.

## The synthesis he made possible

The *Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid* is described as a synthesis of **Ibn Sīnā, Suhrawardī and Ibn
ʿArabī/Qūnavī on the topic of absolute being** (*The Quest*, 6). Those three names are the
three available philosophical positions of the period — peripatetic, illuminationist,
Akbarian — and the fact that Ibn Turka is credited with reconciling them is precisely what
earned him his modern reputation as a mystical philosopher.

The portal's argument is that the reconciliation was **preliminary work**. Having shown that
the three could be held together, he went on to argue that all three are superseded by a
fourth thing. The synthesis is the platform, not the achievement.

## The precedent of his death

Suhrawardi was executed at Aleppo in 1191, at around thirty-six, for teachings judged
dangerous. For a fifteenth-century philosopher working on the boundary of the permissible,
this is not distant history but the field's standing warning. Ibn Turka faced three
tribunals and an exile; the tradition he drew on had a martyr in it, and everyone concerned
knew it.

## What we do not know

- **How directly Ibn Turka read Suhrawardi**, as against receiving Illuminationism through
  later commentators, is not established in these sources.
- The precise charges against Suhrawardi at Aleppo are outside this corpus.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 50-80.

figures.name: Jandi
figures.card: **ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th c.). Persian philosopher-mystic; student of Qunavi and successor in Illuminationist tradition. Elaborated the correspondence between divine names, letters, and cosmic principles. His commentaries on Ibn Arabi and development of divine-names epistemology became foundational to later Islamic occultism. Ibn Turka inherited and systematized Jandi's framework through the Qunavi-Jandi school tradition.
figures.body:
**ʿAbd al-Razzaq al-Jandī** (fl. 13th century) was a Persian philosopher-mystic active in the post-Suhrawardi era. He is best known as a leading figure in the Qunavi-Jandi school tradition—the intellectual lineage that systematized Ibn Arabi's metaphysics for transmission to later generations. Where Qunavi had codified Ibn Arabi, Jandi extended and elaborated. His central contribution was developing the correspondence between divine names (*asmaʾ*), cosmic principles, and the structure of knowledge itself. Jandi argued that the 99 divine names are not merely attributes of God but constitute the framework through which creation manifests and through which the human intellect understands reality. Each name is a lens through which to perceive divine and created being. This doctrine proved transformative for later occultists: Ibn Turka adopted Jandi's framework and radicalized it by mapping the divine names onto the 28 Arabic letters, thereby making lettrism the operative expression of Jandi's metaphysics. Through Jandi, Ibn Turka inherited two centuries of Islamic philosophical synthesis: Ibn Arabi's metaphysics → Qunavi's systematization → Jandi's elaboration → Ibn Turka's operationalization.

## The elaboration, and why it mattered downstream

If [[qunavi|Qūnavī]] made Akbarian metaphysics arguable, Jandī extended it in the direction
that lettrism would need: toward **correspondence**.

The doctrine of [[divine-names|divine names]] as the structure of manifestation invites an
obvious question — if creation unfolds through named attributes, what else is ordered by the
same set? Jandī's development, as the portal receives it through Melvin-Koushki's account of
the school, presses the names into relation with the faculties of the knower and the levels
of the cosmos, so that the same enumeration organises God, world and soul.

That is the structural precondition for [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]. A correspondence system
with the divine names on one side has an empty slot on the other, and Ibn Turka fills it
with the twenty-eight letters. The move looks bold and is, but it is made into a framework
already built to accept it.

## The chain, stated plainly

The portal's genealogy runs: **Ibn ʿArabī → Qūnavī → Jandī → [[saad-al-din-hamuyya|Ḥamūya]]
→ Ibn Turka**, with [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] holding the Akbarian line together
with the al-Būnī line in a single teaching at Cairo. Jandī is the least visible link and one
of the more consequential, because his is the step at which a metaphysics of names becomes a
system of correspondences.

## What we do not know

- **His dates are not fixed** in these sources beyond a floruit in the thirteenth century.
- **Which of his works Ibn Turka used**, and whether directly or through intermediaries, is
  not established.
- The account of his contribution here is **synthesised from the school's shape** rather
  than from a passage in the corpus describing it; treat it as MEDIUM confidence.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism and Imaginal Ontology.

figures.name: Mulla Sadra
figures.card: **Mullā Ṣadrā** (1571–1635), the most celebrated philosopher of Safavid Iran, conventionally named as the terminus of the line running from Ibn ʿArabī through Ibn Turka. **This portal keeps the entry short on purpose.** Ṣadrā appears twice in the forty-three sources it is built on, and the Safavid heir the scholarship actually documents is [[mir-damad|Mīr Dāmād]].
figures.body:
## Why this entry is deliberately short

Mullā Ṣadrā is the most famous philosopher of Safavid Iran and appears in almost every account of Ibn Turka's afterlife. He is also **barely present in this portal's corpus**: a search across all forty-three Melvin-Koushki sources returns **two hits**.

The style guide for these pages sets a floor of 2,500 words and names exactly one acceptable reason to fall short — that the corpus genuinely does not hold more — with the requirement that the page then say so. This is that case, and this is it saying so. Writing five pages on Mullā Ṣadrā here would mean writing from general knowledge rather than from the research this portal is a reading of, which is the one thing these entries are not permitted to do.

## Where the Ṣadrā association comes from

Not from the lettrism. It comes from the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]], whose fame produced the standard picture of Ibn Turka as a **mystical-scholastic thinker lodged unobtrusively somewhere between Naṣīr al-Dīn Ṭūsī (d. 672/1274) and Mullā Ṣadrā (d. 1050/1640)** (*The Quest*, 6).

That framing is precisely what the dissertation exists to dislodge. Being acclaimed as the link between [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] and Mullā Ṣadrā is identified as **the cause of his marginalisation**, since it obscures the occultist tenor of the larger project and abstracts it from its historical context. So the Ṣadrā connection is real, and it is also the specific piece of received opinion this portal is arguing against.

## Who the documented successor is instead

[[mir-damad|Mīr Dāmād]] (d. 1631), with 135 corpus hits and an article substantially devoted to him. He is held largely responsible for the neopythagoreanization of Safavid philosophy, through adherence to a particular brand of Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu philosophical lettrism in at least three of his works — a transmission described in the vocabulary of Ibn Turka's own science rather than in the vocabulary of *wujūd*.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Mullā Ṣadrā engaged Ibn Turka's lettrist works** at all. The sources in hand do not say, and the question is worth someone's attention.
- **What the two corpus mentions contain** beyond situating him as the later terminus of a philosophical line.
- Anything about his own occult-scientific commitments, if he had them — a question Melvin-Koushki's framing of Safavid philosophy makes newly interesting.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 6.
Melvin-Koushki, *World as (Arabic) Text*, on Mīr Dāmād as the documented Safavid lettrist.

figures.name: Ismail I
figures.card: Shah Ismail I (1487–1524), founder of Safavid dynasty. Established Twelver Shi'ism as state religion of Persia. Created court environment that canonized Ibn Turka's intellectual tradition. Safavid support transformed Ibn Turka from Isfahan Circle figure to foundational voice of Islamic philosophy.
figures.body:
Shah Ismail I founded the Safavid dynasty and established Twelver Shi'ism as Persia's state religion. Under Safavid rule, the intellectual networks and traditions established by Ibn Turka achieved institutional stability and court patronage. Ismail's successors, particularly Abbas I, canonized Ibn Turka's works and the Ibn Turka tradition became central to Safavid intellectual establishment. The Safavid court provided resources, protection, and legitimacy for occult philosophers. This political context enabled the transmission of Ibn Turka's system from 15th-century innovation to 16th-17th century canonical status.

## What the dynasty changed for this material

Ismāʿīl's establishment of Twelver Shiʿism as the state religion of Persia is the political
event that turns Ibn Turka's confessional ambiguity from normal into awkward.

The portal argues at [[imamophilism|imamophilism]] that his position — deep reverence for the
Imams held without the juridical commitments of Twelver Shiʿism — was **a defining feature of
9th/15th-century Islamic religiosity**, particularly in Iran and particularly in esotericist
circles. That is a description of a world in which the boundary was soft.

Ismāʿīl hardened it. After 1501 a Persian scholar is Shiʿi or he is a problem, and the
category Ibn Turka actually occupied stops being available. Every subsequent attempt to
classify him — Corbin's "standard-issue Shiʿi esotericist", Lewisohn's "orthodox Sunni Sufi
thinker" — is an attempt to sort a pre-Safavid figure into post-Safavid boxes.

## The reception the dynasty made possible

The Safavid century is also when the science arrived. Melvin-Koushki's account of Safavid
philosophy has it turning **neopythagorean** — a turn few specialists have admitted — with
occult science as the principal mode in which that philosophy was lived as an imperial way of
life. [[mir-damad|Mīr Dāmād]] is the figure held largely responsible, through his adherence
to **Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu philosophical lettrism** (*World as (Arabic) Text*).

So the dynasty that made Ibn Turka hard to classify is the same dynasty in which his
discipline became establishment philosophy. Both things follow from the same consolidation.

## The Ṣafaviyya connection, and its irony

[[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]] — the associate whose company got Ibn Turka
[[exiled-from-herat|exiled from Herat in 1427]] — was a **propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya
order**, the movement that would become this dynasty. Ibn Turka was expelled for association
with the ancestors of the house under which his science would later flourish.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ismāʿīl or his court knew of Ibn Turka** specifically is not established in these
  sources; the transmission is traced at the level of the tradition.
- His dates here follow the standard reign chronology rather than a corpus passage.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.

figures.name: Ulugh Beg
figures.name_full: Muḥammad Ṭaraghay Ulugh Beg b. Shāhrukh
figures.card: **Ulugh Beg** (1394–1449), Shāhrukh's son, governor of Transoxiana and founder of the **Samarkand Observatory** — by a distance the most famous Timurid for history-of-science purposes. He was styled *al-sulṭān al-faylasūf*, the philosopher-sultan. For Ibn Turka he is the **would-be third patron**: the one ruler whose programme — the mathematicalization of the sciences — was the same programme, and whose patronage never quite arrived.
figures.body:
## Ulugh Beg: the patron who should have been

**The sultan-scientist.** Muḥammad Ṭaraghay Ulugh Beg (1394–1449), Temür's grandson and Shāhrukh's son, governed Transoxiana from Samarkand and did something no other Timurid did: he practised the science he patronised. He founded the Samarkand Observatory, breaking ground in 1420, and the *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* produced there stood as the most accurate star table in the world for two centuries. He was awarded the title *al-sulṭān al-faylasūf* — the philosopher-sultan (Fazlıoğlu, *Mathematical-Astronomical School*, 41; on the observatory and the *zīj*, Blake, *Astronomy and Astrology*, ch. 6).
