**Why he belongs in Ibn Turka's story.** Melvin-Koushki's argument makes the connection structural rather than incidental. His thesis is that the occult sciences in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran were **moved out of the natural sciences and into the mathematical sciences** to reassert their legitimacy — and that this mathematicalization is the immediate context for *the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the members of the Samarkand Observatory* (*Powers of One*, 1). Ulugh Beg's observatory and Ibn Turka's [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] are not two subjects that happen to share a century. They are two faces of one movement: the conviction that number is the ground on which a science must stand.

He names the pairing directly — *the model established by Iskandar Sulṭān and Ulugh Beg* ensured that astronomy-astrology and lettrism **in particular** would continue to be heavily patronised by subsequent Timurid and Indo-Timurid dynasts, and by their Safavid and Ottoman competitors (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599). Ibn Turka's first patron and his would-be last are the two poles of that model.

**The would-be.** The sequence of Ibn Turka's patrons is a sequence of losses. [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]], who commissioned *Of Letters* and at whose instance he began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]], was defeated and blinded in 1415. Under Shāhrukh he found a place — he was close to Bāysunghur in particular — and then in **1427 was exiled from Herat**, alongside his old Cairo associate Qāsim-i Anvār, the official excuse being a putative connection with the Ḥurūfīs (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

Samarkand was the obvious remaining door, and the right one. A ruler who had staked his reputation on mathematical astronomy was the natural patron for a man arguing that the occult sciences belong among the mathematical sciences. Ibn Turka died in 1432, seventeen years before Ulugh Beg was killed by his own son's faction in 1449. The patronage that would have made the most sense of his career is the one the record does not show him receiving.

**Afterlife.** The lettrist-astronomical fusion Ulugh Beg's institution made possible outlived them both. Shāhjahān commissioned the *Zīj-i Shāhjahānī*, an updated and corrected version of Ulugh Beg's tables of two centuries prior — and it carries **the first preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be explicitly and thoroughgoingly lettrist in tenor** (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599). Ibn Turka's science reached Ulugh Beg's star tables in the end. It simply took two hundred years.

## The title, and what it was awarded for

Ulugh Beg was styled **al-sulṭān al-faylasūf**, the philosopher-sultan (Fazlıoğlu,
*Mathematical-Astronomical School*, 41, cited in *Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*,
3 n.9). The title is not flattery of the ordinary courtly kind. Melvin-Koushki's study of
Timurid and Mughal rulers is titled *Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists* precisely
because a small number of these men **practised the disciplines they patronised**, and
Ulugh Beg is the clearest case: he computed.

The distinction matters for how his relationship to Ibn Turka should be imagined. A patron
who funds astronomy needs to be persuaded that astronomy is worth funding. A patron who
does the arithmetic himself needs to be persuaded that the arithmetic is *right*. The
second is a harder audience and a better one, and it is the audience Ibn Turka's
[[occult-science-universal|mathematicalized]] science was built for.

## Why the observatory belongs to this portal

The conventional division of labour treats Samarkand as a triumph of exact science and
Timurid occultism as an embarrassment to be handled separately. Melvin-Koushki's thesis
denies the division outright. The mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and
sanctification of occultism in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is, he argues, **the
immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context** for the celebrated mathematization of
astronomy by the members of the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]] — processes
which have **heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation** (*Powers of One*, 1).

The chronology makes the point concrete. The observatory broke ground in 1420. The
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] was completed in 823/1420. Two foundations laid in
one year, a few hundred miles apart, by men acting on the same conviction: that a science
earns its standing by becoming mathematical.

There is also a personal link. [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]], second director of the
observatory, had spent twenty-five years in the same schoolroom as Ibn Turka, taught by Ibn
Turka's own brother. The two institutions share a classroom.

## The model, named

Melvin-Koushki treats Ibn Turka's first patron and his would-be last as a matched pair.
**The model established by [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] and Ulugh Beg** ensured that
astronomy-astrology and lettrism **in particular** would continue to be heavily patronised
by subsequent Timurid and Indo-Timurid dynasts, as well as by their Safavid and Ottoman
competitors (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599).

That sentence is the reason the "would-be third patron" framing is structural rather than
sentimental. Ibn Turka's career opens under one pole of the model and ends within reach of
the other, and the model outlives them all.

## The coda

Two centuries later Shāhjahān — self-proclaimed Second Lord of Conjunction, after Tīmūr the
First — commissioned for his accession the ***Zīj-i Shāhjahānī***, an updated and corrected
version of Ulugh Beg's star tables. Tellingly, it carries **the first preface in the
Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be explicitly and thoroughgoingly lettrist in
tenor** (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599).

The same feature appears in the preface to the *Sirr-i Akbar*, Dārā Shukūh's celebrated
Persian translation of the Upaniṣads. The letter science reached the star tables in the
end; it simply took until the seventeenth century, and Ibn Turka was not there for it.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka ever sought Ulugh Beg's patronage directly** is not documented. The
  "would-be" framing rests on the structural fit and the absence of any record of
  patronage, not on a recorded approach and refusal.
- **Which conjunction** the observatory's own astrological work took as its frame is outside
  these sources.
- The observatory was **abandoned and dismantled** after Ulugh Beg's murder in 1449; its
  foundations were not rediscovered until 1908, so the physical record is largely lost.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 456.
Blake, Stephen P. *Astronomy and Astrology in the Islamic World*, ch. 6.

figures.name: Iskandar Sulṭān
figures.name_full: Iskandar b. ʿUmar Shaykh b. Tīmūr
figures.card: **Iskandar Sulṭān** (1384–1415), Temür's grandson and ruler of Fars — Ibn Turka's first and most consequential patron. He commissioned *Of Letters*, and it was almost certainly at his instance that Ibn Turka began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]]. His court was famous for astrological and occult patronage on a scale that set a model; Shāhrukh marched against him in 817/1414; he fled, was captured and blinded, and was executed afterwards — removing Ibn Turka's protection at a stroke.
figures.body:
**Iskandar Sulṭān b. ʿUmar Shaykh** (1384–1415) ruled Fars from Shiraz and Isfahan as one of the most lavishly bookish and most astrologically preoccupied of the Timurid princes. His patronage is directly responsible for Ibn Turka's two central lettrist works: he commissioned *Of Letters*, and Melvin-Koushki judges that Ibn Turka began the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] shortly afterward, again almost certainly at Iskandar's instance (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

The relationship matters beyond biography. Melvin-Koushki names *the model established by Iskandar Sulṭān and [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]]* as what ensured astronomy-astrology and lettrism in particular would go on being heavily patronised by later Timurid, Indo-Timurid, Safavid and Ottoman courts (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599). Iskandar is the opening term of the pattern that defines the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]].

He rebelled against [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]], who marched against him in Iraq in **817/1414**; Iskandar fled, was captured and blinded, and was executed afterwards, [[baysunghur|his cousin]]'s brother Ibrāhīm Sulṭān being installed in his place (*The Quest*, chronology). An earlier version of this entry compressed that sequence into a single date of 1415; the defeat and blinding belong to 1414. For Ibn Turka the consequence was immediate and lasting: the patron who had commissioned his life's work became, retroactively, a dangerous association — the first of the reversals that would culminate in his exile from Herat in 1427.

**What kind of patron he was.** Iskandar is accounted **the leading Timurid patron of culture in the early Shahrukhid period**, with a particular interest in alchemy and in astrological and astronomical illustrated works, and he was known for his [[imamophilism|imamophilism]] and esotericist bent (*The Quest*, §3.1). He was not a generic prince who happened to employ an occultist; he was looking for one.

**The hereditary judgeship.** Iskandar was presumably responsible for installing Ibn Turka in his **hereditary** office as *qāḍī* of Isfahan — an office established to the Turka family by **Tīmūr himself**, on his appointment of Ibn Turka's elder brother and teacher [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] as *qāḍī* in Samarkand (*The Quest*, §3.1). The judgeship Ibn Turka held, and later lost, was a family possession granted at the founding of the dynasty.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), chronology.

figures.name: Shāhrukh
figures.card: **Shāhrukh** (r. 1405–1447), Tīmūr's son and the ruler under whom Ibn Turka spent almost his entire career. He is not a background figure: he **destroyed Ibn Turka's first patron**, later **received him back into favour**, and his court was the venue of the accusations that ended in exile. In 813/1411 he abrogated the Mongol *yasa* in favour of the sharīʿa and closed the taverns — the turn toward public piety that made an occult philosopher's position permanently precarious.
figures.body:
## Shāhrukh: the ruler who made and unmade him

**Muʿīn al-Dīn Shāhrukh b. Tīmūr** (1377–1447) succeeded to the eastern half of his father's empire and ruled from Herat for forty-two years. By 815/1412 his control was established over Khurasan, Transoxania and Khwarazm. Almost the whole of Ibn Turka's adult career runs inside his reign, and the relationship between them turns twice.

**The pious turn.** In 813/1410 Shāhrukh completed a madrasa-khānaqāh complex at Herat and appointed its teachers. In **813/1411 he declared the abrogation of *yasa* law, enforced the sharīʿa, and closed the taverns** (*The Quest*, chronology). Replacing Mongol customary law with Islamic law was a deliberate re-founding of Timurid legitimacy on religious rather than steppe grounds — and it set the terms on which a man like Ibn Turka would afterwards be judged. A court that has staked its authority on orthodoxy is a dangerous employer for an occultist.

**The destruction of Iskandar.** In 817/1414 Shāhrukh marched against [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] in Iraq. Iskandar fled, was captured and blinded, and was executed afterwards; Shāhrukh replaced him with his own son Ibrāhīm Sulṭān. Ibn Turka had been attached to Iskandar's brilliant Isfahan court in 815–17/1412–14, and had already withdrawn to Shiraz because of what the chronology calls harassment by envious individuals, putting forward his protégé Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb to replace him as *qāḍī*. From 817 to 825 (1414–22) he attempted to retire from public life (*The Quest*, chronology).

**The turn back.** Around 825/1422 his opponents went to Shāhrukh's court at Herat and accused him of **Sufi bias**. Ibn Turka travelled to Herat to clear his name, **gained Shāhrukh's favour, and was given the judgeship of Yazd** (*The Quest*, chronology). This is the first of the tribunals, and he won it — by going in person to the ruler who had destroyed his previous patron, and persuading him.

**And the turn away again.** It did not hold. In 1427 Ibn Turka was exiled from Herat along with [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], the official pretext being a putative connection with the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfīs]] (*The Quest*, 456 n.16). The same court that had vindicated him five years earlier expelled him.

**Why he matters to the argument.** Shāhrukh is the counterweight to the reading of the Timurid century as straightforwardly hospitable to the occult sciences. His son [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] built the observatory and his son [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]] ran the finest book-workshop in the world, but Shāhrukh himself governed through public piety, and the pressure Ibn Turka lived under came from his court. Patronage and prosecution were the same institution.

## What the abrogation of the yasa actually did

The single most consequential act of the reign, for this portal's purposes, is dated
813/1411: **Shāhrukh declares the abrogation of *yasa* law, enforces the sharīʿa, and closes
the taverns** (*The Quest*, chronology).

The *yasa* is the Mongol customary law code attributed to Chinggis Khan, and it had been the
juridical backbone of Chinggisid and early Timurid legitimacy. Abrogating it in favour of
Islamic law is a re-founding: it moves the basis of the dynasty's authority from steppe
descent to religious orthodoxy. The taverns are the visible sign of a policy whose real
content is jurisprudential.

For a man in Ibn Turka's position the consequences are structural rather than immediate. A
court that has staked its legitimacy on public piety acquires (a) an interest in being seen
to police doctrine, (b) a class of religious officials whose standing rises with that
policing, and (c) a vocabulary in which professional rivalry can be conducted as
accusation. All three appear in the tribunals of the 1420s.

## The absolutism argument

Melvin-Koushki sets Shāhrukh against his nephew in a comparison with unusual force: **if the
rise of absolutist politics is one of the benchmarks for early modernity, in 816/1412
Shāhrukh was the last medieval Islamic ruler, and Mīrzā Iskandar was the first early modern
absolutist sovereign** (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 21, citing his own "Eschatological
Absolutism").

Read alongside the *yasa* abrogation, this produces a coherent picture. Shāhrukh's answer
to the legitimacy problem was **conservative and juridical** — govern as a Muslim sovereign
under the sharīʿa. [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar's]] was **eschatological and absolutist** —
claim a sacred role in the unfolding of history, with occultists and philosophers as the
staff who could articulate it. Ibn Turka's science fits the second programme and not the
first, and Iskandar lost.

## The three turns

The relationship reverses twice, and the pattern is the point.

1. **817/1414 — destruction.** Shāhrukh marches against Iskandar in Iraq; Iskandar flees, is
   captured and blinded, and is executed afterwards. Ibn Turka's patron and the
   commissioner of his central works becomes a dangerous association.
2. **c. 825/1422 — vindication.** His opponents go to Shāhrukh's court at Herat and accuse
   him of **Sufi bias**. He travels there to answer in person, **gains Shāhrukh's favour,
   and is given the judgeship of Yazd**. He argued in front of the man who had destroyed his
   patron, and won.
3. **1427 — exile.** He is expelled from Herat with [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], the
   official excuse a putative [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] connection.

And then a fourth movement that is neither: from 1429 he cannot get a hearing at all. A
fruitless attempt at Simnan, a promise of reinstatement at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa around 834/1430, and
**nine months of weekly attendance at Herat** waiting on a review that never came.

## The court as an institution

Shāhrukh completed a madrasa-khānaqāh complex at Herat in 813/1410 and appointed its
teachers; by 815/1412 his control was established over Khurasan, Transoxania and Khwarazm.
His sons ran the century's two most important cultural enterprises —
[[baysunghur|Bāysunghur's]] *kitābkhāna* and [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg's]]
[[samarkand-observatory|observatory]]. The reign is not hostile to learning; it is hostile
to a particular claim about where authority over knowledge lies.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Shāhrukh personally decided any of the three turns** or simply ratified the
  outcome of factional pressure is not recoverable from these sources.
- **The identity of most of the opponents** is unrecorded; only Muḥammad al-Jazarī, who died
  at Herat in 833/1429, is named as a powerful one.
- **Why the 825/1422 vindication did not hold** is not explained in the chronology.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), chronology and 456.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Imperial Talismanic Love*.

figures.name: Ṣadr al-Dīn Turka
figures.card: **Ṣadr al-Dīn Turka**, Ibn Turka's elder brother and his teacher for the first twenty-five years of his life — alongside a fellow student who would become [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]. An eminent scholar of hadith, tafsīr, jurisprudence and *uṣūl al-dīn*. Ibn Turka's own verdict on this education is pointed: his brother taught nothing beyond the outward sciences.
figures.body:
**Ṣadr al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī** was the elder brother of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn and an eminent scholar in hadith, Qur'anic exegesis, jurisprudence and the principles of religion. Ibn Turka studied under him **for the first twenty-five years of his life — and so did [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** (*The Quest*, ch. 1). That single fact reorganises the [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]]: its lettrist and its mathematician were not colleagues who found each other at court but schoolfellows, taught side by side in the same household for a quarter of a century.

**The verdict on the teaching.** Ibn Turka states that his brother taught nothing beyond the outward sciences (*al-ʿulūm al-ẓāhira*). It is a mild sentence with a great deal in it. The education was excellent and, by his own account, insufficient — a complete grounding in the exoteric disciplines that left the *bāṭin* untouched. Everything he later built can be read as the supply of what that education lacked.

**The family and the Ḥurūfīs.** Ḥurūfī sources record that both Ṣadr al-Dīn and their father Afżal al-Dīn sought out Fażl Allāh Astarābādī during his residence in Isfahan to have their dreams interpreted; Naṣr Allāh Nāfajī's *Khwābnāma* preserves Ṣadr al-Dīn's dream of kissing the Prophet's hand. Melvin-Koushki cautions that this implies no [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] inclination in either man — the story's purpose is to show Fażl Allāh's standing as a Sufi before his messianic turn. It nonetheless put a documented family contact with the founder of the Ḥurūfiyya on the record, and that record was available to Ibn Turka's prosecutors.

**The office that came with the name.** Ṣadr al-Dīn was appointed *qāḍī* in Samarkand **by Tīmūr himself**, and that appointment established the judgeship as a Turka family office — the hereditary post his younger brother would later occupy in Isfahan and lose in the tribunals (*The Quest*, §3.1). The family's standing with the dynasty predates Ibn Turka's own career by a generation.

**Why he taught only the outward sciences.** The dissertation gives his reason, and it is not ignorance: he deemed it **too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public** (*The Quest*, 41). The elder brother's caution and the younger brother's career are the same judgement about the same risk, answered in opposite directions — and the tribunals of the 1420s suggest Ṣadr al-Dīn had assessed it correctly.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), ch. 1.
Eichner, Heidrun. 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka.' *Encyclopaedia of Islam*, THREE.

figures.name: Bāysunghur
figures.card: **Bāysunghur b. Shāhrukh** (1397–1433), Timurid prince, governor, and the greatest book-patron of the age — his Herat *kitābkhāna* was the finest manuscript workshop in the world. The dissertation records Ibn Turka's **close relationship to Bāysunghur in particular** among the Timurid amirs. He is the middle term of the patron sequence between [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] and [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]].
figures.body:
**Ghiyāth al-Dīn Bāysunghur** (1397–1433), third son of [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]], was appointed governor of Mazandaran and western Khurasan in 818/1415 and is remembered above all as a patron of the book. The *kitābkhāna* he maintained at Herat gathered calligraphers, illuminators, painters and binders into the most accomplished manuscript workshop of the fifteenth century; he was himself a calligrapher of the first rank.

**The connection to Ibn Turka.** A survey of the *Munshaʾāt-i Ṣāʾin-i Turka* — Ibn Turka's collected letters — shows the frequency of his dealings with various Timurid amirs and **his close relationship to Bāysunghur in particular** (*The Quest*, 136). That the evidence comes from his own correspondence rather than from a chronicle makes it unusually direct.

**Why the pairing is apt.** Bāysunghur's interest was in how a page is *made*. Ibn Turka's science holds that the letter is an ontological entity before it is a written mark — that the shapes on the page participate in what they signify. A prince who cared about letterforms as craft and a philosopher who held letters to be cosmic principles had, unusually, a real subject in common.

**The sequence.** Bāysunghur sits between the patron who was destroyed ([[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar]], 1414) and the patron who never quite arrived ([[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]]). He died in 1433, a year after Ibn Turka. Of the three Timurid patrons the career offers, he is the one that simply worked — which is why he is the least dramatic and the easiest to overlook.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 136 and chronology.

figures.name: Qāsim-i Anvār
figures.name_full: Muʿīn al-Dīn ʿAlī Qāsim-i Anvār Tabrīzī
figures.card: **Qāsim-i Anvār** (c. 1356–1433), Sufi poet, propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya order, and Ibn Turka's charismatic associate from his Cairo days. **Exiled from Herat with him in 1427.** Claimed by Ismāʿīlīs as one of their own, suspected of Ḥurūfī ties: the friendship was a liability, and the record shows exactly what kind.
figures.body:
**Qāsim-i Anvār** was a Sufi poet of great popular reach and a propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya order — the movement that would, three generations later, become the Safavid dynasty. He and Ibn Turka knew each other from Cairo, and the dissertation calls him **Ṣāʾin al-Dīn's charismatic associate from his Cairo days** (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

**The liability.** Qāsim was apparently claimed by Ismāʿīlīs as one of their own, at a moment when that was a dangerous thing to be: [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] attempted a purge of Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415. In **1427 Qāsim was exiled from Herat, and Ibn Turka with him**, on account of such suspect connections — though the official excuse was his putative connection with the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfīs]] (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

The detail worth holding onto is that the stated charge and the operative reason were different. Ibn Turka was not expelled for a doctrine he held; he was expelled for a man he knew, under a label that would carry in court.

**Against the caricature of Ibn Turka the isolate.** His letters show friendly relations with a whole set of prominent Iranian Sufis — Shāh Niʿmat Allāh Valī, Qāsim-i Anvār, Aḥmad Samarqandī, Ḥasan ʿAṭṭār, Sayyid Muḥammad b. Shaykh Kajujī — which sits oddly beside the criticisms of organised [[sufism|Sufism]] he makes in his written work. Melvin-Koushki reads the tension as informative rather than contradictory: the first three of those men were great promoters of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] against often hostile reaction, and that is the likely point of attraction (*The Quest*, 136). He criticised the institution and kept the company.

## The company that cost him

The 1427 expulsion is the clearest case in the biography of a man being punished for an
association rather than a doctrine, and the mechanics deserve setting out.

Qāsim was **a propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya order** and was **apparently claimed by
Ismāʿīlīs as one of their own** (*The Quest*, 456 n.16). Neither is a doctrinal charge
against Ibn Turka; both are facts about someone he knew. And the timing made them dangerous:
[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] had attempted a **purge of Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415**, so the
label named an active security concern rather than a theological abstraction.

The stated charge was different again. What provided the **official excuse** was Qāsim's
**putative connection with the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfīs]]**. So the sequence runs: a real
association (Ṣafaviyya), an alleged one (Ismāʿīlī), and a third label used in the paperwork
(Ḥurūfī). Three different accusations, none of them about Ibn Turka's own work, producing
one exile.

## The corrective to the isolated-philosopher picture

His letters show friendly relations with a set of prominent Iranian Sufis — Shāh Niʿmat
Allāh Valī, Qāsim-i Anvār, Aḥmad Samarqandī, Ḥasan ʿAṭṭār, Sayyid Muḥammad b. Shaykh Kajujī —
which sits oddly beside his criticisms of organised [[sufism|Sufism]] in print, and beside
the admonitory role toward shaykhs he claims in the [[nafsat-al-masdur|apologies]].

Melvin-Koushki reads the tension as informative rather than hypocritical: the first three of
those men were **great promoters of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] in the face of often hostile
reaction**, which suggests the point of attraction (*The Quest*, 136). He criticised the
institution and kept the company, and the company was selected on doctrinal grounds.

## The long irony

The Ṣafaviyya became the Safavid dynasty. Ibn Turka was exiled for association with the
movement whose eventual state would host the [[mir-damad|neopythagorean turn]] in which his
own science became establishment philosophy.

## What we do not know

- **Where Qāsim went** after the 1427 expulsion, and whether he and Ibn Turka were together
  in exile.
- **Whether the Ismāʿīlī claim had any substance**, or was a hostile attribution.
- **Almost nothing of his poetry** is discussed in the sources in hand, though its popular
  reach is what made him worth denouncing.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 136 and 456.
Virani, Shafique. *The Ismailis in the Middle Ages*.

figures.name: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī
figures.card: **ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī** (d. 1454) — the Ottoman arm of the same project. Like Ibn Turka an intellectual heir of [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]], he built a universalist lettrist programme in the Ottoman context that Melvin-Koushki calls **cognate and more successful**. Whether the two men ever met during their long residences in Mamluk Cairo is unclear; that they were doing the same thing at opposite ends of the network is not.
figures.body:
## The other half of the network

**Who he is.** ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī (d. 858/1454) is the leading figure of the [[new-brethren-purity|Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ]] network in the Ottoman lands, and the closest thing Ibn Turka has to a counterpart. The dissertation names them together: the Isfahan Circle may be seen as the eastern arm of a larger network stretching to Anatolia via Cairo, and **they were both the intellectual heirs of Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī**, though it is unclear whether they met during their respective long residences in Mamluk Cairo (*The Quest*, 2).

**Why he matters to a portal about Ibn Turka.** Because of the comparative verdict. Melvin-Koushki describes the Ottoman projects — Bisṭāmī's above all — as **cognate and *more successful*** than Ibn Turka's (*The Quest*, ch. 1). The same programme, inherited from the same teacher, prospered in Anatolia while its Iranian version ended in three tribunals and an exile. That asymmetry is one of the sharpest questions the material raises, and it is a question about politics rather than about ideas.

**The scholarship.** The existence of this network as a network was **posited by İhsan Fazlıoğlu in a 1996 article**, and Melvin-Koushki states plainly that his own understanding of late medieval Islamic occult philosophy depends on the ongoing research of **Cornell Fleischer** and his Chicago Circle into the Ottoman branch. Logistically and conceptually the two networks are **largely coterminous**, so research on either has vital bearing on the whole complex (*The Quest*, ch. 1 n.87–88). Anyone reading this portal should know that half the story is being written by other people.

## The book that became state equipment

The concrete measure of the Ottoman branch's success is a single title. Bisṭāmī's
***Miftāḥ al-jafr al-jāmiʿ*** — the *Key to the Comprehensive Prognosticon* — **came to
function in the 10th/16th century as a dynastic handbook, whereby the political fate of the
House of ʿOs̱mān could be effectively managed over the generations** (*Another Scientific
Revolution*, 2).

Set that beside Ibn Turka's career. Same teacher, same science, same generation. One man's
[[jafr|jafr]] manual becomes an instrument of imperial governance consulted across
centuries; the other man is tried three times, exiled, and dies waiting on a case review
with half his work unedited.

Melvin-Koushki's judgement that the Ottoman projects were **cognate and more successful** is
not a vague comparative impression. This is what it refers to.

## What the asymmetry is actually about

Not doctrine. The inheritance from [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] was the same and the
two men's programmes are described as cognate. What differed was the state.

[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] had [[yasa-abrogated|refounded Timurid legitimacy on the sharīʿa]] in
813/1411 and elevated the class of men who interpret it — creating both the incentive and
the vocabulary for prosecuting an occult philosopher. The Ottoman court of the same decades
made room for exactly this kind of universalist project, and then institutionalised it.

The comparison is the strongest available argument that **Ibn Turka's fate was contingent
rather than deserved**: the same science, in a different polity, became a manual for running
an empire.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 2 and ch. 1 nn. 87–88.
Fazlıoğlu, İhsan. 'İlk Dönem Osmanlı İlim ve Kültür Hayatında İhvanu's-Safâ ve Abdurrahman Bistâmî' (1996).
Fleischer, Cornell. 'Ancient Wisdom and New Sciences: Prophecies at the Ottoman Court in the Fifteenth and Early Sixteenth Centuries.'

figures.name: Mīr Dāmād
figures.card: **Mīr Dāmād** (d. 1631), Twelver Shiʿi philosopher of Safavid Isfahan and — on Melvin-Koushki's argument — the man **largely responsible for the neopythagoreanization of Safavid philosophy**. He did it by adopting a particular brand of Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu philosophical [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] in at least three of his works. He is the documented link by which Ibn Turka's science reaches the seventeenth century, and the reason the tradition's chief opponent ends up inside it.
figures.body:
## Why this entry exists

The portal needs a Safavid successor, and for a long time the obvious candidate was [[mulla-sadra|Mullā Ṣadrā]]. The corpus does not support that: Ṣadrā appears twice in forty-three sources. **Mīr Dāmād appears 135 times**, and one article — *World as (Arabic) Text* — is substantially about him. He is the figure the scholarship actually puts in this position.

## The argument he is used to make

Melvin-Koushki's claim about Safavid philosophy has two halves, and the second is the contentious one.

The **Neoplatonic and perennialist-antiquarian** character of Safavid philosophy is, he grants, widely recognised by specialists. But few have admitted its **equally remarkable neopythagorean turn** — and the principal mode in which that neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy was lived as a Safavid imperial way of life, namely **occult science**, has been **completely ignored**, which makes a history of its practice impossible (*World as (Arabic) Text*, résumé).

That is a strong charge against a field: not that it has the emphasis wrong but that it has omitted the thing that would let the subject be studied at all.

## What he actually did

Mīr Dāmād is described as a **Twelver Shiʿi sage-mage**, known until recently as an occult scientist, and he is held **largely responsible for the neopythagoreanization of Safavid philosophy** — accomplished **through his adherence to a particular brand of Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu philosophical lettrism (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*) in at least three of his many works** (*World as (Arabic) Text*, résumé).

The hyphenated chain in that sentence is the whole transmission history compressed: **Mamluk** (Cairo, al-Būnī, [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]]), **Timurid** (Ibn Turka and the [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]]), **Aqquyunlu** (the Turkman courts between), arriving in Safavid Isfahan. Mīr Dāmād is the terminus, and what he inherited is identified by period rather than by person — a lineage, not a citation.

## The transmogrification of Ibn Sīnā

The most striking consequence, and the portal's favourite piece of irony: the neopythagoreanization Mīr Dāmād drove went as far as **the transmogrification of Ibn Sīnā himself into a neopythagorean occultist** (*World as (Arabic) Text*, résumé; *Powers of One*, 1).

Ibn Sīnā heads the [[peripatetic-philosophy|anti-occultist coalition]] — with [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]], Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Khaldūn — whose four centuries of polemic the [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematicalization]] was built to answer. Two centuries after Ibn Turka, the tradition's chief prosecutor had been posthumously enrolled in the defence. The reclassification did not merely survive its opponents; it absorbed the most formidable of them.

## What he settles about Ibn Turka

**That the project continued.** Melvin-Koushki calls this imperial neopythagorean lettrist crucial for understanding the **continuity** of the tradition. Ibn Turka died in an antechamber at Herat with half his work unedited, and it would be easy to read that as the end of the line. Mīr Dāmād is the evidence that it was not — the science reached the intellectual establishment of the next great Persian empire and helped define its philosophy.

**And that the win was posthumous.** Which is the shape of nearly everything in this biography: the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand tables]] carrying a lettrist preface under Shāhjahān, the [[bistami|Ottoman branch]] prospering while the Iranian one was tried, and now a Safavid philosopher completing the argument its author was exiled for.

## What we do not know

- **Which three works** the lettrist material appears in is not specified in the material in hand; *Mīr Dāmād's on Doffing* is the study to pursue.
- **Whether he read Ibn Turka directly.** The inheritance is identified as Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu lettrism, not as a citation of the *Mafāḥiṣ*.
- **His birth date** is not given in these sources.
- The claim that Safavid occult science has been *completely ignored* is Melvin-Koushki's assessment of a field, and other specialists may weigh it differently.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *World as (Arabic) Text* (BRILL, 2020), résumé and passim.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Mīr Dāmād's on Doffing*.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.

concepts.name: Abjad numerology
concepts.card: **Abjad numerology** (Hisab al-Jumul). The system assigning numerical values to Arabic letters (alif=1, bāʾ=2, etc.), allowing letters and words to be manipulated mathematically. Central to [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]: Ibn Turka used abjad values to establish correspondences between divine names, cosmic principles, and human faculties. Enables the calculation of ''operative words'' whose numerical sum aligns with specific celestial or talismanic purposes.
concepts.body:
## Abjad Numerology (Hisab al-Jumul)

The **abjad system** is an ancient method of letter-to-number correspondence in Arabic and Hebrew. Each of the 28 Arabic letters carries a numerical value:
- alif (a) = 1, bāʾ (b) = 2, jīm (j) = 3... up to ghīn (gh) = 1000

This allowed Arabic letters, words, and verses to be treated as mathematical entities. The sum of a word's letters yields a number; that number can be matched against cosmic cycles, divine names, or talismanic intent.

In Ibn Turka's system, abjad numerology becomes **the bridge between language and mathematics, between expression and causation**. By selecting or composing words whose abjad sum equals a specific number—say, the number corresponding to the planet Venus or to a particular divine name—one creates a linguistic-mathematical object that resonates with that principle. Written or chanted correctly, such a word becomes operative.

Example: the divine name al-ʿAlīm ("the All-Knowing") has a specific abjad value. A talisman inscribed with a word or phrase whose abjad value matches that of al-ʿAlīm would, in theory, embody the properties of divine knowledge and could be used to attract or enhance that quality.

Ibn Turka's genius was systematizing abjad manipulation into a rigorous science rather than leaving it as scattered numerological tricks. He showed how abjad calculations, combined with proper understanding of the barzakh and divine names, provide a methodology for intentional causation grounded in cosmic principles.

## The system itself

The twenty-eight letters carry fixed values in a scheme inherited from the Semitic
alphabetic order rather than the alphabetical order used for dictionaries. Units run
alif = 1 through ṭāʾ = 9; tens yāʾ = 10 through ṣād = 90; hundreds qāf = 100 through
ẓāʾ = 900; and ghayn closes the series at 1000. The mnemonic *abjad hawwaz ḥuṭṭī…* preserves
that order, and gives the system its name.

Two properties make it useful for what Ibn Turka wants. It is **total** — every letter has a
value, so every word has a sum, with no remainder and no exceptions. And it is
**bidirectional** — one can compute the value of a given word, or search for words of a
given value. The second is what turns a notation into a technique.

## What it is doing in this system, and what it is not

Abjad by itself is old, widely known, and not in any interesting sense occult; it is used
for chronograms, for numbering, for dating buildings. Encountering it in a poem does not
imply a cosmology.

What Ibn Turka adds is the claim that the values are **not conventional**. If letters
correspond to [[divine-names|divine names]] and the names are the structure of
manifestation, then a letter's number is a fact about the order of being rather than an
agreed tag. On that reading two words sharing a sum share something real, and the
correspondence can be worked.

This is precisely where the [[hurufism|distinction between the three lettrisms]] bites.
Popular practice uses abjad as a source of resonances and portents. Intellectual lettrism
claims the values are ontologically grounded and reasons from them systematically. Same
arithmetic, incompatible claims about what it is arithmetic *about*.

## Its place in the fourfold analysis

In the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] abjad is one register of four: the letter as counted
(*iḥṣāʾī*), alongside the letter as written (*kitābī*) and as spoken (*kalāmī*), and then,
separately, the letter as it is in itself (*fī anfusi-hā*). Numerology is therefore **a third
of the sensible analysis and a quarter of the whole** — a corrective worth stating, since
lettrism is often described as though it were numerology and nothing else.

## What we do not know

- **Which variant conventions** Ibn Turka used — eastern and western abjad differ on several
  values — is not specified in the sources in hand.
- **His worked examples** survive chiefly in the unedited lettrist treatises.


## Where the arithmetic stops and the science begins

The distinction this entry most needs to hold is between two things that look identical on
the page.

**Abjad as convention** is old, ubiquitous and uncontroversial: chronograms, dating
inscriptions, numbering sections. Encountering it in a poem implies nothing about the poet's
metaphysics.

**Abjad as ontology** is Ibn Turka's claim: that the values are **facts about the order of
being** rather than agreed tags. On that reading two words sharing a sum share something
real, and the correspondence can be worked. The arithmetic is unchanged; what changes is
what the arithmetic is *about*.

This is exactly where the [[hurufism|three lettrisms]] separate. Popular practice uses abjad
for resonances and portents. Intellectual lettrism claims the values are grounded and reasons
from them systematically. A tribunal looking at two practitioners cannot tell them apart by
watching what they compute.

## The corrective the portal needs to keep making

Lettrism is routinely described as though it were numerology and nothing else. In the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] the numerological register (*iḥṣāʾī*) is **one of four** —
alongside the symbological (*kitābī*) and phonological (*kalāmī*), and then the letters **as
they are in themselves** (*fī anfusi-hā*).

So abjad is a third of the sensible analysis and a quarter of the whole. A description of the
science that stops at number has taken the most legible register for the discipline.

## The uneven alphabet

Abjad also has to reckon with the fact that the letters are not equivalent. They divide into
light and dark, with the fourteen *muqaṭṭaʿāt* forming exactly half the alphabet and serving
as the primary matrix. Numerical operations run across a set whose members already differ in
rank before any sum is taken.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Abjad is one of the core technical tools of [[ilm-al-huruf]]; mastery of it is necessary for operative lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, pp. 95-130. Ibn Turka, *Kitab al-Mafahis*, Chapters on Numerology.

concepts.name: Barzakh
concepts.card: **Al-Barzakh** (the Isthmus). In Ibn Turka's system, the intermediate realm between pure matter and pure spirit, between multiplicity and unity. The domain where letters become forms, where [[divine-names]] manifest as causal powers, where mathematics governs physical existence. Central to understanding how lettrism operates—letters do not merely represent reality but constitute the barzakh through which divine principles become concrete.
concepts.body:
## Al-Barzakh: The Intermediate Realm

**Al-Barzakh** (literally, "isthmus" or "barrier") is Ibn Turka's term for the ontological middle ground between pure spirit and pure matter. Qur'anically, the barzakh refers to the barrier between the two seas that prevents them from mixing. Medieval Islamic philosophers, especially Ibn ʿArabī, adopted this to denote the intermediate realm between intellect and sense, between the divine and the created. Ibn Turka transformed this concept into the centerpiece of his metaphysical system.

In Ibn Turka's framework, the Barzakh is not merely a philosophical abstraction but the **actual location where causation operates**. The barzakh is where [[ilm-al-huruf|letters and their numerical values]] exert power. It is the realm in which:

- Divine names (*asmaʾ*) become manifest in forms (*ashkāl*)
- Letters (*hurūf*) function as operative principles
- Mathematics (abjad numerology) governs the unfolding of creation
- Intention (*niyyah*) plus ritual acts produce concrete effects

Understanding the barzakh is essential for understanding how Ibn Turka reconciles rational philosophy with operative magic. Operations that recombine letters work not through mystical intuition but through precise knowledge of how the barzakh functions as the intermediate domain where formal patterns (mathematical, linguistic, geometric) generate effects in material reality.

The barzakh is also the human soul—Ibn Turka argues that human consciousness and will operate in the barzakh, which is why knowledge of letters and divine names grants operative power. Mastery of lettrist science is mastery of the mechanisms by which barzakh-realm knowledge becomes action.

## Where it sits in the hierarchy

The barzakh is defined by its position, so the levels either side of it are part of its definition. Creation is ordered as intelligible, imaginal and sensible: divine names in their unmanifested essence; subtle forms; material existence. The barzakh is the middle term, and the traffic between the outer two has to pass through it.

This is why it carries the operative weight. A cosmology of graded levels alone would describe how being descends. Ibn Turka's addition is that the descent has a **place where it can be worked** — that formal patterns introduced at the intermediate level propagate outward into the sensible one. The hierarchy explains the world; the barzakh is where a practitioner gets a hand on it. See also [[imaginal-realm|the imaginal realm]], which is [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī's]] name for substantially the same domain.

## Why the intermediate is where the work happens

A cosmology of graded levels is common property in this period; almost every school has one.
What is distinctive is the claim that the **middle** level is not merely a stage in a
descent but a **place of operation** — that formal patterns introduced there propagate
outward into the sensible world.

This is what converts a metaphysics into a technology. If causation ran only downward from
the intelligible, the only access would be contemplative ascent, and the tradition would
remain what Sufism largely was: a discipline of the knower. Locating an operative point at
the intermediate level makes it possible to *do* something — and everything operative in
[[talismanic-science|talismanic practice]] depends on that possibility.

## The Qur'anic word and what it originally meant

*Barzakh* appears in the Qur'an for the barrier between two seas that do not mix, and for
the interval between death and resurrection. Both senses are of a **boundary that separates
without merging** — a partition that holds two things distinct while touching both.

The philosophical development retains the structure and changes the application: what is
held apart and joined is no longer two waters or two times but two orders of being.
[[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī's]] [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]] is substantially the same
domain approached from the contemplative side, and the two entries in this portal describe
one thing under two names and two vocabularies.

## Letters as barzakh-entities

The technical payoff is a claim about what letters *are*. A letter is not primarily ink and
not primarily sound; both are its expression in the sensible order. Primarily it is a
barzakh-entity — which is why the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] treats the letters in three
sensible registers (counted, written, spoken) and then, separately, **as they are in
themselves** (*fī anfusi-hā*).

That fourth register is the letter at the level where it operates. A practitioner working
with letters is not manipulating marks that stand for things; he is working at the level at
which the things are constituted.

## The human soul in the same position

The soul occupies the barzakh too, and this is the hinge of the whole system. A being whose
own seat is the intermediate realm can act there natively — which is why knowledge of
letters and [[divine-names|divine names]] grants operative capacity rather than merely
insight. The practitioner is not reaching into a foreign domain; he is already standing in
it.

## What we do not know

- **How Ibn Turka's technical usage differs from Ibn ʿArabī's** is not spelled out in the
  sources in hand; the two are treated as continuous more often than they are compared.
- **The dedicated treatise is unedited**, so the doctrine is known
  chiefly at second hand and through the *Mafāḥiṣ*.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The barzakh is Ibn Turka's foundational cosmological concept; all occult operations depend on understanding it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 150-180.

concepts.name: The Divine Names
concepts.card: **Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya** (The Divine Names and Attributes). Islamic doctrine positing 28 (or 99) divine names—each expressing an aspect of God's nature (The Merciful, The Just, The Mighty, etc.). In [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], each of the 28 Arabic letters corresponds to one divine name, making letters themselves expressions of divine attributes. Ibn Turka's system treats mastery of the divine names through their corresponding letters as the path to aligning human will with cosmic principles.
concepts.body:
## The Divine Names (Al-Asmaʾ al-Ilāhīyya)

Islamic theology recognizes that God is known through His attributes and names. The Qur'an references divine names, and Islamic scholars compiled lists—commonly 99, though sometimes 28. Each name expresses a dimension of divinity: al-Raḥmān (The Merciful), al-ʿAdl (The Just), al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing), al-Qawī (The Mighty), etc.

In [[ilm-al-huruf|Ibn Turka's lettrist system]], the 28 divine names are mapped directly onto the 28 Arabic letters. This creates a correspondence where:
- Each letter IS a divine name
- Each letter carries the properties and powers of that name
- Manipulation of letters becomes invocation of divine principles

For example:
- The letter ʿAyn corresponds to al-ʿAlīm (The All-Knowing)
- The letter Tāʾ corresponds to al-Tāʾib (The Returning/Repenting)
- The letter Qāf corresponds to al-Qawī (The Mighty)

Through understanding these correspondences and using [[abjad-numerology|abjad numerology]], a practitioner can compose words, phrases, or talismans that embody specific divine qualities. The goal is not manipulation (in the magical sense) but **attunement**: aligning human intention and action with divine attributes, thereby participating in the structure of reality itself.

Ibn Turka's treatment of the divine names through letters represents a synthesis of Islamic theology, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist gnosis]], and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]]. It is the theological foundation that legitimizes lettrism as a valid science within Islamic orthodoxy—because engaging with letters is, from this perspective, engaging with divine attributes themselves.

## The mapping, and the arithmetic behind it

The technical claim is a correspondence: the twenty-eight letters of the Arabic alphabet
answer to twenty-eight divine names. The number is doing work. The canonical enumeration of
the names is ninety-nine, and the reduction to twenty-eight is what makes a one-to-one
mapping onto the alphabet possible at all — the correspondence is not found lying about, it
is constructed, and the construction is part of the doctrine.

With the mapping in place, [[abjad-numerology|abjad values]] become theologically loaded.
A word's numerical sum is no longer arithmetic about letters; it is a statement about which
divine attributes that word gathers and in what proportion. This is the machinery
[[talismanic-science|talismanic practice]] runs on.

## Where the doctrine comes from

From [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]], systematised by [[qunavi|Qūnavī]] and elaborated by
[[jandi|Jandī]]: the names are not descriptions of a God who exists apart from them but the
structure through which being manifests. Creation is the self-disclosure of the names.

That metaphysical claim is what makes the lettrist move available. If creation unfolds
through named attributes, and if the letters answer to the names, then the letters are
constitutive of creation and not merely descriptive of it. The whole claim that lettrism is
the [[occult-science-universal|only truly universal science]] rests on this chain, and each
link is inherited except the last.

## Why it keeps the science inside orthodoxy

The divine names are unimpeachably mainstream. They are Qur'anic, they are recited, they are
the common property of every school. A science that presents itself as the disciplined study
of the names is not importing foreign material; it is claiming to systematise something the
tradition already holds.

This is the same defensive structure as the appeal to *iʿjāz* — the miraculous inimitability
of the Qur'an — that [[ilm-al-huruf|the science claims to demonstrate]]. In both cases the
occultist stands on a doctrine his prosecutors also hold.

## What we do not know

- **The full correspondence table** as Ibn Turka gives it is not reproduced in the sources in
  hand; it survives in the unedited lettrist works.
- **How he justified the reduction from ninety-nine to twenty-eight** is not set out in this
  corpus.
- **Whether the mapping was his or inherited** from [[saad-al-din-hamuyya|Ḥamūya]] and the
  earlier tradition is not resolved.


## Light and dark, and what the mapping has to accommodate

The correspondence of names to letters is not a flat table, because the letters themselves
are not uniform. They divide into **light** (*nūrānī*) and **dark** (*ẓulmānī*), the light
ones being the **fourteen isolated letters** — the *muqaṭṭaʿāt* opening twenty-nine Sūras,
**exactly half the alphabet**, and a primary matrix of lettrism (*Being with a Capital B*, 2).

Any mapping of names onto letters therefore inherits a two-tier structure it did not choose,
and has to say what it means that some divine names answer to luminous letters and others to
dark ones. The [[risala-baiyya|*R. al-Bāʾiyya*]] is Ibn Turka working exactly this problem at
its sharpest point: **B**, first of the dark letters and fountainhead of all duality, opens
both the Qur'an and the Torah, where **A**, avatar of divine Oneness, seems far better
suited.

The answer he gives — combining rational and traditional arguments — is not preserved in the
corpus in hand, but the shape of the problem tells us what the doctrine of the names must do.
It cannot simply rank the names by dignity and match them to letters by rank, because
scripture itself refuses that ordering.

## Why the names keep the science inside orthodoxy

The names are Qur'anic, recited, and the shared property of every school. A science
presenting itself as their disciplined study is not importing foreign material; it is
systematising what the tradition already holds. That defensive structure is the same one at
work in the appeal to *iʿjāz*, the miraculous inimitability of the Qur'an, which
[[ilm-al-huruf|the science claims to demonstrate]] rather than to assume.

In both cases the occultist stands on a doctrine his prosecutors also hold — which is what
made the [[first-inquisition|first tribunal]] winnable, and what makes the whole project
something other than the smuggling operation its critics took it for.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The divine names are the theological anchor for [[ilm-al-huruf]]; they ground lettrist practice within Islamic doctrine.
literature: Ibn ʿArabī. *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya*, Treatise on the Divine Names.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, Ch. 3.

concepts.name: Geomancy (ʿilm al-raml)
concepts.card: **ʿIlm al-raml**, the science of sand — divination by generating figures from marks made at random and reading them through a fixed combinatorial system. One of the three sciences Melvin-Koushki tracks as shifting **from the natural to the mathematical** in this period, alongside astrology and [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]. It is also the ground of the portal's sharpest confrontation: **Ibn Khaldūn against [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī]]** — which does not run the way the reputations suggest.
concepts.body:
## What it is

Geomancy generates a set of figures from marks made without deliberation — traditionally in sand, hence the name — and reads them through a fixed system of combination. Each figure is a column of four positions, each either single or double, giving sixteen possible figures; these are then combined by rule to produce further figures and a chart to be interpreted.

The structure is what matters for this portal. **The randomness is at the input only.** Everything downstream is deterministic combination, which is precisely why the discipline could be argued into the mathematical sciences: what a geomancer does after the marks are made is calculate.

## The reclassification

Melvin-Koushki's thesis names three sciences specifically — **astrology, lettrism and geomancy** — as those gradually but definitively shifted **from the natural to the mathematical sciences** as a means of reasserting their scientific legitimacy against four centuries of anti-occultist polemic (*Powers of One*, 1). Geomancy is arguably the easiest of the three to make the case for, since its operations are overtly combinatorial.

## Ibn Khaldūn is not who the reputation says

This is the finding that reorganises the subject, and it is worth stating slowly.

**The received picture.** Ibn Khaldūn's purported objectivity and skepticism about the occult sciences is now much admired — **held up as a shining, solitary example of rationality amidst rampant superstition**, a man ahead of his time, famously rejecting well-patronised sciences like astrology and alchemy out of hand (*In Defense of Geomancy*, 349).

**What is less acknowledged.** That the same Tunisian historian **argues forcefully, and at length, for the incontrovertible reality of magic and divination — with the selfsame sober objectivity** (ibid.).

So the modern hero of Islamic rationalism was not a debunker of the occult. He rejected some occult sciences and accepted others, on grounds he took to be equally rigorous in both directions. The picture of a lone sceptic among credulous contemporaries is a modern construction that survives by not reading him all the way through.

## And Yazdī is not the mirror image

The other side of the confrontation is equally unexpected. [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn ʿAlī Yazdī]] (d. 858/1454) — dynastic historian to the Timurids and **committed occultist** — has theories of historical evolution and human potential **not dissimilar to Ibn Khaldūn's more famous formulations**, yet **predicated precisely on a thoroughgoingly occultist outlook** (*In Defense of Geomancy*, 349).

Two historians of the same generation, arriving at comparable accounts of how societies develop, from opposite metaphysical premises. Both men's views on occultism **go to the heart of their respective sociologies and political theologies, which accordingly converge and diverge in instructive ways**.

The confrontation is therefore not rationalism against superstition. It is two sophisticated theories of history disagreeing about which occult sciences are real.

## What we do not know

- **Whether they met.** Ibn Khaldūn lived in Cairo 785–808/1383–1406, overlapping Yazdī's residence there with Ibn Turka; Melvin-Koushki notes they **possibly met** (*Powers of One*, 37).
- **Ibn Turka's own position on geomancy** specifically is not set out in the corpus in hand, though the science is one of the three named in the reclassification thesis.
- **Which geomantic manuals** circulated in Timurid Iran is treated in *Persianate Geomancy* rather than here.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Geomancy is one of the three sciences (with astrology and lettrism) that the mathematicalization thesis tracks; it is the arena of the Ibn Khaldun–Yazdi confrontation.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *In Defense of Geomancy*, 349.
Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 1, 37.
Melvin-Koushki, *Persianate Geomancy*.

concepts.name: Ḥurūfism
concepts.card: **Ḥurūfism** — the messianic letter-movement founded by Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 796/1394), which read the letters as announcing a new dispensation. It is the heresy Ibn Turka had to be distinguished from, and the charge on which he was exiled from Herat in 1427. The distinction is not technique but **motive**: the Ḥurūfīs proclaimed a new revelation; the lettrists claimed to be working *within* the tradition to extend human knowledge.
concepts.body:
## Ḥurūfism, and the line Ibn Turka had to draw

**The movement.** Fażl Allāh Astarābādī (d. 796/1394) taught that the letters disclose a new phase of revelation, and his followers — the Ḥurūfiyya — carried that claim into open messianism across Iran and Anatolia. Both they and Ibn Turka worked on letters. That shared subject matter is precisely the problem.

**The distinction is motive, not method.** Melvin-Koushki puts the difference plainly: what separates the lettrists from the Ḥurūfīs and the other messianic movements of early 9th/15th-century Iran is motive — *the gnostic Hurufis proclaim a new, Persian dispensation; the messianic Sufis promote themselves as political saviors; the lettrists present themselves as occult philosophers working within the tradition to expand the boundaries of human knowledge* (*The Quest*, 456).

Ibn Turka is himself, by any standard, a profoundly millenarian thinker: he proclaims the advent of a new age, heralded by heavenly portent, in which the occult knowledge of the Imams and the ancients will be made manifest. What keeps this inside orthodoxy is its insistence on **the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad** (*The Quest*, 456). A new age of knowledge, not a new prophecy. The whole of his position rests on that distinction, and it is a fine one.

**Why the charge stuck to him.** Because it was not baseless. Fażl Allāh arrived in Isfahan around 766/1365 and quickly became famous as a dream interpreter, and Ḥurūfī sources record that **Ibn Turka's own father Afżal al-Dīn and his elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] sought him out there to have their dreams interpreted**. Naṣr Allāh Nāfajī's *Khwābnāma* preserves the episode (*The Quest*, ch. 1, and Eichner, 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka', EI3).

Melvin-Koushki is careful about what this does and does not show: the contact does not imply Ḥurūfī inclinations on the part of the two Turkas, and the hagiographical point of the story is to establish Fażl Allāh's fame as a Sufi *before* his messianic transformation — respected scholars of the religious sciences came to him for counsel. But a family documented as having consulted the founder of the Ḥurūfiyya gives a prosecutor something to work with, and in 1427 a prosecutor used it.

**The cost.** [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] court exiled Ibn Turka from Herat alongside [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], the official excuse being a putative Ḥurūfī connection (*The Quest*, 456 n.16). The science and the heresy were close enough in appearance that the difference had to be argued, and arguing it was a lifetime's work.

## Where it sits among the three lettrisms

The clearest way to hold the distinction is to see that lettrism in this period runs in
three strands, and that Ḥurūfism is one of them rather than the whole.
Melvin-Koushki separates **gnostic-messianic**, **Sufi**, and **intellectual** lettrism, and
argues that Ibn Turka's unprecedented elevation of lettrism against philosophy constitutes
the third as a distinct thing (*The Quest*, iii).

He then corrects a standing assumption in the field, and the correction is sharp: **it is
typically — and erroneously — assumed that the Ḥurūfī movement of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī
defines later Islamicate lettrism.** It does not. Ḥurūfism is an instance of *popular*
gnostic-messianic-Sufi lettrism, and what its vigour actually demonstrates is **the
religio-cultural valency of lettrism in Iran at all levels** of society.

That last clause is worth pausing on, because it cuts both ways. The Ḥurūfī movement is
evidence that letter-speculation had penetrated Iranian culture deeply enough to sustain a
mass movement — which is context Ibn Turka benefits from and is endangered by in equal
measure. A science whose vocabulary is in general circulation is a science whose
practitioners can be mistaken for anybody using that vocabulary.

## The millenarianism problem, stated honestly

The entry would be dishonest if it presented Ibn Turka as a sober rationalist accused by
mistake. Melvin-Koushki does not: **Ṣāʾin al-Dīn is a profoundly millenarian thinker by any
standard** (*The Quest*, 456). He proclaims the advent of a new age heralded by heavenly
portent — the [[chronology|Saturn–Jupiter conjunction of 767/1365]] — in which the occult
knowledge of the Imams and the ancients will be made manifest.

The difference from Ḥurūfism is therefore not the presence or absence of millenarian
expectation. It is what the expected age contains. Ibn Turka's is **unimpeachably Islamic in
its insistence on the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad**: a
golden age of *knowledge*, in which what was already revealed becomes fully actual. The
Ḥurūfīs proclaim a new, Persian dispensation. One is an epistemological claim about
timing; the other is a prophetic claim.

## Three movements, three motives

The dissertation's formulation sorts the field by motive rather than doctrine, which is what
makes it usable:

- **the gnostic Ḥurūfīs** proclaim a new, Persian dispensation;
- **the messianic Sufis** promote themselves as political saviours;
- **the lettrists** present themselves as **occult philosophers working within the tradition
  to expand the boundaries of human knowledge** (*The Quest*, 456).

Doctrinally these overlap heavily. By motive they are three different enterprises, and a
tribunal that cannot or will not distinguish motives will convict all three together.

## The political weather that made the charge lethal

Fażl Allāh was executed at the fortress of Alinjaq by Mīrānshāh b. Tīmūr in 796/1394 — the
dynasty had killed the founder within Ibn Turka's own lifetime. [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]]
attempted a purge of Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415. And in 835/1432, the year Ibn Turka
died, there were **Ḥurūfī uprisings in Isfahan and Tabriz**. The label was not an abstract
theological category; it named an active insurgency that the state was killing people over.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka ever addressed the Ḥurūfīs directly** in a surviving text, and in what
  terms, is not established in the sources in hand.
- **What his prosecutors actually alleged** in 1427 beyond the bare "putative connection" is
  not recorded.
- **How the family's consultation of Fażl Allāh became known** to his opponents — whether
  through the Ḥurūfī sources that preserve it or through local memory — is unclear.


## The old sorting problem

The difficulty Ibn Turka faced was not new in his century; it is as old as the science. The
science of letters **entered Islam at its inception in the messianic-gnostic syncretism of
the early *ghulāt***, and was associated **in more sedate Shiʿi circles** with the
*K. al-Jafr wa-l-Jāmiʿa* of ʿAlī, an omniscient text recording past and future history and
all knowledge of the cosmos (*The Quest*, 22).

Two lineages, present from the beginning: an extreme wing and a respectable one, working the
same material. Every subsequent generation had to sort itself against that inheritance, and
the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] episode is a late and violent instance of a problem built into the
discipline's origins.

This is worth knowing because it explains why the distinction Ibn Turka insists on could not
simply be asserted and settled. He was not clarifying a confusion of his own moment; he was
taking a position in an argument the tradition had been having for seven centuries.

## What the movement's success actually demonstrated

Melvin-Koushki's reading of Ḥurūfī vigour is counterintuitive and worth restating: the
movement's strength testifies to **the religio-cultural valency of lettrism in Iran at all
levels** of society (*The Quest*, iii).

That cuts both ways for Ibn Turka. A science whose vocabulary is in general circulation has
an audience, a supply of students and a claim to relevance. It also has practitioners its
theorists cannot control, and a public face over which they have no say. When
[[hurufi-uprisings|the risings came in 835/1432]], the public face was armed rebellion.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Ḥurūfism is the boundary case for [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]: same material, different claim, and the distinction is what Ibn Turka spent his career defending.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 456 and ch. 1.
Eichner, Heidrun. 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka.' *Encyclopaedia of Islam*, THREE.

concepts.name: 'Ilm al-ḥurūf
concepts.card: ***'Ilm al-ḥurūf*** (the science of letters). Islamic science investigating the divine and cosmological meanings hidden in the forms, sounds, and numerical values of Arabic letters. The doctrine that Creation is fundamentally linguistic—that God speaks the world into being through the Arabic alphabet—and that mastery of letter-properties (form, sound, numerical value, and correspondence to divine names and cosmic principles) confers access to hidden causal powers. Central to Ibn Turka's entire philosophical system and foundational to late medieval and early modern Islamic occultism.
concepts.body:
## 'Ilm al-ḥurūf: The Science of Letters

### Definition and Etymology

The term *ʿilm al-ḥurūf* literally means "the science of letters." In Islamic intellectual tradition, it denotes a body of knowledge and practice investigating the divine, mystical, and cosmological meanings encoded in the letters of the Arabic alphabet. Unlike grammar (*ʿilm al-naḥw*) or rhetoric (*ʿilm al-bayān*), which treat letters as vehicles for communication, lettrism treats letters as primary entities carrying inherent causal and spiritual power.

The philosophical foundation of lettrism rests on a radical claim: **Creation is fundamentally linguistic**. God's first act was not merely to think or to will, but to *speak*. The Qur'an expresses this principle in the doctrine that God says *kun* ("Be!") and creation manifests. But if Creation itself is the result of divine speech, then the properties of language—especially the formal, numerical, and phonetic properties of the Arabic letters through which that speech is expressed—must encode the principles of reality itself.

### Historical Development

Lettrism has deep roots in Islamic intellectual history. Early mystical traditions, particularly within Sufism, occasionally invoked letter-symbolism. But lettrism as a systematic science—with formal philosophical grounding and operative methods—emerged gradually in the medieval period.

The key figure in establishing intellectual lettrism was **Ibn ʿArabī** (1165–1240), the Andalusian Sufi metaphysician. In his vast encyclopedic work the *Futūḥāt al-Makkīyya* (Meccan Illuminations), Ibn ʿArabī developed sophisticated theories of letters as expressions of divine names and cosmological principles. His approach was intuitive and poetic—he scattered lettrist insights throughout his work without systematizing them (what Melvin-Koushki calls the principle of *tabdīd al-ʿilm*, "scattering knowledge").

**Saʿd al-Dīn Ḥamūya** (d. 1252), Ibn ʿArabī's Iranian contemporary, took an even more radically lettrist approach, arguing that letters were the foundation of all metaphysics. Indeed, according to sources, Ḥamūya was so committed to lettrist principles that he criticized Ibn ʿArabī for being insufficiently rigorous in his application of lettrist logic.

Yet despite these precedents, lettrism remained scattered and esoteric through the medieval period. The crucial breakthrough came in the late 14th and early 15th centuries with **Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī** and his heir [[ibn-turka]].

### Ibn Turka's Systematization

Ibn Turka's contribution was transforming lettrism from an intuitive, esoteric teaching into a rigorous, scientifically-grounded philosophy. He accomplished this through three moves:

**1. Explicit Pythagorean Modeling.** Ibn Turka grounded lettrism in **Pythagorean mathematical philosophy**—the ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles of reality. By arguing that Arabic letters and their numerical values (*abjad* system) encode cosmic principles in a Pythagorean manner, Ibn Turka gave lettrism mathematical legitimacy.

**2. Integration with Formal Philosophy.** Rather than treating lettrism as a mystical secret, Ibn Turka integrated it with Islamic peripatetic philosophy (*falsafa*), Neoplatonic metaphysics, and rational theology. His treatises are technically sophisticated, employing the logical tools and conceptual apparatus of mainstream Islamic philosophy. This move made lettrism a legitimate intellectual discipline, not marginal mysticism.

**3. Codification and Transparency.** Ibn Turka wrote extensively and clearly on lettrism, replacing the principle of "scattering knowledge" (Achlāṭī's approach, inherited from Ibn ʿArabī) with systematic exposition. His magisterial *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* (Book of Inquiries) lays out lettrist theory in organized chapters, with precise definitions, examples, and arguments. This transparency—making esoteric knowledge available to educated readers—was controversial but effective. It allowed his framework to propagate widely.

### Core Doctrines

**The Letter-Divine Name Correspondence.** The 28 letters of the Arabic alphabet correspond to the 28 divine names recognized in Islamic theology. Each name has properties—creative power, protection, vengeance, mercy—that are encoded in the corresponding letter.

**The Numerical Dimension.** In the *abjad* system, each letter has a numerical value (alif = 1, bāʾ = 2, etc.). These values can be summed, multiplied, and manipulated to yield cosmic and operative results. A Qur'anic verse, understood as a sequence of letters with specific numerical values, encodes mathematical relationships reflecting cosmological structures.

**The Cosmological Scale.** Ibn Turka systematized a correspondence between:
- The 28 letters
- The 28 divine names
- The 28 lunar mansions (in astrology)
- 28 (or seven times four) levels of celestial and sublunary reality
- 28 human faculties and attributes

This integrated system meant that knowledge of letters provided simultaneous access to theology, metaphysics, psychology, and cosmology.

**Operative Power.** Unlike purely theoretical systems, lettrism claims operative efficacy. Operations that recombine letters—anagrams (*taqārīb al-ḥurūf*), numerical rearrangements, geometric configurations—are not mere games but interventions in the fabric of reality. Because letters are the fundamental building blocks of creation, manipulating them (through knowledge, intention, and proper ritual) alters reality itself.

### Distinctions: Intellectual vs. Mystical Lettrism

It is crucial to distinguish **intellectual lettrism** (as developed by Ibn Turka) from earlier **mystical and gnostic lettrism**.

**Gnostic-Messianic Lettrism** (exemplified by the Ḥurūfī movement of Fażl Allāh Astarābādī, d. 1394) treated letters as paths to ecstatic experience, mystical insight, and divine union. It often had popular appeal and sometimes messianic dimensions—the belief that lettrist knowledge would usher in a new age of humanity. This tradition valued direct mystical experience over systematic philosophical reasoning.

**Intellectual Lettrism** (as developed by Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle) treats letters as subjects of rigorous philosophical investigation. While mystical experience might accompany such knowledge, it is not the goal. Rather, lettrism is valued as the truest form of universal science—more comprehensive than logic or mathematics alone because it encompasses both rational and mystical dimensions, integrating them into a coherent system. The operative power of letters is explained through metaphysical principles, not through mystical intuition.

Melvin-Koushki emphasizes that Ibn Turka's intellectual approach did NOT negate the gnostic tradition; rather, it coexisted with it. The vigorous Ḥurūfī movement in 15th-century Iran testifies to the religio-cultural power of gnostic lettrism at all social levels. Ibn Turka's innovation was providing a philosophical framework that made lettrism intellectually respectable among the scholarly elite.

### Later Development and Influence

Ibn Turka's framework became canonical. By the 16th century, virtually every Islamic philosopher engaging seriously with lettrism worked through Ibn Turka's categories. The tradition continued through Safavid Iran (with thinkers like Mullā Ṣadrā), Ottoman Anatolia, and Mughal India. Lettrism remained a living intellectual tradition until the 19th century.

In modern times, the dismissal of lettrism as superstition was part of orientalist ideology. Contemporary scholarship has recognized lettrism for what it was: a legitimate intellectual system with internal coherence, grounded in rigorous reasoning, and integrated with the best scholarship of its era. It was not proto-science awaiting correction by modern physics, but rather a distinct epistemic system with different starting assumptions.

## The correspondence table, and what it is for

The technical core of the science is a mapping: each of the twenty-eight Arabic letters answers to one of the [[divine-names|divine names]], and so carries that name's properties. Working with a letter is therefore working with a divine attribute, and this is what makes the practice more than [[abjad-numerology|arithmetic]] — the numbers are the handle, the names are what is being handled.

Ibn Turka's own analysis in the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] is fourfold rather than simply tabular. He treats the letters in their three forms — numerological (*iḥṣāʾī*), symbological (*kitābī*) and phonological (*kalāmī*) — and then, separately, **as they are in themselves** (*fī anfusi-hā*). The first three are the letter as counted, written and spoken. The fourth is the letter as a being, prior to any of those. A correspondence table alone would give only the first three registers; the fourth is what turns the table into an ontology.

## The three strands, and why the distinction is the whole argument

Lettrism in this period is not a single discipline, and almost every misreading of Ibn
Turka comes from treating it as one. Melvin-Koushki separates:

1. **Gnostic-messianic lettrism** — the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfiyya]], for whom the letters
   announce a new dispensation.
2. **Sufi lettrism** — the devotional and contemplative strand descending through the
   [[ibn-arabi|Akbarian]] tradition and the orders.
3. **Intellectual lettrism** — Ibn Turka's, in which the letters are the object of a
   rigorous universal science grounded in [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematics]].

His **unprecedented lionization of lettrism vis-à-vis philosophy** constitutes the third
strand as a distinct thing (*The Quest*, iii). And the historiographical correction that
follows is sharp: it is **typically and erroneously assumed that the Ḥurūfī movement
defines later Islamicate lettrism**. It does not. The Ḥurūfīs are *popular*
gnostic-messianic-Sufi lettrism, and their vigour testifies to how deeply the material had
penetrated Iranian culture **at all levels** — which is evidence about circulation, not
about definition.

## The claim to universality, stated maximally
