The argument against philosophy is not that philosophy is wrong but that it is
**parochial while believing itself universal**. In the dissertation's formulation: the
faux-universal concepts of philosophical speculation notwithstanding, **only the letter
encompasses all that is and is not, all that can and cannot be; it alone is the
*coincidentia oppositorum*; hence lettrism is the only truly universal science**
(*The Quest*, iii).

The reasoning runs: a philosophical concept ranges over actual and possible being. The
letter ranges over actuality, possibility, **and their negations** — it can signify
non-being and impossibility as readily as being. A science whose object has that range is
the only candidate for a science of everything. Whether one accepts the argument, it is an
argument, and it is aimed precisely at the discipline that held the prestige.

## What the practitioners took themselves to be proving

Two goals, held together. Lettrists of Ibn Turka's kind saw themselves as **advancing human
knowledge of the cosmos** and simultaneously **demonstrating the miraculous inimitability of
the Qur'an (*iʿjāz*) as the clearest transcript of divine Speech in history**
(*The Quest*, iii).

The second is the theologically conservative half, and it is why the science reads as piety
from inside. *Iʿjāz* is mainstream doctrine. If the letters of scripture are the
constitutive principles of creation, the Qur'an's inimitability stops being a literary
verdict and becomes a cosmological one. The science is offered as the *proof* of an
orthodox commitment.

This is also why the whole edifice **necessarily presupposes the uncreatedness of the
Qur'an**. Letters that were created artefacts could not be the principles through which
creation is constituted. Ibn Turka accordingly censures the popularity of Zamakhsharī's
*Kashshāf*, singling out its failure to recognise the intrinsic ontological majesty of the
quranic letters (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66 n.88).

## Reading and writing the world

The operative dimension is best put as Melvin-Koushki puts it: these are thinkers driven by
the prospect of **decoding and recoding the twin Books, the Qur'an and the cosmos**
(*The Quest*, iii).

*Decoding* makes lettrism a hermeneutic — creation is legible. *Recoding* makes it a
technology — a reader fluent in the notation can compose in it. The
[[barzakh|intermediate realm]] is where the writing takes effect, and
[[talismanic-science|talismanic practice]] is the recoding carried out on matter. Everything
operative in the tradition follows from the second verb.

## Style as doctrine

Because letters are entities rather than marks, their arrangement is not presentation. The
dissertation argues that **lettrist theory informs the ornate literary practice of the
period**, and notes Ibn Turka's own standing as a vaunted stylist of Persian prose
(*The Quest*, iii). The prosimetric elaboration of his writing is the doctrine applied to
the page.

## What we do not know

- The **relative chronology of the three strands** is not settled; they overlap and
  cross-fertilise rather than succeeding one another cleanly.
- Most of Ibn Turka's specifically lettrist works are **still unedited**, so the technical
  system is known chiefly through the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] and the treatises
  edited in Part 2 of the dissertation.
- How far the **Ottoman branch** under [[bistami|Bisṭāmī]] developed the same technical
  apparatus is a question for Fleischer's research rather than this portal's sources.


## The letters are not all alike

A technical division the portal has so far left out, and it is fundamental. The Arabic
letters sort into **light** (*nūrānī*) and **dark** (*ẓulmānī*).

The light letters are the **fourteen isolated letters** — the *muqaṭṭaʿāt*, the detached
letters that open twenty-nine Sūras of the Qur'an, whose meaning is one of the oldest
unresolved questions in Qur'anic exegesis. They are **exactly half the alphabet**, and
Melvin-Koushki calls them **naturally a primary matrix of lettrism** (*Being with a Capital
B*, 2).

That numerical fact is doing a great deal of work. A tradition claiming that scripture
encodes the structure of creation is handed, in the *muqaṭṭaʿāt*, a set of letters that
scripture itself sets apart for no stated reason — and which happens to be precisely half
the alphabet. It is the strongest single piece of internal evidence the science has.

**B**, by contrast, is the **first of the dark letters and the fountainhead of all
duality** — which generates the conundrum the [[risala-baiyya|*R. al-Bāʾiyya*]] is written
to solve: why do the Qur'an and the Torah both open on it, rather than on **A**, the avatar
of divine Oneness and of the beginning of creation?

## Jazz, and the theory of jazz

The best short account of Ibn Turka's originality is Melvin-Koushki's. Both
[[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] and [[saad-al-din-hamuyya|Ḥamūya]] can be usefully read as **jazz
philosophers**; Ibn Turka, their **systematizing and Pythagoreanizing lettrist heir**, is a
**philosopher of jazz** (*Being with a Capital B*, 10).

His predecessors improvised on the letters — Ḥamūya's manner is described as radically
free-playing, riffing on the visual and the aural at once. Ibn Turka wrote the theory of
the improvisation: what the changes are, why they work, what makes a run of them correct
rather than merely striking. That is a different activity from playing, and it is the one
nobody had done.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Lettrism is one of five occult sciences in Ibn Turka's classification, considered the highest because it encompasses the others.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context.* In *Islamicate Occult Sciences in Theory and Practice*, pp. 127–199.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology: Lettrism, Alchemy, and the Secrets of the Letters in Medieval Islam.* Berlin: De Gruyter, 2016.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Islamic Pythagoreanism.* 2023.

concepts.name: The Imaginal Realm
concepts.literal_meaning: The realm of forms; the world of imagination
concepts.card: **Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (The Imaginal Realm). In [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] metaphysics, the ontological layer between pure intellect and material sense where forms (*ashkāl*) exist independently of physical matter. The domain where mystical visions occur, where symbols manifest, where divine names express themselves in subtle forms. Central to understanding how knowledge operates in Islamic mysticism and occultism: the imaginal realm is where letters and divine names acquire form, where talismanic operations work, where the barzakh functions.
concepts.body:
## Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl: The Imaginal Realm

**Al-ʿAlam al-Khiyāl** (literally "the imaginal realm" or "the realm of imagination") is [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi's]] term for an intermediate ontological domain between pure intellect (ʿaql) and material sensation (ḥiss). The Arabic word *khiyāl* is often mistranslated as "imagination" in the modern sense (the faculty of fantasy); Ibn Arabi means something far more precise and metaphysically serious: a realm of subtle forms (*ashkāl*) that possess reality independent of physical matter.

The imaginal realm occupies the same position in Ibn Arabi's cosmology that the [[barzakh|barzakh]] occupies in Ibn Turka's refinement of it: the crucial intermediate domain where causation operates, where divine principles become manifest in form, where knowledge acquires structure.

### Three Realms of Being

Ibn Arabi divides creation into three principal domains:

1. **The Intelligible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ʿaql*): Pure intellect, transcendent principles, divine names in their unmanifested essence
2. **The Imaginal Realm** (*ʿālam al-khiyāl*): Forms, symbols, subtle bodies, the world of vision and mystical knowledge
3. **The Sensible Realm** (*ʿālam al-ḥiss*): Material existence, the physical world knowable through sense perception

Each realm participates in the others; none is hermetically sealed. The imaginal realm serves as the *medium* through which the intelligible becomes sensible, through which the transcendent becomes immanent.

### The Imaginal in Mystical Experience

For Ibn Arabi, mystical visions (*mushāhadāt*) are not hallucinations or mere psychological phenomena—they are direct perception of the imaginal realm. When a mystic "sees" an angel, perceives a divine light, or encounters a teacher in a dream, they are perceiving realities that exist in the imaginal realm. These perceptions are as real as sensory experience, though they operate in a different ontological register.

This doctrine revolutionizes Islamic mysticism: it legitimizes mystical experience as a form of genuine knowledge by establishing that there is an objective realm (the imaginal) in which such experiences occur. Mysticism is not projection; it is perception.

### The Imaginal in Occult Practice

[[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]] and the later occult philosophers adopted this framework. When a practitioner creates a talisman by writing letters and numbers with specific intention, the operation works in the imaginal realm first: the talisman, as an imaginal object (a form constituted by [[abjad-numerology|numerical correspondences]] and divine names), exerts influence on the sensible world. The imaginal realm is where the power resides; the physical talisman is the expression.

Similarly, [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrist operations]] work because letters—as forms carrying [[divine-names|divine names]]—are primarily imaginal realities. Mastery of letters grants access to the imaginal realm, whence all material creation flows.

### Legacy and Transmission

[[qunavi|Qūnavī]] elaborated Ibn Arabi's doctrine of the imaginal realm into a full philosophy of knowledge (*gnosis* vs. *reason*). Through the [[qunavi|Qūnavī]]-Jandī school, the imaginal realm became part of the theoretical apparatus available to philosophers, mystics, and occultists across the Islamic world. By Ibn Turka's time, the imaginal realm was accepted as a foundational concept: its reality was presupposed, not debated.

## Why the translation matters

*Khayāl* is routinely rendered "imagination", and the rendering does real damage. In modern
English, imagination names a faculty that produces things which are **not real** — the
opposite of perception. Ibn ʿArabī means something almost inverted: a domain that **is**
real, possessing its own subsistence, which the soul perceives rather than invents.

Hence "imaginal", Henry Corbin's coinage, adopted precisely to block the modern
implication. The imaginal is not the imaginary. A vision occurring there is a perception of
something, and can be true or false in the way perceptions can.

## What follows from granting it reality

Everything operative in the tradition. If the intermediate domain is real and structured,
then:

- **Visions are evidence.** They report on something, and disagreement about them is
  substantive rather than a clash of private impressions.
- **Forms can be introduced there.** A [[talismanic-science|talisman]] is an object composed
  at the imaginal level whose material inscription is secondary — which is why its efficacy
  is held to depend on intention and correspondence rather than on the physical substance
  alone.
- **[[ilm-al-huruf|Letters]] have a native home.** A letter treated *fī anfusi-hā* — as it is
  in itself, apart from being counted, written or spoken — is a letter considered as an
  imaginal entity.

## Two names for one domain

This entry and [[barzakh|barzakh]] describe substantially the same region under two
vocabularies. The imaginal is the Akbarian name, approached from the side of the knower and
what can be perceived. The barzakh is the name Ibn Turka's system leans on, approached from
the side of causation and what can be done. Reading the two entries together gives the
domain from both directions, which is how the sources present it.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka used the two terms interchangeably** or maintained a technical
  distinction between them is not settled in these sources.
- **How the imaginal realm relates to the ordinary faculty of imagination** in his psychology
  — whether they are the same power at different ranges — is not treated in the corpus in
  hand.
concepts.hierarchy_note: The imaginal realm is Ibn Arabi's key metaphysical contribution; all later Islamic occultism presupposes it.
literature: Chittick, William C. *The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination*. Albany: SUNY Press, 1989.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Being with a Capital B: Imaginal Ontology and the New Brethren of Purity*.

concepts.name: Shiʿi-Sunnism (imamophilism)
concepts.literal_meaning: Devotion to the Imams without formal Shiʿi affiliation
concepts.card: **Shiʿi-Sunnism**, or **imamophilism** — reverence for the Imams held without a formal Shiʿi confessional commitment. Melvin-Koushki calls it a **defining feature of 9th/15th-century Islamic religiosity**, particularly in Iran and particularly in esotericist circles, and it is his answer to the long argument about whether Ibn Turka was 'really' a Shiʿi or a Sunni. The question is anachronistic; the position is the period's own.
concepts.body:
## Neither, and deliberately

**The problem it solves.** Ibn Turka's confessional identity has been read both ways. Henry Corbin embraced him as a standard-issue Shiʿi esotericist; Leonard Lewisohn, reading the [[nafsat-al-masdur|apologies]], presents him as an orthodox Sunni Sufi thinker. Melvin-Koushki rejects both: Ibn Turka's ambiguous confessional position is best described as **Shiʿi-Sunnism or imamophilism** (*The Quest*, 7).

**Why it is not fence-sitting.** The category is not a compromise between two real options but a description of what was normal. Deep reverence for the Imams as sources of esoteric knowledge, held without the juridical and political commitments of Twelver Shiʿism, was a defining feature of fifteenth-century Islamic religiosity — most of all in Iran, and most of all among esotericists. Reading the period through the hardened Safavid confessional boundary that came *after* it produces a question the sources are not answering.

**How it shows up in the work.** Ibn Turka identifies the greatest exponents of the perennial philosophy as the Imams and the ancients together with their disciples in every age, the *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*. He reports that Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted the science of letters and that those who cleave to the threshold of his [[walaya|walāya]] have written much on it. The Imams function as guarantors of **knowledge**, which is a different office from the one Twelver jurisprudence assigns them.

**The historiographical payoff.** Insisting on the label 'Shiʿi' or 'Sunni' for Ibn Turka does not sharpen the picture, it flattens it — and, as with the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd*]], the flattening has consequences: a man sorted into a confessional box is easy to file as a mystical philosopher and hard to see as an [[occult-science-universal|occult philosopher]] with a systematic programme.

## What the Imams are for

The distinguishing feature of the position is **what office the Imams hold in it**. In
Twelver Shiʿism they are the legitimate political and juridical authority, and the
consequences are legal and constitutional. In imamophilism they are **guarantors of
knowledge** — the channel through which the occult sciences were transmitted and
authenticated.

The evidence is in what Ibn Turka says about them. Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq **greatly vaunted**
the science of letters, and **those who cleave to the threshold of his [[walaya|walāya]] have
penned numerous works on the subject**. The Imams appear as the head of a *bibliography*.

The strongest instance is [[jafr|jafr]], letter divination, whose inventor is held to be
**ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib** — and who, in this tradition, **was hailed the chief mathematician of
Islam**. That epithet is imamophilism in one phrase: reverence for the first Imam expressed
as a claim about his standing in a *science*.

## Why the period produced it

Because the alternative had not yet hardened. The Safavid consolidation after 1501 made
Persia confessionally Twelver and forced a choice that fifteenth-century scholars had not
been obliged to make. Melvin-Koushki's point is that Shiʿi-Sunnism is **a defining feature of
9th/15th-century Islamic religiosity**, particularly in Iran and particularly in esotericist
circles — the normal condition of the milieu, not a hedge within it.

[[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] himself was **known for his imamophilism and esotericist
bent**, which is presumably part of why he and Ibn Turka suited each other. The patron and
the philosopher occupied the same unnamed middle.

## The damage the anachronism does

Sorting Ibn Turka into a confessional box is not a harmless simplification. Henry Corbin's
warm embrace of him as a **standard-issue Shiʿi esotericist** and Leonard Lewisohn's reading
of him as an **orthodox Sunni Sufi thinker** are opposite errors with a common structure:
each takes a post-Safavid category and applies it to a pre-Safavid man.

And each produces a figure who is easy to file and hard to see. The de facto consensus
presents him as a mystical philosopher, **effectively obscuring his explicitly occultist
project** — and a confessional label is one of the instruments by which that obscuring
happens, because it answers the question of what kind of thinker he was before the question
has been properly asked.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Imamophilism is the confessional setting of the whole project; it explains why the Imams appear as authorities on lettrism without the entry being a Shiʿi one.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Quest for a Universal Science* (PhD diss., Yale, 2012), 6–7.

concepts.name: Jafr
concepts.card: **Jafr** — letter divination, and the political edge of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]]. Its inventor is held to be **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib**, who in this tradition is hailed **the chief mathematician of Islam**; its foundational text is the *K. al-Jafr wa-l-Jāmiʿa*, an omniscient book recording past and future history and all knowledge of the cosmos. The dissertation gives it a chapter, under the heading **political uses of lettrism**.
concepts.body:
## What it is for

Where [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] in general is a science of what letters are, *jafr* is the application that tells you **what is going to happen**. The dissertation places its definition at the head of Chapter 5, **Political uses of lettrism** (§5.1), followed by **lettrist political divination based on the Qur'an** (§5.2). The classification is the argument: this is the branch that touches power.

## The founding attribution

Jafr's inventor is **ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib**, and the phrase Melvin-Koushki records for his standing in the later tradition is remarkable: ʿAlī, inventor of letter divination, **was hailed the chief mathematician of Islam** (*Another Scientific Revolution*, 8).

That is [[pythagorean-cosmology|the reclassification]] in a single epithet. Calling the first Imam a mathematician rather than a gnostic relocates the whole discipline: it is not that the Imams had secret knowledge, it is that they had **exact** knowledge, and exact knowledge belongs among the mathematical sciences.

## The omniscient book

The science of letters entered Islam at its inception in the **messianic-gnostic syncretism of the early *ghulāt***, and was associated in more sedate Shiʿi circles with the ***K. al-Jafr wa-l-Jāmiʿa* of ʿAlī** — **an omniscient text recording past and future history and all knowledge of the cosmos** (*The Quest*, 22).

The dual genealogy matters. Lettrism has, from the beginning, both an extreme wing and a respectable one, and the [[hurufism|three-strand]] distinction Ibn Turka's career depends on is a late episode in a very old sorting problem.

A story preserved in the tradition shows what possession of such a book was taken to mean. Offered the caliphate by al-Maʾmūn, the Imam replied that the compact would come to nothing; asked how he knew, he said: **'It is counterindicated in the Jafr and Jāmiʿ.'** The document of compact itself is said to have carried the line, *I have written this in accordance with your desire, but the Jafr and Jāmiʿ indicate the contrary* (*Better Than Sufi Sex*, 23).

## Incarnating the Imams

The link to [[walaya|walāya]] is direct and is put in strong terms. Occultists of this period seize on these sciences as **both the primary mode of philosophical praxis and the best means of harnessing walāya — which is to say, of magically incarnating the Imams** (*Another Scientific Revolution*, 8).

Jafr is therefore not fortune-telling with letters. It is a claim to participate in the Imams' knowledge, which is why it is simultaneously a science, a devotion and a political instrument, and why a court would pay for it.

## The Ottoman success

The clearest demonstration of what jafr could become is not Iranian. [[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Bisṭāmī's]] ***Miftāḥ al-jafr al-jāmiʿ***, the *Key to the Comprehensive Prognosticon*, **came to function in the 10th/16th century as a dynastic handbook, whereby the political fate of the House of ʿOs̱mān could be effectively managed over the generations** (*Another Scientific Revolution*, 2).

A manual of letter divination operating as an instrument of dynastic management across generations is the most concrete evidence available for Melvin-Koushki's claim that the Ottoman branch of the network was **more successful**. Ibn Turka was tried three times; his counterpart's book became state equipment.

## Ibn Turka's family and jafr

His son **Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb Allāh** appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise entitled ***Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ*** (*The Quest*, 41) — the son of a man exiled on occultist charges writing on the political-divinatory branch specifically.

## What we do not know

- **Ibn Turka's own jafr practice**, if any. The dissertation treats political uses of lettrism as a chapter; whether he cast prognostications himself is not established here.
- **Whether the *K. al-Jafr wa-l-Jāmiʿa* ever existed as a text** in the form the tradition describes.
- **The contents of his son's treatise.**
concepts.hierarchy_note: Jafr is the political-divinatory branch of lettrism; the dissertation treats it under 'political uses of lettrism'.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Another Scientific Revolution*, 2, 8.
Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 22, 41, ch. 5.
Melvin-Koushki, *Better Than Sufi Sex*, 23.

concepts.name: Neoplatonism
concepts.card: **Neoplatonism**. The late-antique emanationist philosophy of Plotinus and Proclus, which reached Islamdom in Arabic translation and was never, in Melvin-Koushki's usage, quite separable from its Pythagorean twin — he writes of *neopythagorean-neoplatonic* philosophy as one tradition. Ibn Turka's contribution was not to receive it but to **reclassify** it: he treated this philosophy as prophetically revealed rather than merely Greek, and made its mathematics the ground on which the occult sciences could be defended as sciences at all.
concepts.body:
## Neoplatonism, and what Ibn Turka did to it

**The tradition.** Neoplatonism — the emanationist system of Plotinus (d. 270), systematised by Porphyry and Proclus — holds that reality flows from a transcendent One through descending grades of being, and that the soul ascends by retracing that descent. It entered Arabic through the translation movement, generally fused with Pythagorean number-metaphysics. Melvin-Koushki treats the pair as a single tradition throughout, writing of **neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy** rather than of two separable schools (*Powers of One*, 127–28).

**The problem it was made to solve.** By Ibn Turka's lifetime the occult sciences — *al-ʿulūm al-gharība*, the 'strange sciences' — had absorbed four centuries of hostile polemic from a formidable coalition. Melvin-Koushki notes that anti-occultism is one of the few subjects on which philosophers like Ibn Sīnā, theologians like Ghazālī, traditionalists like Ibn Taymiyya and historians like Ibn Khaldūn find common cause, joined by al-Ashʿarī, Fārābī, al-Bāqillānī and Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār (*Powers of One*, 1). The charge was that these were not sciences.

**Ibn Turka's contribution.** The Persianate answer, of which he is the central theoretician, was to **move the occult sciences out of the natural sciences and into the mathematical sciences** — a reclassification that reasserted their legitimacy on ground the polemicists could not easily contest (*Powers of One*, 1). Melvin-Koushki names the threefold process **mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification**, and locates it in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran. Neoplatonism is the metaphysics that makes the move coherent: if being descends by graded emanation, and number governs the descent, then a science of number and letter is a science of causation itself.

**The move that was genuinely his.** Ibn Turka did not present this philosophy as a Greek inheritance. He identified its greatest exponents — the Imams and the ancients, with their disciples in every age — with the quranic phrase *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*, 'those possessed of hands and vision': the coterie of inspired thinkers who preserved **prophetically revealed** neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy in written form. The philosophy is therefore not borrowed but recovered, and its authority revelatory rather than merely rational. The phrase appears to have entered common usage as a designation for sages and philosophers generally from Ibn Turka onward (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

**What changed.** The consequences ran well past his death. Melvin-Koushki argues that this mathematicalization is the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context both for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the Samarkand Observatory in the 9th/15th century and for the resurgence of neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy in Safavid Iran in the 10th/16th and 11th/17th — in the course of which **Ibn Sīnā himself, the tradition's most formidable anti-occultist, was posthumously transformed into a neopythagorean-occultist** (*Powers of One*, 1). These processes, he notes, have previously been studied in atomistic isolation.

## Why the pair is never separated

Melvin-Koushki writes throughout of **neopythagorean-neoplatonic** philosophy as one thing,
and the hyphen is a considered position rather than shorthand. In late antiquity the two
were already fused: Plotinus and Proclus are read through number, and the Pythagorean
material reaches the Arabic tradition inside a Neoplatonic frame rather than beside it.

The consequence for reading this portal is that **emanation and number are two descriptions
of one structure**. Emanation says being descends by grades; number says the grades stand in
determinate ratios. A science that works the ratios is therefore working the descent, which
is what licenses the claim that [[ilm-al-huruf|a science of letters]] is a science of
causation.

## The afterlife, and the reversal

The most striking evidence that this framework won is what happened to its opponent.
Melvin-Koushki tracks a **resurgence of neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy in Safavid
Iran in the 10th/16th and 11th/17th centuries**, in the course of which **Ibn Sīnā himself
was transformed into a neopythagorean-occultist** (*Powers of One*, 1).

[[mir-damad|Mīr Dāmād]] is the figure held largely responsible, through adherence to a
particular brand of **Mamluk–Timurid–Aqquyunlu philosophical lettrism** in at least three of
his works. The chain in that phrase is the transmission history compressed: Cairo, then Ibn
Turka's Iran, then the Turkman courts, then Safavid Isfahan.

## The claim about the field

Worth recording as Melvin-Koushki puts it, because it is a charge and not just an emphasis.
The Neoplatonic and perennialist-antiquarian character of Safavid philosophy is, he grants,
**widely recognised**. But few have admitted its **equally remarkable neopythagorean turn** —
and the principal mode in which that philosophy was **lived as a Safavid imperial way of
life**, namely occult science, has been **completely ignored**, which makes a history of its
practice impossible (*World as (Arabic) Text*).
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: The Mathematicalization of the Occult Sciences in the High Persianate Tradition*, 1, 127–28.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.

concepts.name: Occult Science as Universal System
concepts.card: **Occult Science as Universal System**. The core historiographical claim that Ibn Turka and the Isfahan Circle systematized Islamic lettrism, talismanism, and numerology into a comprehensive philosophy claiming universal validity—a science encompassing metaphysics, epistemology, ethics, cosmology, and operative practice. Not marginal superstition but legitimate intellectual achievement rivaling any philosophical school. Melvin-Koushki's central argument.
concepts.body:
The claim that Islamic occultism constitutes a genuine universal science—this is the animating thesis of Melvin-Koushki's entire body of work and the central historiographical claim of Ibn Turka's own project. What did occultism offer that rational philosophy did not? (1) Integration of knowledge and practice: peripatetic philosophy described the cosmos; occult science engaged it operatively. (2) Rigor grounded in systematic principle: not folk magic or superstition but coherent system derived from fundamental doctrines (divine names, letters, Pythagorean numbers). (3) Universality: not provincial tradition but claim to encompass all knowledge—metaphysics via cosmology, epistemology via gnosis, ethics via attunement to cosmic principles. (4) Legitimacy within orthodoxy: by grounding lettrist science in Ibn Arabi's metaphysics and Pythagorean philosophy, Ibn Turka positioned it not as heresy but as sophisticated development within Islamic orthodoxy. The claim to universality is not arrogance but serious metaphysical commitment: if letters are cosmic principles and divine names are ontological foundations, then knowledge of letters and names is knowledge of reality itself—hence universal. This positioning of occult science as universal system represents a major historiographical revaluation: instead of viewing Islamic philosophy as decline into mysticism and formalism, we see a tradition of genuine innovation and intellectual achievement.

## What 'universal' is actually claiming

The word is doing precise work and is worth unpacking, because it is the claim on which everything else rests.

A science is universal, in Ibn Turka's sense, if its object is the principle by which all things are constituted. His argument is that letters and [[divine-names|divine names]] are exactly that: creation unfolds through them, so knowledge of them is knowledge of creation as such, and not of one region of it. This is why he is not content to place [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] among the sciences — a science of everything cannot be one item in a list.

The claim is also what distinguishes his project from what preceded it. Occult practice before him could be defended as *useful*, or as *permitted*, or as *inherited*. Ibn Turka defends it as **systematic**: derived from stated principles, answerable to [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematics]], and therefore assessable as true or false rather than merely effective or ineffective. That is the difference between a body of technique and a philosophy, and it is the difference he spent the *Mafāḥiṣ* establishing.

It should be said plainly that the claim is very strong and was not conceded. The [[neoplatonism|anti-occultist coalition]] — Ibn Sīnā, [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]], Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn Khaldūn — denied that these were sciences at all, and Ibn Turka's move into the mathematical sciences is an answer to them rather than a victory over them.

## The verification claim underneath it

The universality claim is, in the period's own vocabulary, a **[[tahqiq-taqlid|taḥqīq]]**
claim rather than a preference between schools. Ibn Turka is not saying that lettrism suits
him better than philosophy; he is saying the matter has been **worked through to its ground**
and philosophy has been found wanting on terrain it claimed as its own.

That is why the argument is conducted against [[peripatetic-philosophy|the peripatetics]]
rather than against sceptics. A discipline that merely wanted to be tolerated would argue
with its detractors. A discipline claiming to have verified something argues with whoever
currently holds the position it wants.

## The two audiences, and why both were needed

The portal's [[walaya|walāya]] entry sets out the double move — mathematicalization to
answer the philosophers, sanctification to answer the court — and the universality claim
sits on top of both. Neither alone would carry it.

Mathematics establishes that the science *has a subject*, against the charge that it deals
in unverifiable sympathies. Sanctity establishes *who may practise it*, which is what turns a
demonstrated science into a fundable one. Universality is the claim the two together
license: a science whose object is the principles by which all things are constituted, and
whose practitioners stand close enough to God to work them.

## What it cost to claim it

A maximal claim invites a maximal response, and the [[hurufism|three tribunals]] are what a
maximal response looks like. It is worth registering that Ibn Turka could have had a quiet
career: the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]] shows he was entirely capable of
respectable scholastic metaphysics, and it is the book that made his modern reputation.
The universality claim is the thing he did not have to make.
concepts.hierarchy_note: This historiographical frame unites all entries; it is the meta-argument justifying the entire project.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography.

concepts.name: Oneiromancy (ʿilm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā)
concepts.literal_meaning: The science of the interpretation of dream-visions
concepts.card: **ʿIlm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā** — the science of dream interpretation, and the occult science this portal has most consistently underrated. Melvin-Koushki ranks it **second in popularity only to astrology** across the early modern Islamicate world, ahead of [[geomancy|geomancy]] and [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] alike. Its classificatory definition is unusually precise: physiognomy inquires into the inner states of rational souls **while they are conscious**, and oneiromancy does the same **while they are unconscious**. Both are readings of a soul; only the soul's condition differs.
concepts.body:
## ʿIlm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā: The Science of Dream Interpretation

### Where it sits

Oneiromancy (Arabic *ʿilm taʿbīr al-ruʾyā*, Persian *ʿilm-i taʿbīr*) is classified among
the **applied natural sciences** — not the mathematical ones — in the classifications of
the sciences Melvin-Koushki works from. It appears in the standard list alongside medicine,
veterinary medicine and falconry, physiognomy, judicial astrology, magic, talismans and
illusionism.

> Melvin-Koushki, *Another Scientific Revolution*, 6.

Its placement there is argued, not arbitrary, and the argument is the most useful sentence
in the entry:

> "Physiognomy then inquires into the inner states of rational human souls while they are
> conscious, and oneiromancy does the same while they are unconscious."

> *Another Scientific Revolution*, 6, quoting the classification at Melvin-Koushki 2017, 17.

So oneiromancy is not a separate faculty from reading a face. It is the same operation —
inferring an interior state from an exterior sign — performed on a soul that has gone
offline. That is a claim about *continuity between waking and sleeping cognition*, and it is
what makes the science respectable rather than folkloric in these classifications.

### How popular, actually

Very. The ranking is consistent across at least five separate places in the corpus, always
in the same form: geomancy is described as "third in popularity **only to astrology and
oneiromancy**" throughout the early modern Western (variously Islamo-Judeo-Christian,
Helleno-Judeo-Christo-Islamic) world.

> Melvin-Koushki, *Divining Past, Present, and Future in the Sand*, 1;
> *Geomancy in the Islamic World*, 1; *In Defense of Geomancy*, 6;
> Melvin-Koushki and Cummins, *Geomancing Is Googling*, 2.

Read that the other way and it says: **dream divination outranked geomancy, lettrism and
every operative occult science except astrology.** The portal's coverage does not currently
reflect that, which is worth noticing.

It also enjoyed heavy royal patronage in exactly the company you would expect: "astrology,
lettrism, geomancy, oneiromancy and physiognomy in particular enjoyed heavy royal
patronage."

> *Another Scientific Revolution*, 1.

The Ottoman **Sultan Murad III** (r. 1574–1595), "highly sensitive to his own status as
king of the millennium," invested heavily in Sufism and the occult sciences,
"particularly astrology and oneiromancy," while identifying his royal persona with ʿAlī in
the time-honoured Timurid-Safavid manner.

> Melvin-Koushki, *Early Modern Islamicate Empire*, 16.

### Ibn Turka's stake in it

The corpus does **not** preserve a dream narrative of Ibn Turka's own — see the caution
below. What it does preserve is his epistemology, and dreaming is load-bearing in it.
Melvin-Koushki describes Ibn Turka's position as the elegant dissolution of the Science
versus Religion binary, on the grounds that

> "empirical observation and dreamtime intuition are equally important to the business of
> Science."

> Melvin-Koushki, *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 15 (n. 33).

That is not a concession to piety. It is a claim that the sleeping mind is an instrument,
and it belongs beside his demand — against Suhrawardī's ascent-only sensorium — that a
total system requires **descent** (*tanzīl*) as well as ascent.

> *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 2.

### The dream as evidence

One concrete case of dream-vision doing evidentiary work in this literature. The attribution
of the invention of Kufic script is contested between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn Muqla.
Āmulī simply reports that scholars differ. Qāżī Aḥmad, writing an album preface in the
10th/16th-century imperial Twelver context, instead supplies **a dream-vision narrative to
resolve the attribution in favour of ʿAlī**.

> Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 44.

A dream settles a philological dispute. That is oneiromancy operating not as divination
about the future but as a warrant about the past — and it happens inside the album-preface
genre that Melvin-Koushki elsewhere says embodies Ibn Turka's ontogrammatology.

### Caution — an absence, recorded

**No attested dream or vision narrative of Ibn Turka's own has been located in this
corpus.** Searching it for `dream` returns 25 hits in the Yale dissertation alone, but they
are overwhelmingly the term used analytically or metaphorically rather than a report of
something he dreamt. Anything built on "Ibn Turka's visionary life" should therefore be
built as **practice** — a technique the sources describe, with the cost they specify — and
not as an invented anecdote. See
[`docs/VISIONARY_ENVIRONMENTS.md`](../../docs/VISIONARY_ENVIRONMENTS.md), which states this
rule for the game work, and `khalʿ` (doffing the body) for the technique itself.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Classified among the APPLIED NATURAL sciences, not the mathematical ones, and paired with physiognomy: both read the inner state of a rational soul from an outward sign, physiognomy while it is conscious and oneiromancy while it is not. Second in popularity only to astrology across the early modern Islamicate world, ahead of geomancy and lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Another Scientific Revolution*, 1, 6, 7.
Melvin-Koushki, *Early Modern Islamicate Empire*, 16.
Melvin-Koushki, *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 2, 15.
Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 44.
Melvin-Koushki, *In Defense of Geomancy*, 6; *Geomancy in the Islamic World*, 1.

concepts.name: Peripatetic Philosophy
concepts.literal_meaning: Philosophy of those who walk (Aristotelian school)
concepts.card: **Al-Falsafa al-Mashaʾiya** (Peripatetic Philosophy). The Aristotelian philosophical tradition as transmitted and developed in Islamic world. Emphasizes rational inquiry, logical syllogism, study of natural world, metaphysics grounded in being and causation. Ibn Turka synthesized peripatetic logic and metaphysics with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], arguing that occult science achieves what peripatetic philosophy merely attempts—systematic knowledge of causation and being.
concepts.body:
**Peripatetic philosophy** (*al-falsafa al-mashaʾiya*) refers to the Aristotelian tradition as developed and transmitted in the Islamic world. The name derives from Aristotle's practice of teaching while walking (*peripateo*) in the Lyceum. Islamic philosophers—al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Ibn Sina—adopted and adapted Aristotelian logic, metaphysics, and natural philosophy, integrating them with Islamic theology and the philosophical heritage of Greek Neoplatonism. Key commitments: (1) Reason (*ʿaql*) is primary tool for understanding reality. (2) Logic (syllogistic reasoning) provides rigorous methodology. (3) Being (*wujud*) is fundamental category; understanding causation requires understanding gradations and dependencies of being. (4) Metaphysics is possible: systematic knowledge of principles transcending particular things. By Ibn Turka's era, peripatetic philosophy was the dominant intellectual framework across Islamic world. But Ibn Turka and his circle saw its limitations: peripatetic method, while rigorous, remained abstract and speculative. It described cosmic structure but did not engage it operatively. Peripatetic philosophers asked *how* creation unfolds; Ibn Turka asked *how to participate in its unfolding*. By integrating peripatetic logic with [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], Ibn Turka claimed to achieve what peripatetic philosophy merely attempted—systematic, rationally grounded knowledge of causation and being that is simultaneously operative (producing real effects). In this sense, Ibn Turka's system transcends peripatetic philosophy by incorporating and surpassing it.

## The opponent that defines the project

Ibn Turka's argument is not conducted against superstition or against Sufism. It is
conducted against **the discipline that held the prestige**, and the sharpness of his claim
only registers if that is kept in view: the faux-universal concepts of philosophical
speculation notwithstanding, only the letter encompasses all that is and is not, all that
can and cannot be; it alone is the *coincidentia oppositorum*; hence lettrism is **the only
truly universal science** (*The Quest*, iii).

"Faux-universal" is the operative insult. Peripatetic metaphysics claims to treat being *qua*
being — the most general subject there is. Ibn Turka's counter is that a concept ranges over
the actual and the possible and stops there, while the letter reaches also to non-being and
impossibility. On that argument philosophy's universality is a boast its instruments cannot
support.

## The other side of the ledger

The relationship is not simple opposition, and the portal would mislead if it said so. Ibn
Sīnā is one of the three positions the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd al-Qawāʿid*]] synthesises,
alongside [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardī]] and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]]/[[qunavi|Qūnavī]], on
absolute being. Ibn Turka is a competent peripatetic before he is a critic of peripateticism,
and the *Mafāḥiṣ* argues in a vocabulary the philosophers built.

He also has a treatise **against Avicenna on the senses**, and the sensorium article is
devoted to his Pythagorean elevation of sight over hearing as vehicle of total perception —
a technical disagreement conducted on peripatetic ground rather than a refusal of it.

## Ibn Sīnā the anti-occultist, and his afterlife

The most striking fact in this relationship is the reversal. Ibn Sīnā heads the
[[neoplatonism|anti-occultist coalition]] — with Ghazālī, Ibn Taymiyya and Ibn Khaldūn —
whose four centuries of polemic the mathematicalization was designed to answer
(*Powers of One*, 1).

And then, in Safavid Iran, in the resurgence of neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy that
followed, **Ibn Sīnā himself was transformed into a neopythagorean-occultist**. The
tradition's chief prosecutor was posthumously enrolled in the defence.

## What we do not know

- **Which peripatetic texts Ibn Turka taught or commented on** beyond what the *Tamhīd*
  implies is not established here.
- **The treatise against Avicenna on the senses** is discussed in the sensorium article but
  is not edited in the corpus in hand.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Peripatetic philosophy is the dominant rational framework Ibn Turka synthesizes with and transcends through lettrism.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. Powers of One, pp. 100-140.

concepts.name: Pythagorean Cosmology
concepts.card: **Pythagorean Cosmology**. The ancient Greek doctrine that numbers and their ratios are the fundamental principles governing reality. Ibn Turka's distinctive contribution was grounding Islamic [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] explicitly in Pythagorean mathematics, arguing that letters and their [[abjad-numerology|numerical values]] encode cosmic principles just as Pythagoras taught that mathematics is the language of creation. This synthesis gave Islamic lettrism mathematical legitimacy and positioned it as a **truly universal science** encompassing reason, mysticism, and operative power.
concepts.body:
## Pythagorean Cosmology in Islamic Context

Pythagorean philosophy (c. 580–500 BCE) teaches that numbers are the fundamental constituents of reality. Numbers, through their ratios and relationships, generate harmony, order, and all manifestation. This worldview emphasizes that the cosmos is knowable through mathematics, and that mathematical knowledge grants insight into (and potentially influence over) the structure of creation.

The late-antique Neoplatonic tradition preserved and developed Pythagorean thought, eventually reaching the Islamic world through Hellenistic texts, Byzantine commentaries, and the writings of Islamic philosophers like al-Kindī and al-Fārābī. Yet lettrism in the Islamic world developed largely independently, growing from Qur'anic exegesis and gnosis without explicit Pythagorean framing.

### Ibn Turka's Innovation

Ibn Turka's genius was **explicitly connecting Islamic lettrism with Pythagorean principles**. He argued that:

1. **Letters are numbers**: Each of the 28 Arabic letters has a numerical value ([[abjad-numerology|abjad]])
2. **Numbers are cosmic**: Pythagorean mathematics describes the structure of creation
3. **Therefore, letters ARE cosmic principles**: Mastery of letters is mastery of the mathematics of creation

This move was philosophically powerful: it gave lettrism a pedigree reaching back to ancient Greece; it grounded it in mathematical reason rather than mystical intuition alone; and it positioned it as **the supreme science**, encompassing both rational (Pythagorean math) and mystical (gnostic lettrism) approaches.

By adopting the Pythagorean framework, Ibn Turka essentially reinvented lettrism as a **Neopythagorean system**—and in doing so, positioned Islamic occult philosophy as a genuine alternative universal science, rivaling and arguably exceeding the philosophical systems of contemporary Renaissance Europe.

## What the label is claiming

"Neopythagorean" is Melvin-Koushki's term of art and it is chosen against an alternative.
The conventional description of post-classical Islamic thought is *decline*: the Greek
inheritance received, digested, and then dissipated into scholasticism and mysticism.
Calling the fifteenth-century development **Neopythagorean** places it instead in a
comparative frame — as the European Renaissance rediscovered and redeployed Platonic
philosophy, so Islamicate thinkers rediscovered and redeployed Pythagorean principles.

The claim is therefore double: that something genuinely new happened, and that its shape is
recognisable from the European case without being derived from it.

## The move it names

The concrete content is the reclassification described at [[neoplatonism|Neoplatonism]] and
[[walaya|walāya]]: the occult sciences were shifted **from the natural to the mathematical
sciences**, reasserting their legitimacy against four centuries of polemic, and
simultaneously recast as sciences of sanctity (*Powers of One*, 1).

Why mathematics specifically? Because the anti-occultist attack was that these disciplines
had no demonstrable subject matter — that they dealt in sympathies and correspondences no
one could check. Mathematics was the one field whose credentials nobody disputed. Moving
[[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] into it is a jurisdictional claim before it is a metaphysical one.

## Revealed, not borrowed

Ibn Turka's own framing is not that he is importing Greek philosophy. He identifies the
greatest exponents of the perennial philosophy — the Imams and the ancients with their
disciples in every age — with the Qur'anic *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār*, **those possessed of
hands and vision**, who preserved **prophetically revealed** neopythagorean-neoplatonic
philosophy in written form (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

The philosophy is thus recovered rather than adopted, and its authority is revelatory rather
than merely rational. The phrase appears to have entered general usage for sages and
philosophers from Ibn Turka onward — a small piece of evidence that the framing took.

## The consequences downstream

Melvin-Koushki argues the same movement is the immediate context for the mathematization of
astronomy at the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]] and for the resurgence of
neoplatonic-neopythagorean philosophy in Safavid Iran — in the course of which **Ibn Sīnā
himself, the tradition's most formidable anti-occultist, was posthumously transformed into a
neopythagorean-occultist** (*Powers of One*, 1). The reclassification eventually captured
its own chief opponent.

## What we do not know

- **Which Pythagorean sources** were actually available to Ibn Turka in Arabic, and in what
  form, is not detailed in this corpus.
- **How much of the framing is his and how much Melvin-Koushki's analytical vocabulary**
  requires the unedited works to settle.


## Number as the ground of verification

The move into the mathematical sciences is usually described as a bid for prestige, and it
was that. But there is a stronger reason, and it belongs to the
[[tahqiq-taqlid|taḥqīq]] axis.

Mathematics is the discipline in which **verification is possible without appeal to
authority**. A demonstration either goes through or it does not, and no master's endorsement
improves it. For a science under four centuries of attack from a coalition that included the
most authoritative names available — Ibn Sīnā, [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]], Ibn Taymiyya, Ibn
Khaldūn — that property is not merely respectable, it is the only ground on which the
argument could be won at all. You cannot out-cite Ghazālī. You can, in principle, out-demonstrate
him.

This is why [[geomancy|geomancy]] is one of the three sciences named in the reclassification
alongside astrology and lettrism: the randomness is at the input only, and everything
downstream is deterministic combination. What a geomancer does after the marks are made is
calculate.

## Revealed rather than borrowed, and why that framing was necessary

Ibn Turka does not present this as an importation of Greek philosophy. He identifies the
perennial philosophers — the Imams and the ancients with their disciples in every age — with
the Qur'anic ***ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār***, those possessed of hands and vision, who preserved
**prophetically revealed** neopythagorean-neoplatonic philosophy in written form (*Of Islamic
Grammatology*, 66).

The framing does two jobs at once. It gives the philosophy revelatory authority rather than
merely rational authority, which matters in front of a tribunal. And it makes the science
**recovered** rather than adopted, so that pursuing it is a form of fidelity rather than of
innovation — a defence with real force in a tradition where *bidʿa*, innovation, is a charge.

That the phrase appears to have entered general usage for sages and philosophers **from Ibn
Turka onward** is small evidence that the framing took.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Pythagorean cosmology is Ibn Turka's foundational theoretical framework; it structures his entire philosophical system.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Toward a Neopythagorean Historiography*.

concepts.name: Sufism
concepts.card: **Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism). Islamic mysticism emphasizing direct experiential knowledge of the divine through discipline, contemplation, and often ecstatic experience. Developed systematically from 9th century onward; by Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was integral to Islamic orthodoxy. [[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]], and other philosophical predecessors were Sufi-philosophers. Ibn Turka inherited and operationalized Sufi gnosis through lettrism, positioning occult science as Sufi practice systematized into rational discipline.
concepts.body:
## Sufism: Islamic Mysticism and Spiritual Practice

**Al-Tasawwuf** (Sufism) is Islamic mysticism—the disciplined pursuit of direct experiential knowledge (*dhawq*; literally "tasting") of divine reality. Sufism emerged in the 8th-9th centuries as ascetic movement emphasizing renunciation, devotion, and intimate knowledge of God. By the medieval period, it had become systematized into orders (*tariqas*) with formal training, ritual practices, and hierarchical initiation. Key Sufi commitments: (1) Reason alone cannot reach ultimate truth; direct mystical intuition is necessary. (2) The soul possesses faculties beyond intellect—faculties for perceiving divine light and truth. (3) Ascetic discipline, remembrance (*dhikr*), and sincere devotion purify the soul and grant illumination. (4) The spiritual master (*shaykh*) guides disciples on the path. By Ibn Turka's era, Sufism was thoroughly integrated into Islamic orthodoxy. Major philosophical-theologians—[[ibn-arabi|Ibn Arabi]], [[suhrawardi|Suhrawardi]], [[al-ghazali|Al-Ghazali]]—were simultaneously Sufi mystics and systematic philosophers. Sufism provided the conceptual vocabulary and experiential framework for occult philosophy: if the soul can experience divine light directly, if mystical knowledge is genuine, then the soul's interaction with the imaginal realm and its deployment of lettrist gnosis are not irrational but expressions of mystical capacity. Ibn Turka inherited Sufi gnosis and transformed it: where Sufi masters cultivated mystical states through meditation and discipline, Ibn Turka systematized the underlying principles and made them operative through lettrist-talismanic technique. Sufi mysticism became Sufi science.

## Experience as evidence

The Sufi claim that matters most for Ibn Turka's project is epistemological rather than devotional: that direct experiential knowledge — *dhawq*, tasting — is **knowledge**, not feeling. [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]] had established that much for the mainstream, and once it is granted, the soul's perception of the [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]] counts as evidence rather than as reverie.

Ibn Turka takes the concession and does something with it the Sufi tradition largely had not. Where a Sufi master cultivated states through discipline and remembrance, he systematised the principles those states disclose and made them operative through [[ilm-al-huruf|letters]]. Contemplation becomes computation. That is also, precisely, the move his critics objected to — and it is why his relations with organised Sufism were as awkward as [[qasim-i-anvar|his letters]] show them to be: he kept the company of Sufis while criticising the institution in print.

## The specific quarrel

Ibn Turka's relation to Sufism is not the simple debt it is usually described as, and the
sources let us see the friction.

**In print he criticised organised Sufism**, and in the [[nafsat-al-masdur|apologies]] he
describes his dealings with prominent Sufi shaykhs as **primarily admonitory** — he was
correcting them. **In his letters** he maintains friendly relations with the leading Iranian
Sufis of the day: Shāh Niʿmat Allāh Valī, [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], Aḥmad Samarqandī,
Ḥasan ʿAṭṭār, Sayyid Muḥammad b. Shaykh Kajujī.

Melvin-Koushki treats the discrepancy as evidence rather than inconsistency. The letters
**corroborate** what the apologies claim about the contacts, and the first three of those men
were **great promoters of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] in the face of often hostile reaction** —
which identifies the basis of the friendship (*The Quest*, 136). He objected to the
institution and allied with individuals on Akbarian grounds.

## Where the strands separate

The portal's [[hurufism|three-lettrisms]] distinction runs through here. There is a **Sufi
lettrism** — devotional, contemplative, embedded in the orders — and Ibn Turka's
**intellectual lettrism** is defined against it as much as against the
gnostic-messianic strand. Same material, different discipline.

The difference is what the practitioner is for. A Sufi master cultivates states; the
knowledge is the by-product of a transformation. Ibn Turka systematises the principles those
states disclose and makes them operative through [[ilm-al-huruf|letters]] and calculation.
The intersection essay on the Akbarian inheritance calls it contemplation converted to
computation.

## The charge it produced

This is not an abstract taxonomy. Around 825/1422 his opponents went to
[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] court and accused him of **Sufi bias**
([[first-inquisition|the first inquisition]]) — a charge that works precisely because the
associations were real and the doctrinal distance was invisible from outside. He answered it
in person and was given the judgeship of Yazd.

## What we do not know

- **Whether he was formally affiliated** to any order. The sources in hand describe contacts,
  not membership.
- **What his criticisms of organised Sufism actually say** — they are referred to rather than
  quoted in this corpus.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Sufism is the experiential-spiritual foundation upon which Ibn Turka builds his rational occult science; all mystical vocabulary derives from Sufi tradition.
literature: Chittick, William C. The Sufi Path of Knowledge: Ibn Arabi's Metaphysics of Imagination.

concepts.name: Talismanic Science
concepts.card: **ilm al-Talasim** (Talismanic Science). Operative practice of creating talismans inscribed with letters, numbers, divine names. Based on theory that letters, numerical correspondences, and divine names are cosmic principles that, combined correctly with proper intention, exert force through intermediate realm. Central practical application of Ibn Turka's system.
concepts.body:
**Talismanic science** (ilm al-talasim) is the operative discipline of creating objects—rings, seals, parchments, metals—inscribed with carefully chosen letters, numbers, and divine names to accomplish specific aims. Unlike superstition, talismanic science in Ibn Turka's systematization is grounded in rigorous cosmological theory. A talisman works: (1) Each 28 Arabic letter corresponds to divine name and cosmic power. (2) Combining letters by numerical correspondence (*abjad*) aligns word with specific principle (Venus, al-Alim, etc.). (3) Inscribing this word-object on appropriate matter with proper intention embodies the principle. (4) Through intermediate realm, talismanic object exerts influence—attracting love, granting wisdom, protecting. Creating talisman requires: knowledge of letter values and divine correspondences, understanding of cosmic geometry and celestial timing, appropriate mental state, correct materials, proper ritual. In Ibn Turka's framework, talismanic science is not magic compelling spirits but sophisticated technology of imaginal realm. Talismans work because they express cosmic principles; they align practitioner's will with creation's structure. This gives talismanic practice philosophical and theological legitimacy: not sorcery but gnosis applied to practice.

## The theory that makes it not-magic

The distinction the tradition insists on is between compelling a spirit and deploying a
principle. A talisman on Ibn Turka's account does not summon anything. It is an object
composed so that its formal structure — the letters chosen, their
[[abjad-numerology|numerical sum]], the [[divine-names|names]] they answer to, the geometry
of their arrangement, the timing of the making — corresponds to a cosmic principle, and it
takes effect because correspondence at the [[barzakh|intermediate level]] propagates
outward.

That is why the practice can be presented as **science rather than sorcery**: it claims to
work by understood law rather than by negotiation with persons. Whether a tribunal accepts
the distinction is another matter, and the first inquisition turned on exactly this — the
charge framed around Qur'an 2:102 and the angels at Babel, the defence a separation of
theoretical lettrism from sorcery.

## The three-stage history

Melvin-Koushki gives the operative tradition a compact periodisation
(*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70):

1. **Thirteenth century** — the Ibn ʿArabian-Būnian **science of the saints**
   (*ʿilm al-awliyāʾ*) par excellence.
2. **Fourteenth century** — **de-esotericized and adabized** through incorporation into the
   Mamluk literary-political mainstream.
3. **Turn of the fifteenth** — **neopythagoreanized** by the occultists who would form the
   [[new-brethren-purity|Brethren]].

The middle stage is the surprising one and worth holding onto: before it was mathematicised
it was made *literary*, absorbed into the polite letters of the Mamluk court. Operative
lettrism arrived in Ibn Turka's hands having already been domesticated once.

## The al-Būnī inheritance

The practical literature descends from the *Shams al-Maʿārif* tradition attributed to
al-Būnī — magic squares, divine names deployed for effect, procedures with materials and
timings. [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] is described as the **conscious heir of both
al-Būnī and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]]** (*Powers of One*, 6), and that double inheritance is
where the manual meets the metaphysics.

The intersection essay on al-Būnī puts the difference as manual versus system: al-Būnī gives
procedures, Ibn Turka gives the account of why procedures of that kind should work at all.

## The court application

This is not private practice. The [[isfahan-circle|occult court]] entry describes talismanic
knowledge deployed for dynastic protection, campaign timing and political counsel, and
*Imperial Talismanic Love* reads a late work of Ibn Turka's as a **lettrist mirror for
princes**. Talismanic science is, among other things, a service profession with state
clients.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka personally made talismans** is not documented in these sources; the
  [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] treats *al-awfāq* theoretically.
- **The actual procedures** he endorsed survive in the unedited works.
- **How the tribunals' charge was framed in detail** beyond the Qur'anic hook is not
  recorded.


## The charge, and the defence

The [[first-inquisition|first tribunal]] framed its accusation around **Qur'an 2:102 and the
angels at Babel who taught men magic**: whatever you call your *ʿilm al-ḥurūf*, the
prosecution said, this is what it descends from.

That is a well-chosen attack. The verse is the tradition's standard scriptural warrant
against magic, and it works by genealogy rather than by definition — it does not require
showing what the defendant does, only where his discipline comes from.

The defence available is the one the portal states throughout: **a mathematics of letters is
not an operation on spirits.** A talisman does not summon anything; it is an object whose
formal structure corresponds to a cosmic principle and which takes effect because
correspondence at the [[barzakh|intermediate level]] propagates outward. Whether a panel
accepts the distinction is a separate question from whether it is real.

## The literature and its rival

The operative tradition descends from the *Shams al-Maʿārif* corpus attributed to **al-Būnī**
— procedures, magic squares, names deployed for effect. [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] is
the **conscious heir of both al-Būnī and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]]**, which is where the
manual meets the metaphysics.

The portal's intersection essay on al-Būnī puts the difference as **manual versus system**:
al-Būnī supplies procedures; Ibn Turka supplies the account of why procedures of that kind
should work at all. The essay also notes the uncomfortable corollary — that at a tribunal,
**the prosecution borrows the practitioner's own vocabulary**. A science that has explained
its own mechanism has also explained how to indict it.

## Court work

*Imperial Talismanic Love* reads a late work of Ibn Turka's — the *Debate of Feast and
Fight*, 1426, written in the middle of the years of accusation — as simultaneously
philosophical romance and **lettrist mirror for princes**. Talismanic competence in this
world is not private practice; it is counsel, and it is billable.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Talismanic science is primary practical expression of lettrism; demonstrates operative efficacy.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. The Occult Court, Ch. 4.

concepts.name: Walāya
concepts.literal_meaning: Sainthood; sanctity; proximity to God; the authority of the friend of God
concepts.card: **Walāya** — sainthood, or the authority that comes of proximity to God. The most consequential reclassification in Melvin-Koushki's account, and the one usually missed: alongside their move into the mathematical sciences, the occult sciences were recast as **sciences of walāya**. This, he argues, is what *alone* explains the surge in patronage of professional occultists at the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium (1592 CE). A science of walāya is not a technique anyone may practise; it is the prerogative of the sanctified.
concepts.body:
## Walāya: occultism as a science of sanctity

**The term.** *Walāya* denotes sainthood, sanctity, and the proximity to God from which spiritual authority derives; a *walī* is a friend of God. In Shiʿi usage it carries the further charge of the Imams' authority. This is not peripheral vocabulary: it recurs across every major source in the corpus, some two hundred times in total.

**The reclassification.** Melvin-Koushki's thesis has two limbs, and walāya is the one usually overlooked. The occult sciences were shifted from the natural to the [[neoplatonism|mathematical]] sciences to reassert their scientific legitimacy; they were **simultaneously reclassified as the sciences of walāya**. He is emphatic about the explanatory weight the second move carries — it *alone*, he writes, explains the massive increase in patronage of professional occultists at the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium of 1592 CE (*Powers of One*, 1).

**Why the second limb matters.** Mathematicalization answers the epistemological objection: is this a science? Sanctification answers a different and, at court, more urgent question: who may practise it, and why should a ruler pay for them? A science of walāya cannot be picked up by anyone with a manual. It belongs to those near to God — which makes the occultist not a technician but a figure of religious authority, and his patronage a matter of dynastic legitimacy rather than curiosity. This is the mechanism underneath the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]].

**The Shiʿi thread.** The lineage runs through the Imams. Ibn Turka reports that the holy Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted the science of letters, and that 'those who cleave to the threshold of his walāya have penned numerous works on the subject' (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66). Walāya is thus at once the ground of the science's authority and the channel of its transmission — the reason a chain of lettrist writing exists at all.

**Bearing on Ibn Turka.** It positions him. He is not merely systematising a technique; he is claiming for [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] the standing of a sanctified science, whose exponents are the *ūlū l-aydī wa-l-abṣār* — the Imams, the ancients and their disciples in every age — who preserved prophetically revealed philosophy in written form. It also explains how the science travelled after him: what reached the Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts was not a body of techniques but a claim about who stands close to God.

## Why "sanctification" is the second half of a two-part thesis

It is easy to read Melvin-Koushki as arguing one thing — that the occult sciences were
mathematicalized — and to treat walāya as a footnote. The text does not permit that. The
formulation is deliberately double: the occult sciences **were gradually but definitively
shifted from the natural to the mathematical sciences** as a means of reasserting their
scientific legitimacy, and **they were simultaneously reclassified as the sciences of
walāya** (*Powers of One*, 1).

The two moves answer different objections from different audiences.

**Mathematicalization answers the philosophers.** Against Ibn Sīnā, Ghazālī, Ibn Taymiyya
and Ibn Khaldūn, who denied that these were sciences at all, the reply is that they belong
among the mathematical disciplines, whose credentials were not in dispute.

**Sanctification answers the court.** A ruler does not need to be told that a discipline is
epistemically respectable; he needs to know who may practise it and why he should pay them.
A science of walāya is not available to anyone with a manual. It belongs to those near to
God, which makes the practitioner a figure of religious authority and his retention a matter
of dynastic legitimacy.

Melvin-Koushki gives the second limb the heavier causal load, and says so: it is this that
**alone explains the massive increase in patronage of professional occultists at the
Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts in the runup to the Islamic millennium** of 1592
(*Powers of One*, 1). Not mathematics — sanctity — is what opened the treasuries.

## The Imams as the channel

The lineage runs through the Imams, which is what ties walāya to
[[imamophilism|imamophilism]] rather than to formal Shiʿism. Ibn Turka reports that the
**holy Imam Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq greatly vaunted this science, and those who cleave to the
threshold of his walāya have penned numerous works on the subject** (*Of Islamic
Grammatology*, 66).

The phrasing is worth attention. Authorship is attributed not to a school or a lineage of
teachers but to *those who cleave to the threshold of his walāya* — proximity to sanctity
is what qualifies a person to write on letters at all. Walāya is simultaneously the ground
of the science's authority and the channel of its transmission.

## Timing: why the millennium matters

The surge in patronage is dated to the runup to the Islamic millennium of 1592, and the
dating is not incidental. A court approaching a millennial turn has an acute interest in
knowing where it stands in sacred history and in employing people who can say. A science of
walāya supplies both a reading of the times and a sanctified reader. This is the mechanism
underneath the [[isfahan-circle|occult court]], and it explains why the phenomenon is
transregional — Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman courts arriving at the same solution because
they faced the same calendar.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka used the term with the same technical force** the later tradition
  gives it is not laid out in the sources in hand.
- **How the reclassification was argued** — the specific texts in which occult sciences are
  formally reassigned to walāya — is treated by Melvin-Koushki at the level of the movement
  rather than the individual treatise.


## Magically incarnating the Imams

The strongest statement of what the sanctification move actually claims comes in
Melvin-Koushki's account of why occultists seized on these disciplines. They took them up as
**both the primary mode of philosophical praxis and the best means of harnessing walāya —
which is to say, of magically incarnating the Imams** (*Another Scientific Revolution*, 8).

That last phrase is worth not softening. The claim is not that the practitioner studies the
Imams, or venerates them, or transmits their teaching. It is that the operations **make their
sanctity present and operative** in the practitioner. [[jafr|Jafr]] is the clearest case: to
divine by letters is to participate in the knowledge ʿAlī possessed, which is why it is
simultaneously a science, a devotion and a political instrument.

This also explains the phrase in the *Grammatology* passage — that those who **cleave to the
threshold** of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq's walāya have written on the science. Authorship is licensed
by proximity, and proximity is something one can move toward.

## Why courts paid

A ruler acquiring an occultist under this description is not hiring a technician. He is
attaching to his household a man whose competence is a form of sanctity, and whose
prognostications carry the authority of the Imams' own knowledge. That is worth a stipend in
a way that a clever calculator is not.

It also explains the **timing** of the surge Melvin-Koushki dates to the runup to the Islamic
millennium of 1592. A court approaching a millennial turn has an urgent interest in knowing
where it stands in sacred history, and in being seen to employ someone qualified to say. The
phenomenon is transregional — Safavid, Mughal and Ottoman — because the calendar was.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Walāya is the second limb of Melvin-Koushki's thesis, paired with mathematicalization; together they explain the legitimacy and the patronage of the occult sciences.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66.

concepts.name: Taḥqīq and Taqlīd
concepts.card: **Taḥqīq** — verification, working a question through to its ground for oneself — against **taqlīd**, following an authority. The axis on which Islamicate intellectual life sorted itself, and the one Melvin-Koushki uses to compare it with the European Renaissance. His finding runs against the usual story: **taḥqīq was a province dominated by Arabic**, and European humanism's strict Grecism was a *reaction* to Arabism's success, not evidence of its absence.
concepts.body:
## The pair

**Taqlīd** is acceptance on authority: the position is held because a recognised master held it. **Taḥqīq** is verification: the question is worked through to its grounds, and the conclusion held because it has been established. Every discipline in the tradition has a view about which is appropriate where, and the pair functions as the standing axis of intellectual self-description.

It is not a straightforward good-and-bad. Taqlīd in law is a virtue — it is what makes a legal system predictable — and a jurist who verified everything from first principles would be a menace. The argument is always about **scope**.

## Where Ibn Turka stands

On the side of verification, aggressively. The whole claim that [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] is the [[occult-science-universal|only truly universal science]] is a taḥqīq claim: it says the matter has been worked through and philosophy has been found wanting on its own ground. His invidious comparison with philosophy is not a preference between schools but an assertion that one of them has verified something the other has not.

The same commitment shows in the treatment of scripture. He censures the popularity of Zamakhsharī's *Kashshāf* for failing to recognise **the intrinsic ontological majesty of the quranic letters** — an attack on the standard exegesis of his century for not having gone far enough into its own subject.

And it shows in the family. Where his brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] taught only the outward sciences because he deemed it **too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public**, the younger brother delved. Same material, opposite judgement about how far verification should be pushed in the open.

## The comparative claim, which is the striking part

Melvin-Koushki uses the pair to compare the Islamicate and European renaissances, and the result inverts a familiar narrative.

European humanists, **committed to a purely European *prisca sapientia*, pushed for an extreme *taqlīd* of Greek sources to the exclusion of Arabic** — but they did this **in reaction to the unprecedented success of Arabism in European scholarly circles**, whence the boom in printing Latin editions of Arabic texts in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries (*Taḥqīq vs. Taqlīd*, 195).

And the purificationists could not hold the line: **even these ideological purificationists could not avoid the scientific seductions of taḥqīq, a province dominated by Arabic**, which their strict Grecism was far too narrow and too impractical to sustain. **Scholarly compromises abounded. Arabism thus remained essential to Renaissance scientific-philosophical inquiry** (ibid.).

Two consequences follow, and both matter for how this portal frames its subject. European humanism's turn to the Greeks was a **defensive** move against a live rival, not the natural recovery of an obvious inheritance. And on the axis that mattered for getting science done — verification — **the Arabic tradition held the advantage**, which is why the humanists' own programme kept leaking.

## Why this belongs in a portal about Ibn Turka

Because it supplies the comparative frame the intersection essays work in. When the portal sets Isfahan 1420 against Cusa 1440 and Pico 1486 without asserting contact, this is the ground of the comparison: two renaissances arguing about the same epistemological pair, in which the Islamicate side is not the belated one.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka uses the terms as a formal pair** in the unedited works, or whether the framing is Melvin-Koushki's analytical vocabulary applied to him.
- **How far the Arabism thesis is accepted** by historians of the European Renaissance; it is a strong claim made in a comparative venue.
concepts.hierarchy_note: Tahqiq/taqlid is the epistemological axis on which the portal's comparative claims about the two renaissances rest.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Taḥqīq vs. Taqlīd in the Renaissances of Western Early Modernity*, *Philological Encounters* 3 (2018), 193–249, at 195.

bibliography.author: Matthew Melvin-Koushki
bibliography.title: The Quest for a Universal Science: The Occult Philosophy of Ṣāʾin al-Dīn Turka Iṣfahānī (1369–1432) and Intellectual Millenarianism in Early Timurid Iran
bibliography.card: Matthew Melvin-Koushki's Yale dissertation is the foundational modern treatment of Ibn Turka's life, thought, and historical significance.
