Within this milieu, Ibn Turka's circle could flourish—court patronage provided resources, institutional sanction provided protection, and the cosmopolitan court environment created space for intellectual experimentation.

### Transregional Network: The Ikhwan al-Safa Connection

Most significantly, the Isfahan Circle saw itself as part of a larger, transregional network stretching from Anatolia through Isfahan to Cairo and Mamluk Syria. Members referred to themselves cryptically as the *Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ* (Brethren of Purity), invoking the name of the famous 10th-century Brethren while claiming to represent a "new" order. This network included Ottoman scholars in Anatolia, Mamluk court practitioners in Cairo, and Persian philosophers scattered across Timurid lands. The network's coherence lay not in formal organization but in shared commitment to the project of [[ilm-al-huruf|occult science as universal system]].

### Legacy

The Isfahan Circle disbanded with Ibn Turka's death (1432) and the gradual fragmentation of Timurid power. However, its intellectual legacy persisted: the systematization of [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], the integration of [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], and the claim that occultism constitutes rational science became foundational to later Safavid, Ottoman, and European occultist traditions. The Circle's members—especially [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]] through his *Ẓafarnāma*—achieved considerable influence: their works circulated, were copied, were commented upon. By the early 16th century, as Ottoman and Safavid courts consolidated power, the intellectual project inaugurated by the Isfahan Circle had become canonical.

## Where it sits in a larger structure

The Circle is not self-standing and was never meant to be. The dissertation places it
precisely: Ibn Turka and the members of his Isfahan Circle **may be seen as the eastern arm
of a larger network of intellectuals stretching to Anatolia via Cairo and calling
themselves, cryptically, the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ** (*The Quest*, 2). The
[[new-brethren-purity|New Brethren]] entry treats the network; this entry treats its
Iranian node.

The word **cryptically** is doing work. They took the name of the tenth-century Basran
encyclopedists — a name with its own reputation, some of it Ismāʿīlī — without announcing
what they meant by it. A borrowed name is a claim of succession and a partial concealment
at once, which is a fair description of the whole enterprise.

## The schoolroom underneath the circle

The most surprising thing the corpus yields about this group is that its two principal
minds had been in the same classroom for twenty-five years. Ibn Turka studied under his
elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] for the first twenty-five years of his life
**along with [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** (*The Quest*, 41 n.17).

That reorganises the Circle's intellectual history. The lettrist and the astronomer are not
specialists who converged at a Timurid court to compare notes; they are schoolfellows who
divided a shared inheritance between them. Ṣadr al-Dīn taught only the outward sciences,
deeming it too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public — and his two pupils then
spent their careers on the two disciplines by which the hidden order of things might be made
calculable. They died in the same year, 835/1432.

## What each member contributed

- **Ibn Turka** — the [[ilm-al-huruf|theory]], and the claim that it is universal.
- **[[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** — mathematical astronomy, and, as second director of
  the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]], the institutional bridge between the
  letter science and the star science.
- **[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī]]** — not a peer but Ibn Turka's **disciple
  and closest associate**, who accompanied him from Samarkand to Cairo around 795/1393,
  attended his *majālis*, travelled with him to Herat, and cared for his children after his
  death (*The Quest*, 135–36). He applied the framework to history and to the defence of
  divination.

## The political weather

The Circle formed and worked under conditions the entry should name. [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]]
abrogated *yasa* law in favour of the sharīʿa in 813/1411 and closed the taverns; the same
ruler destroyed [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] in 817/1414, exonerated Ibn Turka in
825/1422, and exiled him in 1427. A circle of occult philosophers operating inside a court
that had refounded its legitimacy on public piety is not a comfortable arrangement, and the
tribunals were its predictable expression.

## What we do not know

- **Membership is not a list.** The Circle is a modern historiographical construct built
  from correspondence and association, not an institution with a roll.
- **Whether it had a meeting place, a rule, or a formal name** among its members is not
  attested; the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ designation is cryptic by nature.
- **How far its members agreed** is largely unrecoverable — we have Ibn Turka's system in
  detail and much less of the others' on the same questions.


## The patronage economy it ran on

Timurid court patronage is the material condition for everything in this entry, and it worked on terms worth naming. Princes competed for prestigious scholars because scholarship was an instrument of legitimacy in a dynasty whose claim was recent and contested; the fragmentation that followed Tīmūr's death in 807/1405 turned that competition into a seller's market, which is why a returning occult philosopher found [[returns-isfahan|a receptive audience]] in 810/1408.

The terms were not generous in the modern sense. Patronage was personal, revocable, and tied to a specific prince's fortunes — so a scholar's standing collapsed when his patron did. Ibn Turka attached himself to four Timurid princes and every one of those relationships ended in murder, blinding, death or deferral. The career sim's contract mechanic, in which each delivery raises what the patron demands next, is the accurate model of what this economy felt like from inside.

## The Cairo precedent

The model was not invented in Iran. Mamluk Cairo — the largest city in the Islamic world and the centre of its scholarly life — had already produced a version of it under Sultan Barqūq (r. 784–801/1382–1399), whose personal physician-alchemist was [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] and whose courtiers included Ibn Turka himself. Melvin-Koushki asks whether Barqūq was **the first Mamluk sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and so an inspiration for Timurid rivals**, and answers *likely so* (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70).

If that holds, the Isfahan Circle is not the origin of the occult court but its second instance — and Ibn Turka had watched the first one operate before he was thirty.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth-Century Isfahan*. Boston: BRILL, 2025.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One: Pythagorean Cosmos in Islamic Context*, pp. 20–50.

institutions.name: New Brethren of Purity
institutions.card: **Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid** (The New Brethren of Purity). Transregional network of late 14th- and 15th-century scholars, occultists, and courtiers claiming succession to the 10th-century Brethren of Purity. Members included [[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]], [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlati]], [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]], and figures across Ottoman, Mamluk, and Persian courts. United by commitment to [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], [[abjad-numerology|numerology]], and the integration of occult sciences with [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean philosophy]]. Represented a self-conscious intellectual movement to establish occultism as legitimate, rational universal science.
institutions.body:
## Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid: The New Brethren of Purity

The **New Brethren of Purity** (Ikhwan al-Safa al-Jadid) was a transregional network of scholars and practitioners spanning three major power centers—Ottoman Anatolia, Mamluk Egypt/Syria, and Timurid Persia—in the late 14th and 15th centuries. They invoked the name of the legendary 10th-century Brethren of Purity (*Ikhwan al-Safa*), but understood themselves as a *new* order inaugurating a fresh era of occult science.

### Network Structure

Unlike formal institutions, the New Brethren functioned as a loose confederation bound by shared intellectual commitments rather than hierarchy or bylaws. Key nodes included:
- **Isfahan Circle** ([[ibn-turka|Ibn Turka]], [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Din Yazdi]], [[qazizada-rumi|Qazizada Rumi]])
- **Cairo/Mamluk court** ([[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Sayyid Husayn Akhlati]], Ottoman and Mamluk occultists)
- **Anatolian scholars** (Ottoman court philosophers and talismanic practitioners)

### Core Project

The New Brethren were united by a single grand project: to establish that [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]], [[abjad-numerology|numerology]], [[pythagorean-cosmology|Pythagorean mathematics]], and [[divine-names|divine-names doctrine]] constitute a comprehensive, rational science encompassing metaphysics, ethics, cosmology, and operative practice. This was not mysticism in the Sufi sense but *rational occultism*—grounded in logic, mathematics, and philosophical rigor.

### Historical Significance

Melvin-Koushki's research demonstrates that the New Brethren were not marginal occultists but central intellectual figures in their respective courts, commanding patronage, commanding audiences, and exerting real influence over political and administrative thought. They succeeded in their project: by the early 16th century, their intellectual synthesis had become canonical in Ottoman and Safavid philosophy.

The New Brethren represent a crucial moment in global intellectual history—when Islamic occult philosophy achieved systematic articulation, international coordination, and institutional legitimacy, rivaling and arguably exceeding contemporary European and Chinese philosophical achievements.

## Who established that this network existed

The network is not a category the sources hand over ready-made; it is a modern reconstruction, and the portal should say whose. Its existence was **posited by İhsan Fazlıoğlu in a 1996 article** on the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ and [[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]] in early Ottoman intellectual life. Melvin-Koushki states that his own understanding of late medieval Islamic occult philosophy is **dependent on the ongoing research of Cornell Fleischer** and his Chicago Circle into the cognate Ottoman projects (*The Quest*, ch. 1 nn. 87–88).

The two branches are described as **largely coterminous both logistically and conceptually**, so work on either has vital bearing on the whole complex. The [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]] is the eastern arm of something that reached Anatolia through Cairo, and reading the Iranian half alone produces a partial picture by construction.

One comparative fact is worth sitting with: Melvin-Koushki calls the Ottoman projects **cognate and more successful**. The same inheritance from the same teacher flourished at one end of the network and ended in tribunals at the other.

## Why the name, and why cryptically

Taking the name of the tenth-century Basran encyclopedists was a considered act with a cost.
The original *Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ* had produced the most ambitious encyclopedia of the sciences
Arabic had seen, unified by a Neoplatonic-Pythagorean conviction that **number is the ladder
by which the soul climbs back toward its origin** — which is precisely the fifteenth-century
programme, four hundred years early.

But the name also carried Ismāʿīlī associations, and Ismāʿīlism was dangerous:
[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] attempted a purge of Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415, and
[[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]] was **apparently claimed by Ismāʿīlīs as one of their own** —
part of what got him and Ibn Turka expelled from Herat in 1427.

Hence **cryptically**. A borrowed name that announces succession to the right readers and
nothing to the wrong ones is the only way to claim that inheritance safely, and the fact that
they needed the manoeuvre tells you the conditions they worked in.

## The two arms, and the comparison

The network's eastern arm is the [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]]; the western is Ottoman,
led by **[[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]]**. Both men were **intellectual heirs of
[[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]]**, and it is unclear whether they met during their
overlapping Cairo residences.

The outcomes diverged sharply, and the portal should not soften it. Melvin-Koushki calls the
Ottoman projects **cognate and more successful**, and the concrete measure is that Bisṭāmī's
*Miftāḥ al-jafr al-jāmiʿ* **came to function in the 16th century as a dynastic handbook, by
which the political fate of the House of ʿOs̱mān could be managed over the generations**
(*Another Scientific Revolution*, 2).

Same teacher, same science, same generation. One branch's manual becomes imperial equipment;
the other branch's theorist is tried three times and dies waiting on a case review. The
difference is political, not doctrinal, and it is the strongest argument available that Ibn
Turka's fate was contingent.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The New Brethren of Purity: Occult Science and Statecraft in the Islamic World*. Boston: BRILL, 2019.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *The Occult Court: Magic, Medicine, and Mathematics in the Fourteenth and Fifteenth-Century Isfahan*. Boston: BRILL, 2025.
Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 2 and ch. 1 nn. 87–88.
Fazlıoğlu, İhsan (1996); Fleischer, Cornell, *A Mediterranean Apocalypse* (in progress).

institutions.name: The Samarkand Observatory
institutions.card: **The Samarkand Observatory**, founded by [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] in 1420 around a meridian arc of unprecedented scale. Its *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* was the most accurate star table in the world for two centuries. Melvin-Koushki's argument places it inside Ibn Turka's story rather than beside it: the mathematization of astronomy achieved here and the [[neoplatonism|mathematicalization of the occult sciences]] are the same movement, and have been studied in isolation only by accident of modern disciplinary boundaries.
institutions.body:
## The Samarkand Observatory

**The institution.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] broke ground in 1420 on what became the largest astronomical instrument on earth: a meridian arc sunk into bedrock, housed in a three-storey building, staffed by the best mathematical astronomers of the age — Qāḍīzāda Rūmī among them, and later Jamshīd al-Kāshī and ʿAlī Qushjī. The *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* it produced remained the most accurate star catalogue in the world for roughly two centuries.

**Why it belongs to this portal.** The conventional account treats Samarkand as a triumph of exact science and Timurid occultism as a separate, embarrassing phenomenon. Melvin-Koushki's thesis denies the separation. He argues that the mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification of occultism in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is *the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context* for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy by the members of the Samarkand Observatory — processes which, he notes, have heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation (*Powers of One*, 1).

The observatory and the [[kitab-al-mafahis|Book of Inquiries]] were begun in the same year, 1420, a few hundred miles apart, by men working out the same conviction: that a science earns its standing by becoming mathematical. [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]] worked at both ends of it.

**The end.** Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 and the observatory was abandoned and dismantled not long after; its foundations were not rediscovered until 1908. The tables outlived the building, and reached Mughal India, where Shāhjahān's *Zīj-i Shāhjahānī* updated them behind the first thoroughly **lettrist** preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition (*Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599).

## The argument for putting it in this portal at all

The observatory's presence here is a thesis, not a courtesy. The standard division treats
Samarkand as exact science and Timurid occultism as a separate embarrassment.
Melvin-Koushki's claim is that this separation is an artefact of modern disciplinary
boundaries: the mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification of occultism
in Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is **the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical
context** for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy achieved here — processes which
have **heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation** (*Powers of One*, 1).

Three concrete links support it.

**The year.** Ground was broken in 1420; the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] was
completed in 823/1420.

**The classroom.** [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]], the observatory's second director, spent
twenty-five years being taught alongside Ibn Turka by Ibn Turka's own brother. He died in
835/1432, the same year as Ibn Turka.

**The patron.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] was styled *al-sulṭān al-faylasūf* and did the
mathematics himself — the audience Ibn Turka's mathematicalized science was constructed for.

## The instrument

The defining feature was a meridian arc of unprecedented scale, sunk into bedrock and housed
in a three-storey building — an instrument whose accuracy came from sheer size, since a
larger radius means finer graduations. The *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* produced from its observations
remained the most accurate star catalogue in the world for roughly two centuries, and was
still in use in Europe long after.

## The afterlife the tables had

The lettrist connection surfaces explicitly two centuries later. Shāhjahān commissioned the
***Zīj-i Shāhjahānī***, an updated and corrected version of Ulugh Beg's tables, and its
preface is **the first in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be explicitly and
thoroughgoingly lettrist in tenor** (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599).

Whatever was separate in 1420 was not separate by the 1650s: the most prestigious
astronomical project of Mughal India introduced itself in Ibn Turka's idiom.

## The end

Ulugh Beg was killed in 1449 by his own son's faction. The observatory was abandoned and
dismantled not long after, and its foundations were not rediscovered until 1908. The
institution lasted under thirty years; its tables lasted two centuries.

## What we do not know

- **Whether Ibn Turka ever visited**, or corresponded with anyone there beyond Qāḍīzāda.
- **What the observatory's staff thought of lettrism.** The link is argued at the level of
  intellectual context, not documented as an exchange of views.
- **Almost nothing of the physical instrument** survives to be examined.


## The staff, and the shared classroom

The observatory's directors and computers are the other half of Melvin-Koushki's argument
about disciplinary isolation. **[[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]** was its **second**
director; Jamshīd al-Kāshī and ʿAlī Qushjī worked there.

Qāḍīzāda is the link that makes the claim concrete rather than thematic. He had studied under
Ibn Turka's elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] **alongside Ibn Turka**, for
twenty-five years, in an education that stopped deliberately at the outward sciences because
their teacher deemed it **too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public**.

Two pupils of one household then spent their careers making the hidden order of things
calculable — one through the stars, one through the letters. They died in the same year,
835/1432.

## What was actually built

A meridian arc of unprecedented radius sunk into bedrock and housed in a three-storey
building. The principle is simple and the engineering was not: angular precision scales with
the instrument's size, so accuracy was bought by sheer scale. The *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* compiled
from its observations remained **the most accurate star catalogue in the world for roughly
two centuries**, and was still consulted in Europe long after.

## The lettrist preface, two centuries on

The clearest evidence that the two sciences were never as separate as the modern division
assumes comes from the tables' afterlife. Shāhjahān — self-proclaimed **Second Lord of
Conjunction**, after Tīmūr the First — commissioned for his accession the ***Zīj-i
Shāhjahānī***, an updated and corrected version of Ulugh Beg's tables of two centuries prior.

**Tellingly, it features the first preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical tradition to be
explicitly and thoroughgoingly lettrist in tenor** (*Philosopher-Kings*, 599). The same
feature appears in the preface to the *Sirr-i Akbar*, Dārā Shukūh's Persian translation of
the Upaniṣads.

The most prestigious astronomical project of Mughal India introduced itself in Ibn Turka's
idiom.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Powers of One*, 1.
Melvin-Koushki, Matthew. *Timurid-Mughal Philosopher-Kings as Sultan-Scientists*, 599.
Blake, Stephen P. *Astronomy and Astrology in the Islamic World*, ch. 6.

timeline_events.title: Ibn Turka born in Isfahan
timeline_events.card: Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī is born into an established Isfahani scholarly family. His father Afżal al-Dīn and elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn are both men of the religious sciences; the brother will be appointed *qāḍī* and will teach him for his first twenty-five years.
timeline_events.body:
**The family.** Ibn Turka was born into an established Isfahani scholarly house, not into
obscurity. His father **Afżal al-Dīn Turka** is a figure of sufficient standing to have an
*Encyclopaedia of Islam* article of his own (Eichner, 'Afḍal al-Dīn Turka', EI3). His elder
brother **[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]]** was an eminent scholar of hadith, Qur'anic
exegesis, jurisprudence and *uṣūl al-dīn*, and was appointed *qāḍī*.

**The office waiting for him.** The most consequential inheritance was institutional. Tīmūr
appointed Ṣadr al-Dīn *qāḍī* in Samarkand, and in doing so **established the judgeship to
the Turka family** (*The Quest*, §3.1). The post Ibn Turka would later hold in Isfahan, and
lose in the tribunals, was a family possession dating to the founding of the dynasty. He was
born into a claim.

**What the date sits next to.** The conventional dates are 770–835/1369–1432. Two years
before, around 766–67/1365, Fażl Allāh Astarābādī had arrived in Isfahan and become famous
as an interpreter of dreams — and Ibn Turka would later hold that a celestial conjunction of
that same moment heralded his generation as the best in history. The two facts sit oddly
together: the portent he claimed and the heresy he was accused of belong to the same year
and the same city.

**What we do not know.** The month and day are not recorded. His mother is not named. Of
the household's circumstances beyond its scholarly standing the sources say nothing.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fażl Allāh Astarābādī in Isfahan
timeline_events.card: The future founder of the Ḥurūfiyya arrives in Isfahan and becomes famous as an interpreter of dreams. Ibn Turka's father and elder brother both consult him — a documented family contact that prosecutors would still be able to use sixty years later.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Fażl Allāh Astarābādī arrived in Isfahan around **766/1365** and quickly
gained fame as an interpreter of dreams. He would later found the
[[hurufism|Ḥurūfiyya]] and be executed for it in 796/1394.

**The awkward fact.** Ḥurūfī sources record that Ibn Turka's father **Afżal al-Dīn** and his
elder brother **[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]]** both sought Fażl Allāh out during this
Isfahan residence to have their dreams interpreted. Naṣr Allāh Nāfajī's *Khwābnāma* preserves
the episode: Khwāja Ṣadr al-Dīn Turka attended an afternoon *majlis* of Fażl Allāh's and
presented a dream in which he saw the Prophet seated, went up to kiss his hand, and then
noticed he had inadvertently left saliva on the back of his own hand and felt ashamed
(*The Quest*, 58 n.16).

**What it does and does not show.** Melvin-Koushki is careful in both directions. The contact
**does not imply Ḥurūfī inclinations** on the part of the two Turkas; the hagiographical
point of preserving such stories is to establish Fażl Allāh's fame as a Sufi **before his
messianic transformation**, such that respected scholars of the religious sciences sought his
counsel. In 766/1365 consulting him was unremarkable.

**Why it nonetheless mattered.** Because it is on the record, in the movement's own sources,
and it was still on the record sixty years later when Ibn Turka's opponents needed a charge
that would carry at [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] court. A documented family connection to the
founder of a proscribed movement is exactly the kind of material a prosecutor can use
without having to prove anything about doctrine.

**What we do not know.** Whether Ibn Turka's opponents drew on the Ḥurūfī sources directly,
on local memory, or on something else entirely.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Studies under his brother, with Qāḍīzāda Rūmī
timeline_events.card: For the first twenty-five years of his life Ibn Turka studies under his elder brother Ṣadr al-Dīn — **alongside Qāḍīzāda Rūmī**, the future director of the Samarkand Observatory. He later remarks that his brother taught nothing beyond the outward sciences.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ibn Turka studied under his elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr
al-Dīn]] **for the first twenty-five years of his life**, and so — the detail that
reorganises everything — did **[[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]]**, the future second
director of Ulugh Beg's observatory (*The Quest*, 41 and n.17).

**Why it matters.** The [[isfahan-circle|Isfahan Circle]] is usually described as an
intellectual network that formed at Timurid courts. This shows that its two principal minds
had been in the same household classroom for a quarter of a century first. The lettrist and
the mathematical astronomer are not specialists who converged; they are schoolfellows who
divided an inheritance.

**What was and was not taught.** Ibn Turka's own verdict is that his brother **taught
nothing beyond the outward meaning of the sharīʿa**, deeming it **too dangerous to delve
into esoteric matters in public** (*The Quest*, 41). The reason is not ignorance but
assessment of risk — and the tribunals of the 1420s suggest the assessment was correct.

**The shape this gives the life.** A complete grounding in the exoteric disciplines,
deliberately stopping short of the *bāṭin*, delivered by a brother who thought the *bāṭin*
was dangerous to teach openly. Everything Ibn Turka built afterwards can be read as the
supply of what that education withheld — and as a demonstration that his brother's caution
was warranted.

**What we do not know.** The curriculum's contents beyond the named disciplines; whether
other students shared it; and whether Ṣadr al-Dīn's caution extended to private teaching.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Leaves Samarkand for Mecca and Cairo, with Yazdī
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka departs for the Ḥijāz and then Cairo. **Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī accompanies him** — the disciple is with him from the beginning of the formative journey, not acquired later at court.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around **795/1393** Ibn Turka left Samarkand for Mecca and then Cairo.
**[[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī]] accompanied him** (*The Quest*, chronology).

**Why the companion matters.** Yazdī is usually introduced as a member of the Isfahan
Circle, which makes him sound like a colleague acquired at the height of Ibn Turka's career.
He was there at the start. The fifteen formative years under
[[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] were shared, and Melvin-Koushki notes that Yazdī spent at
least part of 795–810/1393–1408 in Cairo with him (*Powers of One*, 37). The relationship the
dissertation calls **disciple and closest associate** runs the whole length of the adult
life.

**Why Samarkand, why leave.** The family had standing there — Tīmūr had appointed his
brother *qāḍī* in the city. Departing for the Ḥijāz and Egypt at around twenty-four means
leaving a secure position for a long absence, and the chronology gives no stated reason. The
*ḥajj* is the conventional occasion; fifteen years abroad is not conventional.

**What we do not know.** Whether the journey was planned as a long stay or extended once
begun; who funded it; and whether the choice of Cairo — rather than Damascus or Baghdad —
was made in advance or arrived at.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fifteen years abroad: study under Akhlāṭī in Cairo
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka studies under Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī, Sirāj al-Dīn al-Bulqīnī and others, remaining abroad fifteen years. Akhlāṭī — summoned to Cairo as personal physician to Sultan Barqūq — is the pivot of the network that will call itself the New Brethren of Purity.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** From roughly **795/1393 to 810/1408** — fifteen years — Ibn Turka studied
in Mamluk Cairo under **Sayyid Ḥusayn [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]]**, **Sirāj al-Dīn
al-Bulqīnī** and others, remaining abroad the whole time (*The Quest*, chronology).

**What he trained in.** Melvin-Koushki lists three fields: **law, Arabic letters and occult
science** — and adds that he launched his writing career there, and that his prose from this
period is masterfully prosimetric (*Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 5). The combination
is the whole later career in miniature: the jurist, the stylist and the occultist are formed
together, not sequentially.

**Bulqīnī matters as much as Akhlāṭī.** Sirāj al-Dīn al-Bulqīnī was a mainstream Shāfiʿī
authority of the first rank. Studying under him is what makes Ibn Turka a credentialed
jurist — and it is why he could later hold the chief judgeship of two cities and argue his
own case in front of a ruler. The occult philosophy was written by a man with impeccable
orthodox training, and that is not incidental to how he defended it.

**What Cairo was at the time.** The largest city in the Islamic world and the centre of its
scholarly life, under a sultan — [[chronology|Barqūq]] — whose personal physician-alchemist
was Ibn Turka's own master, and whose choice of courtiers included Ibn Turka himself. The
[[new-brethren-purity|network]] that would call itself the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ was forming in
these rooms.

**The cost.** The same years produced **mortal enemies at court**. The opposition that
culminated in the tribunals of the 1420s begins in Egypt, decades before it bore fruit.

**What we do not know.** What he wrote before 806/1404; how he supported himself; and the
identity of the Cairo enemies.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fażl Allāh Astarābādī executed
timeline_events.card: The founder of the Ḥurūfiyya is executed at the fortress of Alinjaq by Mīrānshāh b. Tīmūr. The movement he leaves behind becomes the heresy from which Ibn Turka's own science must afterwards be distinguished.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Fażl Allāh Astarābādī was executed at the **fortress of Alinjaq by
Mīrānshāh b. Tīmūr** in 796/1394 (*The Quest*, chronology).

**Who killed him.** The detail worth registering is the executioner's house. Mīrānshāh was
Tīmūr's son. The dynasty under which Ibn Turka would spend his entire career had killed the
founder of the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfiyya]] within Ibn Turka's own lifetime, when he was
twenty-five and already abroad.

**What it made the charge worth.** When Ibn Turka was exiled in 1427 on a **putative Ḥurūfī
connection**, the label did not name an abstract theological error. It named the movement
whose founder the ruling family had personally executed, and which would rise in armed
revolt at Isfahan and Tabriz in 835/1432. The accusation carried the weight of a live
security question.

**The distinction that had to be held.** Ibn Turka's own position is millenarian — he
proclaims a new age heralded by heavenly portent — but it is a golden age of **knowledge**
in which the legacy transmitted by the Imams and the ancients becomes actual, insisting on
**the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad**. The Ḥurūfīs proclaimed a
new dispensation. The difference is real and it is fine, and a court that will not attend to
it convicts both.

**What we do not know.** The formal grounds of Fażl Allāh's execution, and whether Ibn Turka
ever wrote about him directly.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Akhlāṭī dies in Cairo
timeline_events.card: The master of the Cairo circle dies. Ibn Turka will present himself thereafter as the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's teachings, and was received as such by the later lettrist tradition.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Sayyid Ḥusayn [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] died in Cairo in
**799/1397** (*The Quest*, chronology). Ibn Turka had been studying under him for roughly
four years and would remain abroad another eleven.

**What was lost and what was inherited.** Akhlāṭī was the **pivot** of the network that would
call itself the [[new-brethren-purity|Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ]], and had proclaimed a new era of
human development through the retrieval and open promulgation of the occult sciences
(*The Quest*, 2). He was also **personal physician-alchemist to Sultan Barqūq**, and the
conscious heir of both al-Būnī and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] (*Powers of One*, 6) — the
operative and metaphysical traditions held together in one teaching.

**The succession.** Two men inherited it in opposite directions. Ibn Turka took it east;
**[[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]]** took it into the Ottoman lands. They were **both the
intellectual heirs of Akhlāṭī**, and it is unclear whether they ever met during their
overlapping Cairo residences (*The Quest*, 2). Melvin-Koushki judges the Ottoman outcome the
**more successful**.

**How Ibn Turka positioned himself afterwards.** As **simply the systematizer of Akhlāṭī's
teachings** — and he was received as such by the later lettrist tradition (*The Quest*, 2).
The modesty is partly genuine debt and partly the prudence of a man in a dangerous field,
for whom a chain of transmission is a defence. It also understates the case: Akhlāṭī does not
appear to have argued lettrism into the [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematical sciences]].

**What we do not know.** The circumstances of the death; whether Barqūq's interest in the
occult sciences survived his physician; and almost anything of Akhlāṭī's own writings.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr
timeline_events.card: His first major work, in Persian: a commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's *al-Tāʾiyya al-kubrā*, a favourite teaching text of the Ibn ʿArabī school. It timuridizes the Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre and is the first such commentary to re-poeticize that tradition.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ibn Turka completed the *Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr* in **806/1404**, toward the
end of his Cairo residence — his **first major work** (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70).

**What it is.** An ornate Persian commentary on Ibn al-Fāriḍ's (d. 1235) *al-Tāʾiyya
al-kubrā*, a favourite teaching text of the [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] school. Formally a
commentary; in practice an anthology, since it answers each line of the poem with several
further lines of Persian or Arabic verse, contemporary and classical.

**Why it matters more than a first book usually does.** Three claims are made for it. It
**closely tracks high Mamluk Arabic literary culture**; it **timuridizes** the new hybrid
Mamluk anthology-as-commentary genre pioneered by Ibn Nubāta (d. 768/1366) and his student
al-Ṣafadī (d. 764/1363); and it is **the first such commentary to effectively re-poeticize
that tradition** (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70; *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 38).

**The direction of travel.** The Akbarian school had spent two centuries turning a visionary
inheritance into scholastic philosophy. This book runs the other way, returning the material
to verse. That is not a detour from the later lettrism: if
[[ilm-al-huruf|letters are ontological entities]], their arrangement is participation rather
than decoration, and a book whose method is the conjunction of verses is a book about how
arrangements of letters answer to one another.

**Its role in modern scholarship.** It is the base text for **Akram Jūdī-Niʿmatī's edition**,
whose introduction supplies the list of works from which Melvin-Koushki builds the annotated
catalogue in §2.1. The bibliography of the whole oeuvre rests partly on this book's edition.

**What we do not know.** For whom it was written, and how it was received in the Cairo
literary culture whose genre it adapted.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Tīmūr dies at Utrar
timeline_events.card: The founder of the dynasty dies on campaign, opening the succession struggle out of which Shāhrukh will emerge and within which Ibn Turka's patrons will rise and fall.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Tīmūr died at Utrar in 807/1405 while campaigning (*The Quest*,
chronology). Ibn Turka was in Cairo, three years from returning home.

**What it opened.** A succession contest among sons and grandsons that would not resolve for
years. The competing courts of the Timurid princes of western Iran — Pīr-Muḥammad at Shiraz,
then [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar]] in Fars and Isfahan — are products of it, and they are the
courts that would employ Ibn Turka within five years.

**The pairing worth noticing.** Ibn Khaldūn died in Cairo the following year, 808/1406. The
two men had met at Damascus in 803/1401, where — Melvin-Koushki notes — Ibn Khaldūn
attempted to palm himself off to Tīmūr as a seasoned occultist. Within twelve months the
conqueror and his most famous interviewer were both dead, and Ibn Turka was still in the city
where the second of them had lived.

**What we do not know.** Whether news of the death shaped Ibn Turka's decision to return to
Iran c. 810/1408.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Returns to Isfahan and takes up teaching
timeline_events.card: After fifteen years abroad Ibn Turka comes home and begins to teach. The Cairo formation is complete; the Persian career begins.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around **810/1408**, after fifteen years abroad, Ibn Turka returned to
Isfahan and took up teaching (*The Quest*, chronology).

**What he came back with.** A Shāfiʿī legal training under Sirāj al-Dīn al-Bulqīnī, a decade
under [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] in the occult sciences, a completed major work in the
[[sharh-nazm-al-durr|*Sharḥ-i Naẓm al-Durr*]] (806/1404), a mastery of Mamluk literary form,
membership in a transregional [[new-brethren-purity|network]], and a set of mortal enemies.

**What he came back to.** A political landscape being reorganised. Tīmūr had died at Utrar in
807/1405 and the succession was unresolved; the Timurid princes of western Iran were
building competing courts. Melvin-Koushki's judgement is that Ibn Turka **found a receptive
audience for his occult philosophy at the courts of the Timurid princes of western Iran**
(*The Quest*, §3.1) — a seller's market for exactly what he had.

**Why the timing was fortunate and then wasn't.** The fragmentation that made princes
compete for prestigious scholars is the same fragmentation that would destroy
[[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar]] in 817/1414 and leave Ibn Turka attached to a defeated house.
The conditions that made the career possible are the conditions that ended it.

**What we do not know.** Where he taught, and to whom, in these first years back.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: At Pīr-Muḥammad's court in Shiraz
timeline_events.card: A first Timurid attachment, to the court of Pīr-Muḥammad b. ʿUmar-Shaykh — cut short when Pīr-Muḥammad is murdered in 812/1409 and his brother Iskandar rises to power in Fars.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around **810–12/1408–9** Ibn Turka was a member of the court of
**Pīr-Muḥammad b. ʿUmar-Shaykh** at Shiraz. In 812/1409 Pīr-Muḥammad was **murdered**, and
his brother [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar]] rose to power in Fars (*The Quest*, chronology,
§3.1).

**The first patron, and the first loss.** This is the forgotten entry in the patronage
sequence. The story is usually told as Iskandar → Bāysunghur → the unreached Ulugh Beg;
Pīr-Muḥammad comes before all of them, and his court lasted Ibn Turka perhaps a year before
its holder was killed.

**The pattern it starts.** Every Timurid patron in this life ends badly or ends inaccessible.
Pīr-Muḥammad murdered in 1409. Iskandar defeated, blinded and executed in 1414–15.
[[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]] dead in 1433, a year after Ibn Turka. [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] never
quite reached, then murdered in 1449. Attaching yourself to a Timurid prince in this
generation was a structurally unsafe career move, and Ibn Turka did it four times.

**The continuity.** Iskandar was Pīr-Muḥammad's brother, and Ibn Turka moved from the one
court to the other. The transition was lateral within a family — which is presumably how a
scholar attached to a murdered prince avoided sharing his fate.

**What we do not know.** What Ibn Turka did at this court; who murdered Pīr-Muḥammad and
why; and whether the move to Iskandar was immediate.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Appointed qāḍī at Iskandar Sulṭān's court
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka joins the court of Iskandar Sulṭān, appointed *qāḍī* and teacher. Iskandar commissions *Of Letters* and, shortly after, the Book of Inquiries — the patronage that produces his central work.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** From **812–15/1409–12** Ibn Turka was a member of
[[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān's]] court in Isfahan, **appointed *qāḍī* and teacher**
(*The Quest*, chronology).

**The office was his family's.** Melvin-Koushki judges that Iskandar was presumably
responsible for installing him in his **hereditary** office as *qāḍī* of Isfahan — a post
established to the Turka family by Tīmūr himself when he appointed
[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] *qāḍī* in Samarkand (*The Quest*, §3.1). The appointment
was a restoration as much as a favour.

**Why this patron in particular.** Iskandar was known for his **imamophilism and esotericist
bent**, is accounted **the leading Timurid patron of culture in the early Shahrukhid
period**, and showed a particular interest in **alchemy and astrological and astronomical
illustrated works** (*The Quest*, §3.1 and n.1). He was not a generic prince who happened to
employ an occultist; he was looking for one. [[imamophilism|Imamophilism]] is precisely the
confessional position the portal ascribes to Ibn Turka too.

**What the patronage produced.** It is possible that Iskandar **personally commissioned** the
[[risalat-huruf|*R. Ḥurūf*]], Ibn Turka's first treatise on lettrism; and the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] was begun shortly afterwards, again almost certainly
at his instance. The two central lettrist works of the century have one patron behind them.

**What we do not know.** Whether the commission is documented or inferred — Melvin-Koushki
writes "it is possible that" and "almost certainly", not that a record survives.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Shāhrukh abrogates yasa law for the sharīʿa
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh declares the abrogation of Mongol *yasa* law, enforces the sharīʿa and closes the taverns. Timurid legitimacy is refounded on religious rather than steppe grounds — and the ground on which an occult philosopher will be judged shifts with it.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In 813/1411 Shāhrukh declared the abrogation of *yasa* law, enforced the
sharīʿa, and closed the taverns (*The Quest*, chronology). The previous year he had
completed a madrasa-khānaqāh complex at Herat and appointed its teachers.

**What the yasa was.** The Mongol customary law code attributed to Chinggis Khan, which had
served as the juridical backbone of Chinggisid and early Timurid authority. Timurid rulers
governed as heirs to a steppe legal order as much as to an Islamic one, and the two
coexisted uneasily.

**What the abrogation did.** It relocated the basis of dynastic legitimacy from descent and
custom to religious orthodoxy. This is a re-founding rather than a reform: a ruler who
governs under the sharīʿa is answerable to the class of men who interpret it, and elevates
that class in the act of submitting to it.

**Why it matters for Ibn Turka.** Not because it targeted him — it did not, and he was in
Iskandar's Isfahan at the time — but because it set the conditions under which his career
would be judged. A court that has staked its legitimacy on public piety acquires an interest
in policing doctrine, a class of officials whose standing rises with that policing, and a
vocabulary in which professional rivalry can be pursued as accusation. All three appear in
the tribunals of the 1420s.

**The contrast with Iskandar.** Melvin-Koushki sets the two rulers against each other:
if the rise of absolutist politics is a benchmark for early modernity, then in 816/1412
**Shāhrukh was the last medieval Islamic ruler and Mīrzā Iskandar the first early modern
absolutist sovereign**. Shāhrukh's answer to the legitimacy question was conservative and
juridical; [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar's]] was eschatological, with occultists on the staff.
Ibn Turka's science belonged to the programme that lost.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam
timeline_events.card: A commentary on Ibn ʿArabī's *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam*, completed in the year he travels to the Ḥijāz and invites Sharaf al-Dīn to join him. A corrected version follows in 817/1415.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In **813/1411** Ibn Turka completed the *Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam*, a
commentary on [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī's]] *Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam*, in the same year he travelled to
the Ḥijāz — possibly on pilgrimage — and invited [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn]] to
join him. He completed **a corrected version in 817/1415** (*The Quest*, chronology).

**What it establishes.** That Ibn Turka was a working Akbarian commentator, not merely an
inheritor of Akbarian ideas at second hand. The *Fuṣūṣ* is the central text of the school and
commenting on it is the standard way of entering the tradition's scholarly conversation.

**Why it complicates the reception story.** This is the kind of work that produced the modern
picture of Ibn Turka as a mystical philosopher linking Ibn ʿArabī to Mullā Ṣadrā — the
picture the [[tamhid-al-qawaid|*Tamhīd*]] entry argues obscured everything else. He really
did write Akbarian commentary, and a great deal of it; the error is not in noticing that but
in stopping there.

**The revision.** A corrected version four years later, in the year after
[[iskandar-falls|Iskandar's fall]]. Ibn Turka returned to his own texts — this one in 1415,
the [[mafahis-revised|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] in 828/1425 — which is worth knowing when using colophon
dates: a date may record a revision rather than a first composition.

**What we do not know.** What the 817/1415 corrections changed; whether the Ḥijāz journey was
in fact a pilgrimage (the chronology marks it with a question mark); and whether Yazdī
accepted the invitation.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Iskandar takes Isfahan and builds a brilliant court
timeline_events.card: Iskandar Sulṭān establishes at Isfahan one of the most lavishly bookish and most astrologically preoccupied courts of the age. Ibn Turka is attached to it — then moves back to Shiraz under harassment by envious individuals, putting forward his protégé Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb to replace him as *qāḍī*.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Between **815 and 817/1412–14** Iskandar took Isfahan and established
what was **by every measure a brilliant though short-lived court** there
(*The Quest*, §3.1). Ibn Turka was attached to it — and then **moved back to Shiraz due to
harassment by envious individuals**, putting forward his protégé **Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb** to
replace him as *qāḍī* (*The Quest*, chronology).

**The withdrawal is the important half.** This is the first documented instance of the
pattern that would end the career, and it happens at the height of his patron's power, a
decade before the first tribunal. He was not driven out by doctrinal opposition or by the
state. He was driven out by **colleagues**, and the chronology's phrase for their motive is
*envy*.

**What he did about it.** He left, and he installed his own protégé in the post. That is a
managed retreat rather than a rout: the office stays within his influence even as he vacates
it. It also tells us he had protégés worth placing.

**The absolutism experiment.** This court is the setting for what Melvin-Koushki treats as a
turning point in Islamic political history — the [[eschatological-absolutism|experiment of
815/1412]] involving Iskandar, Shāh Niʿmatullāh Valī and Sayyid Sharīf Jurjānī, from which he
concludes that Iskandar was **the first early modern absolutist sovereign**. Ibn Turka was
attached to the court where that happened.

**What we do not know.** Who the envious individuals were; whether Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb is
connected to [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Sharaf al-Dīn Yazdī]] (the sources in hand distinguish
them); and how long the Shiraz interval lasted.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Shāhrukh destroys Iskandar Sulṭān
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh marches against Iskandar in Iraq. Iskandar flees, is captured and blinded, and is executed afterwards; Ibrāhīm Sulṭān is installed in his place. Ibn Turka's first patron is destroyed by the ruler he must now live under.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In **817/1414** [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] marched against
[[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] in Iraq. Iskandar **fled, was captured and blinded, and
was executed afterwards**; Shāhrukh installed his own son Ibrāhīm Sulṭān in his place
(*The Quest*, chronology). Iskandar's death is generally dated 818/1415.

**A correction this portal has had to make.** Earlier versions of the entries here compressed
the sequence into "defeated, blinded and killed in 1415". The chronology separates the
defeat and blinding (817/1414) from the execution that followed. The distinction matters
because blinding was the standard Timurid method of disqualifying a rival from rule without
killing him — the execution was a second decision.

**What it cost Ibn Turka.** Everything, in slow motion. The patron who had installed him in
his hereditary judgeship and commissioned his two central lettrist works was destroyed by the
man who would rule for the next thirty-three years. The commission became a liability; the
association became a fact on a file. From **817 to 825/1414–22** Ibn Turka **attempted to
retire from public life**.

**The deeper problem.** It was not merely a change of employer. Iskandar and Shāhrukh
represented incompatible answers to the legitimacy question — eschatological absolutism with
occultists on staff, against a conservative juridical order refounded on the
[[yasa-abrogated|sharīʿa]]. Ibn Turka's science belonged to the programme that lost the war.

**What we do not know.** Where Ibn Turka was during the campaign, and whether he was ever
formally associated with Iskandar's rebellion.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Writes the Risālat al-Ḥurūf in Shiraz
timeline_events.card: *Of Letters*, written for Iskandar Sulṭān — the treatise that first proposes the fourfold analysis of the letter which the Book of Inquiries will expand.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In **817/1414** Ibn Turka wrote the *Risālat al-Ḥurūf* — *Of Letters* —
in Shiraz, apparently for [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] (*The Quest*, chronology; the
chronology marks the attribution with a question mark).

**The timing is extraordinary.** 817/1414 is the year Shāhrukh marched against Iskandar and
had him captured and blinded. Ibn Turka's first treatise on lettrism was written **for a
patron in the act of being destroyed**, or immediately after.

**What it contains.** The **fourfold schema** of the letter that the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] would later massively expand: the letters treated
according to their numerological (*iḥṣāʾī*), symbological (*kitābī*) and phonological
(*kalāmī*) forms, and then as they are in themselves (*fī anfusi-hā*)
(*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66). The technical architecture of the whole system is present
in this short treatise.

**Its place in the oeuvre.** It is the first lettrist work, and the summa was begun **shortly
after completing it**. Read together, 817/1414 and 823/1420 bracket the period in which the
science took its mature form — a period that begins with the destruction of his patron and
ends in the year Ulugh Beg broke ground at Samarkand.

**What we do not know.** Whether Iskandar commissioned it — the chronology's question mark is
deliberate. Whether Iskandar ever saw it. And whether it survives in edited form.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Attempts to retire from public life
timeline_events.card: For eight years after Iskandar's fall Ibn Turka tries to withdraw. It is the most productive stretch of his life: the Book of Inquiries is completed inside it.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** From roughly **817 to 825/1414–22** — eight years, following
[[iskandar-falls|Iskandar's destruction]] — Ibn Turka **attempted to retire from public
life** (*The Quest*, chronology).

**Why "attempted" is the right word.** The retirement did not hold: it ends with his
opponents denouncing him at Herat around 825/1422 and his travelling there to answer them.
A man whose patron has been executed by the reigning sovereign does not get to withdraw
quietly by choosing to.

**What the retirement produced.** The most important eight years of his working life. The
[[mafahis-completed|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] was completed in 823/1420, inside this window. The
summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism is the work of a man in political eclipse, without a
patron, trying to stay out of view.

**The pattern worth naming.** Much of what survives was written in the gaps between
disasters. *Of Letters* in the year his patron fell; the *Mafāḥiṣ* during the attempted
retirement; the *Kitāb al-Manāhij* wintering at Natanz in exile; the second
[[nafsat-al-masdur|apology]] and the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya* during nine months of waiting at
Herat. The productivity is not despite the trouble; it tracks it.

**What we do not know.** Where he spent these years, how he supported himself, and whether
the retirement was formal — a resignation of office — or simply a withdrawal from court.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Completes the Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ
timeline_events.card: The Book of Inquiries is finished — the first Arabic summa of Islamic neopythagoreanism. It is revised and expanded in 828/1425. **Ulugh Beg breaks ground on the Samarkand Observatory the same year**: two foundations laid in one year, one in stone and one on paper.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ibn Turka completed the *Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ* in 823/1420, in Isfahan or
Yazd — the chronology is uncertain which. He revised and expanded it in 828/1425
(*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

**What was finished.** Melvin-Koushki calls it **the first Arabic summa of Islamic
neopythagoreanism** and the fullest expression of Ibn Turka's lettrist metaphysics. It
massively expands the fourfold schema first proposed in the earlier *Of Letters*, treating
the letters in their numerological (*iḥṣāʾī*), symbological (*kitābī*) and phonological
(*kalāmī*) forms, and then separately **as they are in themselves** (*fī anfusi-hā*).

**Who it was for.** Begun shortly after *Of Letters* and, like it, almost certainly at the
instance of [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] — though by 1420 Iskandar had been dead for
five years. The summa was completed for a patron who no longer existed.

**The coincidence worth noticing.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] broke ground on the
[[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]] in the same year. Two foundations laid in
1420, a few hundred miles apart, by men acting on one conviction: that a science earns its
standing by becoming mathematical. Melvin-Koushki's argument is that these are not
neighbouring events but one movement, studied separately only by accident of modern
disciplinary boundaries.

**How we know the date.** From the colophons of [[ms-majlis-10196|MS Majlis 10196]], the
codex in which the incipit and explicit of this very text are written in Ibn Turka's own
hand. For this work specifically, the evidence is about as good as the corpus offers —
though even here the general caution applies that a colophon may record transcription rather
than composition.

**What the revision changed** is not stated in the sources in hand. We know the work was
expanded in 828/1425, in the same window in which two-thirds of the surviving oeuvre was
being copied, and immediately before the exile.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Ulugh Beg founds the Samarkand Observatory
timeline_events.card: Ground is broken on the largest astronomical instrument on earth. Melvin-Koushki argues that the mathematicalization of the occult sciences is the immediate context for the mathematization of astronomy achieved here — the two are one movement, not two.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] broke ground on the
[[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]] in 1420 — a meridian arc of unprecedented
scale sunk into bedrock, housed in a three-storey building, staffed by the best mathematical
astronomers of the age.

**The coincidence, and the argument built on it.** The [[mafahis-completed|*Kitāb
al-Mafāḥiṣ*]] was completed in 823/1420. Two foundations laid in one year, a few hundred
miles apart. Melvin-Koushki's claim is that this is not coincidence but a single movement
seen twice: the mathematicalization, neopythagoreanization and sanctification of occultism in
Ilkhanid–Timurid–Aqquyunlu Iran is **the immediate intellectual and sociopolitical context**
for the celebrated mathematization of astronomy achieved at Samarkand — processes which have
**heretofore been studied in atomistic isolation** (*Powers of One*, 1).

**The human link.** [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]], the observatory's second director, had
spent twenty-five years in the same schoolroom as Ibn Turka, taught by Ibn Turka's own
brother. The two institutions share a classroom.

**Why the size.** A meridian arc's precision scales with its radius: a larger instrument
resolves finer angles. The *Zīj-i Sulṭānī* produced from its observations remained the most
accurate star catalogue in the world for roughly two centuries.

**What we do not know.** Whether Ibn Turka knew of the founding, and whether any
communication passed between Isfahan and Samarkand in this year.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Accused of Sufi bias; clears his name at Herat
timeline_events.card: His opponents go to Shāhrukh's court and accuse him of Sufi bias. Ibn Turka travels to Herat to answer them in person, **gains Shāhrukh's favour, and is given the judgeship of Yazd**. The first tribunal, and he wins it.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around 825/1422 Ibn Turka's opponents went to [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]]
court at Herat and accused him of **Sufi bias**. He travelled to Herat to clear his name,
**gained Shāhrukh's favour, and was given the judgeship of Yazd** (*The Quest*, chronology).

**The shape of the win.** This is the most impressive thing in the biography and it is easy
to skip past. He answered the charge in person, in front of the ruler who had destroyed his
previous patron eight years earlier, and left not merely acquitted but **promoted**. The
accusation of Sufi bias was converted into an additional judicial office.

**Why "Sufi bias" was the charge.** It is a revealing choice. Ibn Turka criticised organised
[[sufism|Sufism]] in his written work while maintaining friendly relations with prominent
Sufi shaykhs, several of them promoters of [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]] against hostile
reaction. A prosecutor could point at the associations without engaging the doctrine — which
is easier than arguing about [[ilm-al-huruf|lettrism]] and, in a court that had recently
refounded itself on public orthodoxy, more likely to land.

**Where it sits in the sequence.** Historically he faces three inquisitions, winning the
first two and losing the third. This is the first. The chronology dates it; the second and
third are **not dated in the sources in hand**, which is a real gap given that the whole
dramatic arc of the life turns on them.

**What it did not settle.** Five years later he was exiled from Herat anyway, on a different
charge, from the same court. The vindication of 825/1422 bought time rather than security —
and the chronology gives no explanation for why it failed to hold.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Exiled from Herat with Qāsim-i Anvār
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka is expelled alongside Qāsim-i Anvār, his charismatic associate from the Cairo years, over suspect connections — the official excuse being a putative Ḥurūfī link. The stated charge and the operative reason are not the same.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In 1427 Ibn Turka was expelled from Herat together with
[[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]], his charismatic associate from the Cairo years. The
dissertation is specific about the mechanism: they were exiled **for suspect connections**,
though it was Qāsim's **putative connection with the Ḥurūfīs that provided the official
excuse** (*The Quest*, 456 n.16).

**The distinction that matters.** The stated charge and the operative reason are not the
same, and the sources let us see the gap. The operative worry was association — Qāsim was a
propagandist of the Ṣafaviyya order and was apparently claimed by Ismāʿīlīs as one of their
own, at a moment when that was dangerous: [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] had attempted a purge of
Ismāʿīlīs in Quhistan in 1415. The [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] label was the charge that would
carry in court.

**Why the label was available.** Because it was not baseless in the family's case. Ḥurūfī
sources record that Ibn Turka's father Afżal al-Dīn and his elder brother
[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] had consulted Fażl Allāh Astarābādī during his Isfahan
residence, presenting dreams for interpretation. Melvin-Koushki cautions that this implies
no Ḥurūfī inclination and that the story's hagiographical purpose is to show Fażl Allāh's
standing *before* his messianic turn — but the episode is on the record and a prosecutor
could reach it.

**What it cost.** The exile ends the settled portion of the career. What follows is the
sequence the [[chronology|chronology]] records: a fruitless attempt at a hearing in Simnan
around 833/1429, a winter at Natanz, a promise of reinstatement at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa around
834/1430, and then nine months of weekly attendance at court in Herat waiting for a review
that had not come when he died in 835/1432.

**The irony of the timing.** In 835/1432, the year of his death, there were **Ḥurūfī
uprisings in Isfahan and Tabriz**. The charge that had removed him five years earlier
acquired, at exactly the wrong moment, the appearance of foresight.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Muḥammad al-Jazarī, his powerful opponent, dies
timeline_events.card: The death in Herat of the man the chronology names as Ibn Turka's powerful opponent. It does not restore him: the machinery of the case outlives its instigator.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** **Muḥammad al-Jazarī**, described in the chronology as Ibn Turka's
**powerful opponent**, died at Herat in 833/1429 (*The Quest*, chronology). The same year saw
[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] second Azarbayjan campaign against the Qara Quyunlu.

**Why the entry exists.** Because he is **the only opponent the chronology names**. The
tribunals are attributed throughout to rival colleagues and envious individuals, and the
record is otherwise silent about who they were. Al-Jazarī is the single face on the other
side.

**What his death did not do.** Restore him. Ibn Turka was two years into exile when his
powerful opponent died, and the machinery outlived the man: the very next entries in the
chronology are the **fruitless attempt to obtain a hearing at Simnan** in the same year, and
then a further two years before even a promise of reinstatement. Removing the instigator did
not reverse the case.

**What that suggests.** That by 1429 the matter had ceased to depend on anyone's animus. An
accusation that has been processed by a court acquires an institutional existence of its own,
and reversing it requires a positive decision that nobody had an interest in making.

**What we do not know.** Al-Jazarī's office and standing; what specifically he did against
Ibn Turka; and whether he was involved in the first inquisition of 825/1422, the exile of
1427, or both.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Fruitless attempt to obtain a hearing at Simnan
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka tries and fails to get in front of Shāhrukh. The exile is now a matter of waiting on access.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around **833/1429** Ibn Turka made a **fruitless attempt to obtain a
hearing with [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] at Simnan** (*The Quest*, chronology).

**What the exile had become by then.** Not a sentence being served but a case awaiting
attention. Two years after the expulsion from Herat, the obstacle was no longer a verdict —
it was **access**. Ibn Turka needed to be in front of the sovereign, and could not get
there.

**Why he thought it would work.** Because it had, once. In 825/1422 he had travelled to
Herat to answer an accusation of Sufi bias in person, **gained Shāhrukh's favour and been
given the judgeship of Yazd**. The [[first-inquisition|first inquisition]] was won by exactly
this method. Simnan is an attempt to repeat a proven manoeuvre, and it fails.

**The shape of the last years.** Simnan 833/1429, refused. Natanz 833/1430, wintering and
writing. Ṣāʾin Qalʿa c. 834/1430, a hearing obtained at last and a promise given. Herat
834–35/1431–32, nine months of weekly attendance. Death. The pattern is not persecution
intensifying but a man repeatedly *nearly* getting through.

**What we do not know.** Why the hearing was refused, who refused it, and whether Shāhrukh
knew it had been sought.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Winters at Natanz and writes for his son
timeline_events.card: He sends for his family and, while there, writes the *Kitāb al-Manāhij* for his son Muḥammad. The transmission problem has become domestic.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** In **833/1430** Ibn Turka wintered at **Natanz**, sent for his family,
and while there wrote the ***Kitāb al-Manāhij*** for his son **Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad** — a
**manual of logic** (*The Quest*, chronology, 41).

**The domestic detail.** He sent for his family. After three years of exile and a refused
hearing at Simnan, the arrangement had lasted long enough to require a household. This is
the only entry on the chronology that records him doing something ordinary.

**What he wrote, and for whom.** Not a lettrist treatise, not an apology — **a logic manual
for his son**. Of ten children (three sons and seven daughters) only two sons are known by
name, and both appear in connection with texts: Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad receives this book, and
**Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb Allāh** appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise of his own,
the *Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ*.

**Why a logic manual matters here.** Logic is the propaedeutic — the discipline you teach
first, the entry to everything else. A man in political eclipse, whose own career was being
dismantled on charges of doctrinal irregularity, spent a winter writing his son the
elementary textbook. The transmission problem had become domestic, and his answer to it was
to start at the beginning.

**What we do not know.** Whether Jamāl al-Dīn continued the work; the dissertation notes he
**may have been a key player** in something the passage does not complete.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: A promise of reinstatement at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka finally obtains a hearing at Shāhrukh's camp and **receives a promise of reinstatement**. It is the high point of the last years and it is only a promise.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Around **834/1430** Ibn Turka **obtained a hearing at [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]]
camp at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa near Sultaniyya, and received a promise of reinstatement**
(*The Quest*, chronology). Shāhrukh returned to Herat from the Azarbayjan campaign the same
year.

**The high point of the last five years.** After the refusal at Simnan, he finally got in
front of the sovereign — in a military camp, on campaign, rather than at court — and was told
he would be restored.

**And it is only a promise.** The chronology's next entries are the journey to Herat and
[[nine-months-waiting|nine months of weekly attendance]] waiting on a review that never came.
Whatever was said at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa did not convert into an order.

**Why this may be the cruellest entry on the chronology.** A refusal can be answered:
appealed, worked around, waited out with a clear view of the obstacle. A promise cannot. It
removes the grounds for further pleading while producing nothing, and it obliges the
recipient to keep attending in good faith. The last two years of the life are structured by
a commitment that was probably sincere and certainly never actioned.

**The rhyme.** This is the same shape as the [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] problem — interest that
is real, an arrangement to be settled later, and *later* turning out to have a great deal of
court business in front of it. Ibn Turka's career ends twice over in a deferral rather than a
refusal.

**What we do not know.** Who conveyed the promise, in what terms, and whether it was ever
recorded in writing.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Nine months in weekly attendance, waiting on a case review
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka travels to Herat and for nine months attends court weekly, waiting for his case to be reviewed. In that interval he writes *Nafsat al-Maṣdūr II* and the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya* for Bāysunghur. The review does not come.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Having obtained a promise of reinstatement at Shāhrukh's camp at Ṣāʾin
Qalʿa near Sultaniyya around 834/1430, Ibn Turka travelled to Herat. There, across
834–35/1431–32, he was **for nine months in weekly attendance at court waiting for the
review of his case** (*The Quest*, chronology). The review did not come. He died at Herat
in 835/1432.

**What he did with the time.** He wrote. The chronology places two works in this interval:
the second recension of the [[nafsat-al-masdur|*Nafsat al-Maṣdūr*]] — the apologies — and
the *Risāla Iʿtiqādiyya*, composed **for [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur]]**. Both are documents of
a man arguing for himself: one a defence, one a statement of belief addressed to the
Timurid prince he had been closest to.

**How to read the apology written here.** With care. Melvin-Koushki's warning about the
genre applies with maximum force to a text produced in these conditions: the self-image Ibn
Turka presents in the apologies, **produced under great duress**, is hardly reflective of
his primary concerns (*The Quest*, 6–7). Leonard Lewisohn's reading of him as an orthodox
Sunni Sufi thinker rests on exactly this material. A creed written in the ninth month of
waiting on a tribunal is evidence about the tribunal.

**Why the shape of it matters.** This is not a dramatic ending. There is no verdict, no
condemnation, no scene. There is an old man attending court once a week for the better part
of a year because a promise had been made, and then there is a death. The most consequential
occult philosopher of Timurid Iran spent his last year in an antechamber.

**The rhyme with Samarkand.** [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]] — the patron whose programme was his
own programme — had seventeen years left. The [[samarkand-observatory|observatory]] was
running. The patronage that would have made sense of the whole career was three weeks' ride
away and never arrived, for the same reason the case review never arrived: not refusal, but
a court's ordinary capacity to defer.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Ḥurūfī uprisings at Isfahan and Tabriz
timeline_events.card: In the year of his death the movement he had spent a career being distinguished from rises in his own city. The charge that exiled him is, at exactly the wrong moment, politically vindicated.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] uprisings broke out at **Isfahan and Tabriz in
835/1432** — the year Ibn Turka died at Herat (*The Quest*, chronology).

**The timing.** He had been exiled from Herat five years earlier on a **putative Ḥurūfī
connection** — a charge Melvin-Koushki describes as the official excuse for an expulsion
actually driven by association with [[qasim-i-anvar|Qāsim-i Anvār]]. In the year of his
death, the movement he had spent a career being distinguished from rose in arms in his own
city.

**What it did to the record.** Nothing good. A distinction that was difficult to maintain in
1427 became harder still once Ḥurūfīs were in open revolt at Isfahan, and posthumous
reputation is made in exactly such conditions. The [[tamhid-al-qawaid|reception history]]
that reduced him to a mystical philosopher had, among its other causes, a strong incentive
after 1432 to keep his lettrism out of view.

**The distinction, one more time.** The Ḥurūfīs proclaimed a new, Persian dispensation. Ibn
Turka proclaimed a golden age of **knowledge** in which what the Imams and ancients had
already transmitted becomes actual, insisting on the binding finality of the dispensation
given through Muḥammad. Both are millenarian. Only one is a prophetic claim
(*The Quest*, 456).

**What we do not know.** The scale and outcome of the risings; and whether Ibn Turka, at
Herat, heard of them before he died.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: Dies at Herat
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka dies still waiting on the review of his case. Ulugh Beg — the patron whose programme was his own — has seventeen years left; the Samarkand tables will carry an unsigned debt to the letter science for two centuries.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ṣāʾin al-Dīn ʿAlī ibn Turka Iṣfahānī died at **Herat in 835/1432**
(*The Quest*, chronology), in the ninth-or-so month of weekly attendance at a court that had
promised to review his case.

**What was unfinished.** The reinstatement promised at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa. The judgeship of Isfahan
and Yazd, a hereditary family office granted by Tīmūr, lost. Over half his roughly forty-five
works unedited — a state of affairs that would persist for six centuries.

**Who else died that year.** [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]], the schoolfellow of
twenty-five years, second director of the [[samarkand-observatory|Samarkand Observatory]],
also died in 835/1432. Two men taught side by side in one Isfahani household, who then
divided the century's work between the stars and the letters, went in the same season.

**And what happened in Isfahan.** [[hurufi-uprisings|Ḥurūfī uprisings]] broke out at Isfahan
and Tabriz in the same year. The charge that had exiled him five years earlier acquired, at
exactly the wrong moment, the appearance of foresight.

**What outlived him.** [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī]], who looked after his children.
[[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]], for another seventeen years. [[bistami|Bisṭāmī]] in the Ottoman
lands, for twenty-two — pursuing the same inheritance from the same teacher, more
successfully. And the tables at Samarkand, which two centuries later would be reissued by
Shāhjahān behind the first thoroughly lettrist preface in the Arabo-Persian astronomical
tradition.

**What we do not know.** The cause of death, the place of burial, and what became of the
promised review.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: MS Majlis 10196 copied, partly in the author's hand
timeline_events.card: The earliest, most complete and most reliable collection of Ibn Turka's works, copied over the last eight years of his life and three years past his death. **The incipit and explicit of the Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ, ff. 52a and 118b, are in Ibn Turka's own hand** — the copyist was in close contact with the author. It is the basis for dating most of the oeuvre.
timeline_events.body:
**What it is.** [[ms-majlis-10196|MS Majlis 10196]], the earliest, most complete and most
reliable collection of Ibn Turka's works — copied across **the last eight years of his life
and three years past his death**, so roughly 827–839/1425–1435 (*The Quest*, §2.1).

**The autograph.** The **incipit and explicit of the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]],
folios 52a and 118b, are in Ibn Turka's own hand**, which suggests the copyist was in close
contact with the author at various points. Opening and closing lines are exactly where an
author would be asked to sign off.

**Why it is the portal's foundation.** Melvin-Koushki relies on its colophons wherever
possible to date the oeuvre, and nearly every date on this chronology descends from it. The
