chain runs: colophon → his analysis → the chronology in the addenda → these pages.

**The limits, which are real.** In many instances it is **impossible to tell whether a date
records composition or transcription**. And **fully half the manuscript, representing almost
two-thirds of the preserved works, was copied between 827–29/1425–27** — the window
bracketing the exile. That clustering may record a burst of writing; it may equally record a
**copying campaign undertaken because the author's position was collapsing and the works
needed securing**. The evidence does not decide, and the second reading is at least as
plausible as the first.

**What we do not know.** Who the copyist was; who paid for the collection; what was omitted
and why; and whether other autograph fragments survive in it beyond the two named folios.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), chronology, 33–36

timeline_events.title: A Saturn–Jupiter conjunction in Scorpio
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka holds that his own generation's evolution was heralded by a portentous celestial conjunction — **likely Saturn–Jupiter in Scorpio in 767/1365**. His generation, poised on the edge of history and encompassing all that went before, is therefore the best generation, and the late 8th/14th century the **beginning of a golden age in which the prophetic legacy transmitted by the Imams and the ancients would be actualized**. Melvin-Koushki flags his own uncertainty about which conjunction is meant.
timeline_events.body:
**What the claim is.** Ibn Turka holds that the evolution of his own generation was heralded
by a portentous celestial conjunction. Melvin-Koushki identifies it as *likely* the
Saturn–Jupiter conjunction in Scorpio of 767/1365, while stating in a footnote that he is
**not entirely sure which conjunction Ibn Turka has in mind** (*The Quest*, 21 n.8). The
uncertainty is preserved here because it is the scholar's own.

**Why a conjunction.** Saturn–Jupiter conjunctions are the backbone of Islamicate
historical astrology. They recur roughly every twenty years, shift triplicity every couple
of centuries, and complete a full cycle in something under a millennium; the tradition
reads the greater ones as marking dynastic and religious turning points. To claim one as
the herald of your own generation is to place that generation in a cycle of world-history,
not merely to note an omen.

**The claim it licenses.** From the portent Ibn Turka draws a strong conclusion: his
generation, **poised on the edge of history and encompassing all that went before, is
therefore the best generation**, and the late 8th/14th century is **the beginning of a
golden age in which the prophetic legacy transmitted by the Imams and the ancients would be
actualized** (*The Quest*, 21).

**Why this is not Ḥurūfism.** The structure is millenarian, and Melvin-Koushki grants
without hesitation that Ibn Turka is a profoundly millenarian thinker by any standard. What
keeps it inside orthodoxy is the object: a golden age of **knowledge**, in which what the
Imams and ancients already transmitted becomes fully actual — not a new revelation. The
insistence on the binding finality of the dispensation given through Muḥammad is what
separates this from the [[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] claim (*The Quest*, 456).

**Consequences.** Almost everything programmatic in the career follows from this dating.
If the golden age has begun, then the occult knowledge of the ancients is due to be made
manifest, and a man who systematises it is not an antiquarian but a participant in a
scheduled event. The urgency of the project, and its confidence, are both downstream of a
conjunction.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 21 and n.8

timeline_events.title: The reign of Tīmūr
timeline_events.card: Tīmūr rules the empire into which Ibn Turka is born and which will employ, elevate and eventually prosecute him. It is Tīmūr who appoints his brother Ṣadr al-Dīn *qāḍī* in Samarkand, establishing the judgeship as a Turka family office.
timeline_events.body:
**The frame.** Tīmūr ruled 771–807/1370–1405 (*Powers of One*, 34), and the empire he built
— the Timurid, 771–912/1370–1507 — is the whole political container of Ibn Turka's life.

**The specific debt.** Tīmūr appointed [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] *qāḍī* in Samarkand
and thereby **established the judgeship as a Turka family office** (*The Quest*, §3.1). The
post Ibn Turka held in Isfahan and lost in the tribunals descends from a personal act of the
founder.

**The instability it bequeathed.** Tīmūr's death at Utrar in 807/1405 opened a succession
struggle that structured everything after: [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] against
[[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar]], the Timurid princes of western Iran competing for prestige and
scholars. That competition is why a returning occult philosopher found a receptive market in
810/1408, and why his patron was destroyed six years later.

**What we do not know.** Whether the Turka family had standing before Tīmūr's appointment, or
whether it made them.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The reign of Sultan Barqūq at Cairo
timeline_events.card: Al-Malik al-Ẓāhir Barqūq rules the Mamluk sultanate. **Akhlāṭī serves as his personal physician-alchemist**, and under that influence Barqūq develops a keen interest in the occult sciences — evidenced by his personal library and his choice of courtiers, Ibn Turka among them. Melvin-Koushki asks whether he was the first Mamluk sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and answers: likely so.
timeline_events.body:
**The reign.** Al-Malik al-Ẓāhir Barqūq ruled the Mamluk sultanate 784–801/1382–1399
(*Powers of One*, 6) — the sultan under whom Ibn Turka spent his first Cairo years.

**The physician at the centre.** [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] was summoned to Cairo as
Barqūq's **personal physician-alchemist**. A court physician has repeated private access to
the ruler's body, and that access is the mechanism behind what follows: under his influence
Barqūq **seems to have developed a keen interest in the occult sciences**
(*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 70).

**The evidence, which is good.** Not testimony about the sultan's opinions but two things a
historian can check: **his personal library and his choice of courtiers** — among whom was
**Ibn Turka himself**. Ibn Turka was not merely a student in Cairo; he was a courtier of
Barqūq's, at the beginning of his career and in his twenties.

**The question, and its answer.** Melvin-Koushki asks whether Barqūq was **the first Mamluk
sultan to aspire to occult-philosopher-kingship, and so an inspiration for Timurid rivals**,
and answers: **likely so**. If that holds, the model of the occult court that
[[isfahan-circle|Isfahan]] would develop has a Cairene prototype, and Ibn Turka saw it
working before he ever served a Timurid.

**What we do not know.** What was in the library; whether Barqūq's interest survived his
physician's death in 799/1397; and how far the aspiration was realised in policy.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 6

timeline_events.title: Ibn Khaldūn settles in Cairo
timeline_events.card: Ibn Khaldūn lives in Cairo from 785/1383 until his death in 808/1406 — overlapping the years Ibn Turka and Yazdī spent there. Melvin-Koushki notes that **the two historians possibly met**: Yazdī spent at least part of 795–810/1393–1408 in the city with Ibn Turka. The most formidable critic of the occult sciences and their most consequential defender may have been in the same rooms.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ibn Khaldūn lived in Cairo from **785/1383 until his death in 808/1406**
— overlapping almost the whole of Ibn Turka's fifteen-year residence, and Yazdī's.

**The possible meeting.** Melvin-Koushki notes that **the two historians possibly met**:
Yazdī spent at least part of 795–810/1393–1408 in the city with Ibn Turka
(*Powers of One*, 37). The claim is carefully limited — *possibly* — and the portal keeps it
that way.

**Why it would matter.** Ibn Khaldūn belongs to the [[neoplatonism|anti-occultist
coalition]] whose four centuries of polemic the whole mathematicalization project was built
to answer, alongside Ibn Sīnā, [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]] and Ibn Taymiyya (*Powers of One*, 1).
And [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī]] would go on to write in defence of divination against
precisely that critique — the subject of the portal's intersection essay on geomancy.

If the defence was written by a man who had argued with Ibn Khaldūn in person, it reads
differently: not a scholar answering a book but a scholar answering someone he had met.

**The complication.** Melvin-Koushki also notes that Ibn Khaldūn attempted, at his Damascus
interviews with Tīmūr in 803/1401, **to palm himself off as a seasoned occultist**. The
period's most rigorous critic of the occult sciences was willing to claim competence in them
in front of a conqueror.

**What we do not know.** Whether any meeting occurred. No source in hand records one; the
inference rests on overlapping residence in a shared scholarly world.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 37

timeline_events.title: Ibn Khaldūn's Damascus interviews with Tīmūr
timeline_events.card: At the famous Damascus interviews, Ibn Khaldūn — the age's leading anti-occultist — attempts, in Melvin-Koushki's reading, **to palm himself off as a seasoned occultist**. The hypocrisy is instructive about how much occult competence was worth in front of a conqueror.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** At the famous Damascus interviews of **803/1401**, Ibn Khaldūn attempted
— in Melvin-Koushki's reading — **to palm himself off as a seasoned occultist**, and did so
with some hypocrisy, given his own disallowing of occultism elsewhere
(*In Defense of Geomancy*, 36).

**Why it is worth a chronology entry.** Because it establishes the market value of occult
competence at the top of the political world. Ibn Khaldūn is the most formidable critic the
occult sciences had — a member of the [[neoplatonism|anti-occultist coalition]] with Ibn
Sīnā, [[al-ghazali|Ghazālī]] and Ibn Taymiyya. In front of a conqueror he claimed to be one
of the practitioners he elsewhere dismissed.

**What it implies about the tribunals.** If occult competence was worth claiming falsely
before Tīmūr in 1401, then the accusations levelled at Ibn Turka two decades later were not
straightforward expressions of a settled hostility. The same courts that prosecuted
occultists also employed them, and the difference between the two treatments has more to do
with faction than with doctrine.

**The connection to Yazdī.** [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī]] would write in defence of
divination against precisely Ibn Khaldūn's critique — the subject of the portal's
intersection essay on geomancy. Melvin-Koushki also notes the two historians **possibly met**
in Cairo. The defence may have been aimed at a man its author had encountered.

**What we do not know.** What Ibn Khaldūn actually said at Damascus about the occult
sciences; the accounts in hand are Melvin-Koushki's characterisation rather than a quoted
transcript.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *In Defense of Geomancy*, 36

timeline_events.title: Akhlāṭī as heir of al-Būnī and Ibn ʿArabī
timeline_events.card: Melvin-Koushki characterises Akhlāṭī as the **conscious heir of both al-Būnī and Ibn ʿArabī**, and master to the most important occult philosophers of the following generation. The two streams the portal treats separately — operative talismanic lettrism and Akbarian metaphysics — are joined in one teacher before Ibn Turka inherits them.
timeline_events.body:
**The characterisation.** Melvin-Koushki calls [[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Akhlāṭī]] the
**conscious heir of both al-Būnī and [[ibn-arabi|Ibn ʿArabī]]**, and master to the most
important occult philosophers of the following generation (*Powers of One*, 6).

**Why "both" is the point.** These are two different inheritances that do not obviously
combine. From **al-Būnī** comes the operative talismanic literature — the *Shams al-Maʿārif*
tradition, magic squares, divine names deployed for effect, procedures with materials and
timings. From **Ibn ʿArabī** comes a metaphysics: the [[divine-names|divine names]] as the
structure of manifestation, the [[imaginal-realm|imaginal realm]], an orientation that is
contemplative rather than operative.

One is a manual; the other is an ontology. Holding both **consciously** — as a single
teaching rather than as two competencies — is the achievement, and it is what Ibn Turka
inherited as a going concern.

**What it let his student skip.** Because the manual and the metaphysics arrived already
joined, Ibn Turka did not have to spend his career reconciling them. He could take the
combination as given and spend the effort on something neither predecessor had attempted:
arguing the result into the [[pythagorean-cosmology|mathematical sciences]].

**The periodisation this sits in.** *Imperial Talismanic Love* gives the three stages:
thirteenth-century Ibn ʿArabian-Būnian **science of the saints**; fourteenth-century
de-esotericization and adabization through the Mamluk mainstream; and neopythagoreanization
at the turn of the fifteenth by the occultists who would form the
[[new-brethren-purity|Brethren]]. Akhlāṭī stands at the hinge between the second and third.

**What we do not know.** Whether Akhlāṭī himself argued for the combination in writing, or
simply taught it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 6

timeline_events.title: Iskandar Sulṭān rules Fars
timeline_events.card: Iskandar Sulṭān — grandson of Tīmūr, ruler of Fars and contender with his uncle Shāhrukh for control of Iran — is described by Melvin-Koushki as **Ibn Turka's first and most important patron**.
timeline_events.body:
**The reign.** [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] ruled Fars 812–817/1409–1414, grandson of
Tīmūr and contender with his uncle [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] for control of Iran. Melvin-Koushki
calls him **Ibn Turka's first and most important patron** (*Powers of One*, 34).

**What kind of court it was.** Accounted **the leading Timurid patron of culture in the early
Shahrukhid period**, with a particular interest in **alchemy and astrological and
astronomical illustrated works**, and known for his **imamophilism and esotericist bent**
(*The Quest*, §3.1 n.1). Brilliant and short-lived, in the chronology's phrase.

**Why "most important" is right.** Iskandar installed Ibn Turka in his hereditary judgeship,
possibly commissioned the [[risalat-huruf|*R. Ḥurūf*]], and was almost certainly behind the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]]. The two central lettrist works of the century have one patron
behind them — a patron who was blinded before the second was finished.

**The larger claim.** Melvin-Koushki argues that **the model established by Iskandar Sulṭān
and [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg]]** is what ensured astronomy-astrology and lettrism would continue
to be heavily patronised by later Timurid, Indo-Timurid, Safavid and Ottoman courts
(*Philosopher-Kings*, 599). Ibn Turka's first patron and his would-be last are the two poles
of a model that outlived them both.

**What we do not know.** Whether Iskandar read the works he commissioned.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The eschatological-absolutism experiment
timeline_events.card: Melvin-Koushki devotes a study to Mīrzā Iskandar, Shāh Niʿmatullāh Valī and Sayyid Sharīf Jurjānī in 815/1412 as an experiment with eschatological absolutism, and draws a sharp conclusion: **if the rise of absolutist politics is a benchmark for early modernity, then in 816/1412 Shāhrukh was the last medieval Islamic ruler and Mīrzā Iskandar the first early modern absolutist sovereign.** Ibn Turka is attached to the court where this happens.
timeline_events.body:
**What the study argues.** Melvin-Koushki devotes an article to **Mīrzā Iskandar, Shāh
Niʿmatullāh Valī and Sayyid Sharīf Jurjānī in 815/1412** as an experiment with
eschatological absolutism, and draws from it a conclusion about periodisation that is
unusually blunt: **if the rise of absolutist politics is one of the benchmarks for early
modernity, in 816/1412 Shāhrukh was the last medieval Islamic ruler, and Mīrzā Iskandar was
the first early modern absolutist sovereign** (*Imperial Talismanic Love*, 16, 21).

**The two answers to one problem.** Both rulers faced the same question — on what basis does
a Timurid govern, now that Tīmūr is dead? Their answers were incompatible.
[[shahrukh|Shāhrukh's]] was **conservative and juridical**: abrogate the
[[yasa-abrogated|Mongol *yasa*]], enforce the sharīʿa, rule as a Muslim sovereign answerable
to the religious classes. [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar's]] was **eschatological and
absolutist**: claim a sacred role in the unfolding of history, with occultists,
astrologers and philosophers on the staff to articulate it.

**Where Ibn Turka stood.** On the losing side, and not by accident. A science that reads
cosmic cycles, dates golden ages from [[saturn-jupiter-conjunction|conjunctions]] and
supplies rulers with a place in sacred time is precisely staff work for the second
programme. It has no comparable role in the first.

**Why this reframes the tribunals.** They stop looking like a clash between religion and
magic and start looking like the aftermath of a political defeat. The man prosecuted in the
1420s had been the intellectual furniture of a rival claim to sovereignty, and the
prosecution was conducted by the winners' court.

**What we do not know.** What Ibn Turka's personal involvement in the 815/1412 experiment
was, if any; the sources in hand place him at the court rather than in the episode.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Imperial Talismanic Love*, 16, 21

timeline_events.title: The reign of Shāhrukh
timeline_events.card: Shāhrukh rules for thirty-eight years, spanning almost the whole of Ibn Turka's Persian career — the patron who received him back into favour in 825/1422 and the court that exiled him in 1427.
timeline_events.body:
**The reign.** [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] ruled 811–850/1409–1447 (*Powers of One*, 34) — thirty-
eight years, spanning almost the whole of Ibn Turka's Iranian career and outlasting him by
fifteen.

**Three turns and a silence.** He destroyed [[iskandar-falls|Iskandar]] in 817/1414;
[[first-inquisition|vindicated Ibn Turka and gave him the judgeship of Yazd]] around
825/1422; [[exiled-from-herat|exiled him]] in 1427; and thereafter would not see him — a
refused hearing at Simnan in 833/1429, a
[[promise-of-reinstatement|promise at Ṣāʾin Qalʿa]] around 834/1430, and
[[nine-months-waiting|nine months of unanswered weekly attendance]] at Herat.

**Not a hostile reign, exactly.** He completed a madrasa-khānaqāh complex at Herat in
813/1410 and appointed its teachers. His sons ran the century's two greatest cultural
enterprises: [[baysunghur|Bāysunghur's]] *kitābkhāna* and
[[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg's]] [[samarkand-observatory|observatory]]. This is not a court
indifferent to learning. It is a court hostile to a particular claim about where authority
over knowledge lies.

**The mechanism.** By refounding legitimacy on the sharīʿa he elevated the class of men who
interpret it — and gave professional rivals a vocabulary in which envy could be prosecuted
as heresy. The tribunals are the predictable output of that arrangement rather than an
expression of the ruler's own animus, and the 825/1422 vindication suggests Shāhrukh
himself was persuadable.

**What we do not know.** Whether he personally decided any of the three turns, or ratified
factional outcomes.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Powers of One*, 34

timeline_events.title: The judgeship of Isfahan becomes a Turka family office
timeline_events.card: Tīmūr appoints Ibn Turka's elder brother **Ṣadr al-Dīn** as *qāḍī* in Samarkand, establishing the office to the Turka family. The judgeship of Isfahan that Iskandar later installs Ibn Turka in — and that the tribunals take from him — is a **hereditary** family possession dating to the founding of the dynasty.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Tīmūr appointed Ibn Turka's elder brother [[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr
al-Dīn]] as *qāḍī* in Samarkand, and in doing so **established the office to the Turka
family**. When [[iskandar-sultan|Iskandar Sulṭān]] later installed Ibn Turka as *qāḍī* of
Isfahan, he was presumably filling a post the family already held by right
(*The Quest*, §3.1).

**Why this reframes the career.** It changes what the tribunals were taking. Read without
this fact, Ibn Turka is a scholar who obtained a good appointment and later lost it through
controversy. Read with it, he is the holder of **a hereditary family office granted at the
founding of the dynasty**, and the accusations of the 1420s are an attempt to strip a
lineage of a possession, not merely to remove an individual from a job.

**The precise office.** Melvin-Koushki describes him as **Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and
Yazd** (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 13) — a senior magistracy, in a named legal school,
across two cities. This is a full working career in its own right. Everything in the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] was written around it.

**What it explains about the opposition.** Rival colleagues engineered the inquisitions,
and a hereditary judgeship is exactly the kind of thing colleagues covet. The chronology
notes that he had already moved back to Shiraz once, in 815–17/1412–14, **due to harassment
by envious individuals**, putting forward his protégé Sharaf al-Dīn Yaʿqūb to replace him as
*qāḍī*. The pattern of professional envy is attested a decade before the tribunals.

**What we do not know.** Whether the Isfahan judgeship was formally the same grant as the
Samarkand one, or a family claim honoured by a later prince, is not spelled out in the
sources in hand.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), §3.1

timeline_events.title: Ten children; two sons known by name
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka states that he had **ten children — three sons and seven daughters**. Only two sons are known by name: **Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad**, for whom he wrote his manual of logic the *K. al-Manāhij*, and **Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb Allāh**, who appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise of his own, the *Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ*. The science stayed in the family for at least one generation.
timeline_events.body:
**What the sources say.** Ibn Turka **states that he had ten children** — three sons and
seven daughters (*The Quest*, 41).

**The two named sons.** Only two are known by name, and both are known through texts.
**Jamāl al-Dīn Muḥammad**, for whom he wrote his manual of logic the *Kitāb al-Manāhij*
while [[natanz-winter|wintering at Natanz]] in exile in 833/1430; and **Najīb al-Dīn Ḥabīb
Allāh**, who **appears to have written a brief lettrist treatise** of his own, the
*Qavāʿid-i Jafr-i Jāmiʿ*.

**Why the second matters.** Because it means the science stayed in the family for at least
one further generation. *Jafr* is the divinatory-lettrist discipline; a son writing on it,
after his father had been tried three times and exiled once, is a small piece of evidence
about how the household understood what had happened to it. Nothing further is known about
Najīb al-Dīn.

**The eight who are not named.** Seven daughters and a third son leave no trace in these
sources. This is normal for the period and worth stating anyway, because a chronology that
records only the named risks implying the rest did not exist.

**What the family cost him, and vice versa.** [[sharaf-al-din-yazdi|Yazdī's]] letters show
concern for Ibn Turka's children (*makhdūm-zādagān*) **after their father's death** — the
detail that establishes the character of that friendship. And the exile years include sending
for the family to Natanz: the case that consumed his last five years was being pursued by a
man with a household to move.

**What we do not know.** The names of eight children; whether Jamāl al-Dīn continued the work
— the dissertation says he **may have been a key player** in something the passage in hand
does not complete; and anything of his wife or wives.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 41

timeline_events.title: Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and Yazd
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka's office is described precisely by Melvin-Koushki as **Shāfiʿī chief judge of Isfahan and Yazd** — a working senior magistracy in two cities, in a named legal school. The occult philosophy was written by a man with a full-time judicial day job.
timeline_events.body:
**What the office was.** Melvin-Koushki's description is exact: **Shāfiʿī chief judge of
Isfahan and Yazd** (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 13). Three things are specified — the legal
school, the rank, and the fact that it covered two cities.

**Why the precision matters.** *Shāfiʿī* places him in a named madhhab and settles that his
legal training was mainstream; he studied under Sirāj al-Dīn al-Bulqīnī, a Shāfiʿī authority
of the first rank, in Cairo. *Chief judge* is a senior appointment with jurisdiction and
staff, not an honorific. *Isfahan and Yazd* means the workload was doubled, and that Yazd was
added by [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] in 825/1422 as the reward for surviving the first inquisition.

**The bearing on how the work was written.** Everything in the
[[kitab-al-mafahis|*Mafāḥiṣ*]] was produced around a full-time senior magistracy. This is not
the leisure of a court philosopher; it is the second job of a working judge who heard cases,
supervised subordinates and administered a jurisdiction. The career sim's obligation
mechanic — an office that taxes every turn — is the accurate model.

**The vulnerability it created.** A hereditary chief judgeship in two prosperous cities is
exactly the sort of prize that generates the **envious individuals** the chronology blames
for driving him out of Isfahan in 815–17/1412–14. The office that made the intellectual work
possible is also what made him worth attacking.

**What we do not know.** The dates of appointment to each city (Yazd is fixed at c. 825/1422;
Isfahan is not precisely dated); whether he held both simultaneously; and when he lost them.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 13

timeline_events.title: Makes mortal enemies at the Cairo court
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka launches his writing career during the fifteen-year Cairo tenure, where he trains in law, Arabic letters and occult science — **and makes mortal enemies at court**. The opposition that culminates in the tribunals of the 1420s begins in Egypt, decades before it bears fruit.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** During the fifteen-year Cairo tenure Ibn Turka **made mortal enemies at
court** (*Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 5).

**Why it belongs on a chronology.** Because it relocates the origin of the tribunals. The
inquisitions of the 1420s are easy to read as a late-career collision between an occultist
and a pious Timurid establishment — a story about Iran, [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] and the
[[hurufism|Ḥurūfī]] scare. This entry says the enmity is older than that and began somewhere
else, in a different sultanate, before he had written the works he would be tried for.

**The pattern it establishes.** The chronology records the same dynamic again in Iran:
between 815 and 817/1412–14 he moved back to Shiraz **due to harassment by envious
individuals**, putting his protégé forward to replace him as *qāḍī*. Twice, in two countries,
the record uses the language of personal rivalry rather than doctrinal objection.

**What this suggests about the charges.** That the accusations were instruments rather than
motives. Colleagues who wanted a hereditary judgeship reached for the vocabulary the court
would respond to — Sufi bias in 1422, a Ḥurūfī connection in 1427 — because those were the
charges available, not because they described what was actually at stake.

**What we do not know.** Who they were. Only one opponent is named anywhere in the
chronology: **Muḥammad al-Jazarī**, who died at Herat in 833/1429 and is described as
powerful — and he belongs to the Iranian phase, not the Egyptian one.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Ibn Turka's Pythagorean Sensorium*, 5

timeline_events.title: Qāḍīzāda Rūmī dies
timeline_events.card: The second director of Ulugh Beg's observatory dies **in the same year as Ibn Turka**. The two had studied together under Ibn Turka's brother for twenty-five years and had divided the work between the stars and the letters; they leave it in the same season.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** [[qazizada-rumi|Qāḍīzāda Rūmī]] — noted astronomer and mathematician, and
the **second director** of [[ulugh-beg|Ulugh Beg's]]
[[samarkand-observatory|observatory at Samarkand]] — died in **835/1432**, the same year as
Ibn Turka (*The Quest*, 41 n.17, citing Ragep, 'Ḳāḍī-zāda Rūmī', EI2).

**The symmetry.** They had studied together under Ibn Turka's elder brother
[[sadr-al-din-turka|Ṣadr al-Dīn]] for the first twenty-five years of their lives — an
education that stopped deliberately at the outward sciences because their teacher deemed it
too dangerous to delve into esoteric matters in public.

Both pupils then spent their careers on disciplines by which the hidden order of things
might be made **calculable**: one took the stars, the other the letters. Melvin-Koushki's
argument is that these were not two projects but one, studied separately only by accident of
modern disciplinary boundaries.

They died in the same year, one in an observatory that would be dismantled within two
decades, the other in an antechamber at Herat waiting on a case review.

**What we do not know.** Whether they were in contact in later life; whether Qāḍīzāda knew of
the tribunals; and whether anything passed between the observatory and Ibn Turka's circle
beyond the shared schooling.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 41

timeline_events.title: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī dies
timeline_events.card: The Ottoman arm of the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network outlives its Iranian counterpart by twenty-two years. Bisṭāmī and Ibn Turka were both heirs of Akhlāṭī pursuing the same universalist lettrist project; Melvin-Koushki judges the Ottoman version **more successful**.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** ʿAbd al-Raḥmān [[bistami|Bisṭāmī]] died in **858/1454**, twenty-two years
after Ibn Turka.

**The comparison the portal cannot avoid.** They were **both the intellectual heirs of
[[sayyid-husayn-akhlati|Sayyid Ḥusayn Akhlāṭī]]**, and it is unclear whether they ever met
during their respective long residences in Mamluk Cairo (*The Quest*, 2). The same teaching
went east with one and west with the other.

Melvin-Koushki's judgement on the outcome is the uncomfortable one: the Ottoman projects are
**cognate — and more successful**. The Iranian version produced three tribunals, an exile,
and an oeuvre half of which is still unedited. The Ottoman version produced a durable
tradition at a court that wanted it.

**What the asymmetry is about.** Not ideas. The inheritance was the same and the doctrines
were close. What differed was politics: [[shahrukh|Shāhrukh]] refounded Timurid legitimacy on
the sharīʿa and elevated the class of men who interpret it, while the Ottoman court of the
same decades made room for exactly this kind of universalist project. The comparison is the
sharpest available argument that Ibn Turka's fate was contingent rather than deserved.

**Why the portal is only half the story.** Because the Ottoman half is being written
elsewhere — by **Cornell Fleischer** and his Chicago Circle — and the two branches are
described as **largely coterminous**, so research on either bears on the whole.

**What we do not know.** Whether they met. Nothing in the sources in hand settles it.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), 2

timeline_events.title: The Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network is identified by modern scholarship
timeline_events.card: İhsan Fazlıoğlu posits the existence of the fifteenth-century Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network in a 1996 article; Cornell Fleischer and his Chicago Circle develop the Ottoman side. Melvin-Koushki's account of the Isfahan Circle is explicitly dependent on that work — the two branches are **largely coterminous**, and neither can be read alone.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** **İhsan Fazlıoğlu** posited the existence of the fifteenth-century
Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ network in a **1996 article** on the Brethren and
[[bistami|ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Bisṭāmī]] in early Ottoman intellectual and cultural life
(*The Quest*, ch. 1 n.88).

**Why a 1996 event belongs on a fifteenth-century chronology.** Because the network is a
**modern reconstruction**, not a category the sources hand over. The men involved called
themselves the Ikhwān al-Ṣafāʾ **cryptically**; no roll, rule or manifesto survives. That
there was a coherent transregional network at all is a scholarly finding with a date and an
author, and a portal that presents it as simple fact would be concealing its own
foundations.

**Who is building it.** Melvin-Koushki states that his understanding of late medieval Islamic
occult philosophy is **dependent on the ongoing research of Cornell Fleischer** and his
Chicago Circle into the cognate Ottoman projects; Fleischer's *A Mediterranean Apocalypse* is
expected to provide definitive corroboration of the network's transregional and transcultural
character (*The Quest*, ch. 1 nn. 87–88).

**What follows for the reader.** The two branches are **largely coterminous both
logistically and conceptually**, so research on either has vital bearing on the whole
complex. This portal treats the Iranian arm in detail and the Ottoman arm at second hand,
which means it gives a partial account **by construction** — and the partiality is a
property of the sources chosen, not an oversight.

**What we do not know.** Whether the reconstruction will hold in its present form.
Fleischer's corroborating work is described as forthcoming.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *The Quest for a Universal Science* (Yale diss., 2012), ch. 1 nn. 87–88

timeline_events.title: The Book of Inquiries revised and expanded
timeline_events.card: Ibn Turka returns to the summa five years after finishing it and expands it — in the same period, 827–29/1425–27, in which two-thirds of the surviving oeuvre was being copied into MS Majlis 10196. The revision belongs to the years immediately before the exile.
timeline_events.body:
**What happened.** Ibn Turka revised and expanded the [[kitab-al-mafahis|*Kitāb al-Mafāḥiṣ*]]
in **828/1425**, five years after completing it (*Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66).

**Where it falls.** Inside the window 827–29/1425–27, in which half of
[[ms-majlis-10196|MS Majlis 10196]] — two-thirds of the surviving oeuvre — was being copied,
and immediately before the [[exiled-from-herat|exile of 1427]]. The chronology also assigns
to 828/1425 the writing or copying of four further treatises: *R. al-Inzāliyya*, *R. Anjām*,
*R. Bāʾiyya* and *R. Nuqṭa*.

**What that concentration might mean.** Two readings, and the sources choose neither. Either
these were extraordinarily productive years, or this is what it looks like when a man under
mounting accusation puts his corpus in order — revising the summa, gathering the shorter
treatises, and having the whole copied while he still can. The second reading fits the
political chronology better; the first is what a bare list of dates suggests.

**The pattern of revision.** He returned to his own work more than once: the
[[sharh-fusus|*Sharḥ Fuṣūṣ al-Ḥikam*]] was corrected in 817/1415, four years after
completion; the *Mafāḥiṣ* expanded in 828/1425, five years after. A colophon date in this
oeuvre may record a second pass rather than a first composition.

**What we do not know.** What the revision changed. That it was expanded is recorded; the
content of the expansion is not described in the sources in hand.
literature: Melvin-Koushki, *Of Islamic Grammatology*, 66
